findings.title: Trot bounce is inverted: the trunk is highest at mid-stance and lowest in the suspension
findings.observed: BODY.trot sets spine y = rest - 0.03 + 0.022*cyc(g,2,0.32). That puts the maximum at g = 0.16 / 0.66 and the minimum at g = 0.41 / 0.91. Measured withers y: 1.619 m at g = 0.156 and 1.617 at 0.19 (mid-stance of the LF+RH diagonal, which is planted 0-0.4), then 1.571 at g = 0.41 and 1.572 at 0.44 (lift-off and suspension). Croup and poll follow the same curve: croup max 1.586 at 0.156, min 1.564 at 0.41; poll max 1.867 at 0.17, min 1.797 at 0.42. So the horse rises while both legs of a diagonal are loaded and drops while it is airborne. Shoulder-to-toe length keeps shortening until g = 0.31, after mid-stance. In sheet 02-trot, tiles g = 1/8 and 2/8 (mid-stance) show the body higher than g = 3/8 (end of stance). The code comment says 'lowest as each diagonal pair takes the weight', and the code does not do that either.
findings.expected: The trot is a bouncing, spring-mass gait. The centre of mass, the withers and the tuber sacrale reach their lowest point at mid-stance of each diagonal, when the limbs are most compressed and ground reaction force peaks. They reach their highest point in mid-suspension, with two sinusoidal cycles per stride. This head-down/pelvis-down-at-mid-stance pattern is what every objective lameness system measures (HDmin/PDmin). A half-sine ground reaction force with the model's own timing (T 0.72 s, duty 0.4) gives a ~66 mm excursion with its minimum at g ≈ 0.20 / 0.70 and its maximum at g ≈ 0.45 / 0.95. The model is about 180° out of phase with that.
findings.evidence: index.html:1572 (BODY.trot spine.position), index.html:1573-1579 (pitch, neck and head use the same phase constants 0.3-0.42), index.html:221-226 (GAITS.trot land/duty); measurements.json gaits.trot samples k=5 (g .156) vs k=13 (g .406); sheet 02-trot tiles g=1/8, 2/8, 3/8

fixOptions.label: Re-phase the sinusoid
fixOptions.approach: Put the minimum at diagonal mid-stance: y = rest - c - A*cyc(g, 2, 0.4), i.e. lowest at g = 0.2 and 0.7, highest at 0.45 and 0.95. Shift the neck/head/pitch phase constants by the same amount so the head still moves with the withers.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The legs are shortest at mid-stance, which the two-bone IK and fetlock sag already allow. Check that no leg hits full extension at touchdown.

fixOptions.label: Derive height from the stance legs
fixOptions.approach: Compute the body offset each frame from the summed 'load' (sin² of stance progress) of the planted legs, plus a ballistic arc in suspension. The bounce then follows GAITS land/duty automatically, for every running style (tuneGait changes T and duty).
fixOptions.risk: Medium. The shared code path also drives canter, gallop and race, so their hand-tuned BODY curves would need the same treatment or an opt-out.

fixOptions.label: Per-gait spring-mass table
fixOptions.approach: Precompute vertical displacement per gait from T and duty (half-sine GRF integration, as in the review's check) and sample it in BODY.*.
fixOptions.risk: Low to medium. It needs a small integrator at build time. Stays exact when the stride or duty is customised.

references: Cavagna GA, Heglund NC, Taylor CR (1977) Mechanical work in terrestrial locomotion: two basic mechanisms for minimizing energy expenditure. Am J Physiol 233:R243-R261
Farley CT, Glasheen J, McMahon TA (1993) Running springs: speed and animal size. J Exp Biol 185:71-86

Buchner HHF, Savelberg HHCM, Schamhardt HC, Barneveld A (1996) Head and trunk movement adaptations in horses with experimentally induced fore- or hindlimb lameness. Equine Vet J 28:71-76 (PMID 8565958)
Keegan KG (2007) Evidence-based lameness detection and quantification. Vet Clin North Am Equine Pract 23:403-423

findings.title: Trot vertical excursion is too small, and the croup moves less than half as much as the withers
findings.observed: Peak-to-peak vertical travel at the trot: withers 48 mm, croup 22 mm, poll 70 mm. The mean of withers and croup (a centre-of-mass proxy) moves about 36 mm. The croup stays small because spine.rotation.z (0.6°) and hips.rotation.z (1.5°) pitch the hindquarters against the translation.
findings.expected: The model's own timing (duty 0.4, 72 ms suspension) implies about 6-7 cm of centre-of-mass excursion. Treadmill studies at 3.5-4 m/s find the head, withers and tuber sacrale oscillating with similar sinusoidal patterns and amplitudes of roughly 6-10 cm (Buchner 1996). Trunk pitch at a sound trot is small, so the sacrum should travel about as far as the withers, not half as far.
findings.evidence: index.html:1572-1575 (amplitude 0.022 m, pitch terms); measurements.json gaits.trot withers y range 1.571-1.619, croup 1.564-1.586

fixOptions.label: Raise the amplitude and drop the counter-pitch
fixOptions.approach: Raise the translation amplitude to about 0.03-0.035 m (60-70 mm peak-to-peak). Cut spine.rotation.z and hips.rotation.z in the trot to ~0.3°, or put them in phase, so withers and croup travel the same distance.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The legs compress more at mid-stance, so check the pastern and fetlock for clipping.

fixOptions.label: Tie the amplitude to duty and stride time
fixOptions.approach: Use the spring-mass integration from the previous finding, so a customised running style (stride/duty from tuneGait) changes the bounce consistently.
fixOptions.risk: Low to medium.

references: Buchner et al. 1996 Equine Vet J 28:71-76
Faber M et al. (2001) Basic three-dimensional kinematics of the vertebral column of horses trotting on a treadmill. Am J Vet Res 62:757-764 (PMID 11341399): flexion-extension only 2.8-4.9°

findings.title: Walk: the hindquarters do not vault over the hind legs, so the croup is nearly flat
findings.observed: At the walk the withers rise and fall 34 mm, twice per stride, peaking at fore mid-stance (g ≈ 0.06 / 0.56), which is correct. The croup moves only 6 mm (1.587-1.593 m) and the hip joints 11 mm. The spine pitch (0.8° about x = 0) and the hips pitch (1.2°) cancel most of the translation at the back end. The whole bob reads as a forehand nod.
findings.expected: A walking quadruped behaves like two inverted pendulums: the forequarters vault over each fore stance and the hindquarters over each hind stance. Each end rises and falls twice per stride. For a lateral-sequence walk the hind peaks fall at hind mid-stance (g ≈ 0.3 / 0.8), about a quarter stride after the fore peaks, so withers and croup move roughly in anti-phase and the trunk rocks fore and aft. At walk the tuber sacrale shows a vertical pattern comparable to the withers (Buchner 1996, 1.6 m/s). Back flexion-extension at walk runs about 7° per two-cycle stride (Faber 2000); the model's back angle changes 1.3° and its pitch 1.9°.
findings.evidence: index.html:1622-1626 (BODY.walk spine.position / rotation.z / hips.rotation.z); measurements.json gaits.walk croup y range 0.006 vs withers 0.034; sheet 01-walk g=0..7/8 (level croup line)

fixOptions.label: Add a hind vault term
fixOptions.approach: Give the hindquarters their own vertical term peaking at hind mid-stance, e.g. hips.position.y += 0.012*cyc(g, 2, 0.6). Or pitch the spine about the trunk middle with amplitude chosen so the croup moves ±10-15 mm in anti-phase with the withers.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The hind legs must reach slightly further at the trough, and the walk already has ≥2.5% reach margin.

fixOptions.label: Derive fore and hind heights from their own stance legs
fixOptions.approach: Compute the forehand and hindquarter heights separately from the stance progress of the fore pair and the hind pair (inverted-pendulum arc), then set chest and hips offsets from them.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. Interacts with the skin-weight blend between the spine, chest and hips bones.

references: Griffin TM, Main RP, Farley CT (2004) Biomechanics of quadrupedal walking: how do four-legged animals achieve inverted pendulum-like movements? J Exp Biol 207:3545-3558 (PMID 15339951)
Faber M et al. (2000) Basic three-dimensional kinematics of the vertebral column of horses walking on a treadmill. Am J Vet Res 61:399-406 (PMID 10772104)
Buchner et al. 1996 Equine Vet J 28:71-76

findings.title: Walk side-to-side sway is on the wrong side: the trunk sways away from the legs bearing the weight
findings.observed: spine.position.z = 0.012*sin(TAU*(g-0.1)) and roll = 1°*sin(TAU*(g-0.15)). Withers and croup z reach +0.019 m (toward the right) at g ≈ 0.34-0.38 and stay at +0.015 at g = 0.47. In exactly that window, g 0.35-0.50, the horse stands on its left lateral pair (LH + LF) with both right legs in the air. Mirror-wise, it is at -0.019 m (left) during right lateral support (0.85-1.0). The comment says 'the trunk sways over whichever side is bearing weight', but the phase does the opposite.
findings.expected: The body sways toward the legs bearing its weight. When only the left legs are planted, their ground reaction forces point medially (rightward), which accelerates the trunk to the right while it is displaced left. The left-most point therefore falls inside the left support phase. A trunk displaced away from the only planted legs cannot be produced by ground forces. Lateral bending at walk is one cycle per stride (Faber 2000).
findings.evidence: index.html:1621-1624 (BODY.walk, comment and code); index.html:236-242 (land LH 0, LF .25, RH .5, RF .75; duty 0.6); measurements.json gaits.walk withers z max +0.019 at k=11-12; sheet 01-walk front/rear tiles

fixOptions.label: Shift the phase by half a stride
fixOptions.approach: Negate both sway terms or add 0.5 to their phase (z = -0.012*sin(TAU*(g-0.1)), and the same for rotation.x), so the extreme to each side falls inside that side's lateral support.
fixOptions.risk: Very low.

fixOptions.label: Derive the sway from the planted feet
fixOptions.approach: Set the trunk z to a weighted mean of the z of the planted toes, scaled to ~±15-20 mm and smoothed. It then stays correct if the footfall timing is customised.
fixOptions.risk: Low. It needs smoothing so it does not step at each touchdown.

references: Faber et al. 2000 Am J Vet Res 61:399-406
Griffin, Main & Farley 2004 J Exp Biol 207:3545-3558

findings.title: Walk and trot trunk moves as one rigid block: no pelvic roll, no lateral bending, and a single-cycle roll at the trot
findings.observed: Withers and croup z are identical to within 1 mm at every phase, and the yaw of the withers-croup line spans only 0.12° (walk and trot). The roll is a single rigid-body spine.rotation.x of ±1° (walk) and ±1.2° (trot), one cycle per stride. The hip joints differ in height by at most 6 mm (walk) and 7 mm (trot). The hips bone only ever gets rotation.z (pitch), never roll or yaw. In the rear tiles of sheets 01 and 02 (g = 1/4, 3/4) the croup stays level.
findings.expected: Bone-pin kinematics (Faber 2000, walk at 1.6 m/s): lateral bending of up to 5.6° (cranial thorax and pelvic region), one cycle per stride. Axial rotation rises from 4° at T6 to 13° at the tubera coxae, so the hips visibly rock up and down alternately, by several cm at each tuber coxae. Trot (Faber 2001, 4 m/s): lateral bending 1.9-3.6° (one cycle), axial rotation 4.6-5.8° as a double sinusoid (two cycles per stride). At the trot the withers drift toward the planted fore and the sacrum toward the planted hind, which are opposite sides, so the trunk bends rather than translating.
findings.evidence: index.html:1572-1575 and 1622-1626 (only spine.rotation.x rolls; hips/chest have rotation.z only); index.html:701-703 (hips, chest bones available); measurements.json walk/trot withers z == croup z, hip y difference ≤ 7 mm

fixOptions.label: Add pelvic roll and opposed lateral bend
fixOptions.approach: Walk: hips.rotation.x ≈ ±5-6° with the stance-side hip up at hind mid-stance; hips.rotation.y and chest.rotation.y ≈ ±2-3° in opposite directions. Trot: hips.rotation.x as a two-cycle term, ±2.5°; lateral bend ±1-1.5°.
fixOptions.risk: Low to medium. solveLeg already abducts each limb plane to keep hooves in their track. Check the skin at the loin and flank for creasing, and keep the tail and saddle following the hips.

fixOptions.label: Distribute rotations along the spine
fixOptions.approach: Split the trunk roll and yaw across spine, chest and hips with Faber's regional weights (small at the withers, largest at the pelvis) instead of one rigid spine.rotation.x.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. The saddle and jockey read rowAt along the trunk and would need to follow the chest/spine blend.

references: Faber et al. 2000 Am J Vet Res 61:399-406 (PMID 10772104)
Faber et al. 2001 Am J Vet Res 62:757-764 (PMID 11341399)

findings.title: Walk is a short, collected-type walk that does not track up: hind hooves land 3 cm short of the fore prints
findings.observed: Stride 1.585 m (1.6 before makeGait rounds it to the 65 m loop), T 1.1 s, speed 1.44 m/s. In ground coordinates the LF toe print is at x = 1.580 m. The next LH toe lands at 1.549 m, 3.1 cm behind the fore print (overtrack = (xc_h - xc_f) + 0.75*stride = -1.22 + 1.19 = -0.03 m). The GAITS comment says 'the hind print lands just past the fore print', which is not true.
findings.expected: Clayton (1995), six dressage horses: collected walk 1.37 m/s with a 157 cm stride; medium walk 1.73 m/s; extended walk 1.82 m/s with a 193 cm stride and a stride time of about 1.06 s. The longer stride comes almost entirely from greater over-tracking. A Thoroughbred walking freely on a loose rein (paddock, post parade) walks at a medium/free walk and overtracks its fore prints, typically by about a hoof length or more (~10-25 cm). The model's numbers match a collected walk with no overtrack.
findings.evidence: index.html:235-242 (GAITS.walk stride 1.6, T 1.1, xc fore 0.64 / hind -0.58, comment line 235); index.html:267-275 (makeGait rounding); measurements.json gaits.walk meta strideM 1.585, speedMs 1.44; LF ground print 1.580 vs LH next landing 1.549

fixOptions.label: Lengthen the walk stride
fixOptions.approach: Set stride to ~1.8 m and T to ~1.05 s (≈1.7 m/s). Overtrack becomes ≈ -1.22 + 0.75*1.8 = +0.13 m.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. The stance length becomes 1.08 m. The comment notes the legs keep only ≥2.5% reach, so duty may need to drop to ~0.58, or xc be re-centred, to avoid locking the knee or hock at touchdown or lift-off.

fixOptions.label: Re-centre the stances
fixOptions.approach: Move hind xc forward and/or fore xc back by ~0.06-0.08 m each so the existing stride overtracks by ~10 cm.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. The hind stance moves further under the belly, so check hind reach at lift-off and fore/hind interference (forging) in mid-swing.

fixOptions.label: Make walk length a running-style parameter
fixOptions.approach: Expose an overtrack or walk-length control (tuneGait already scales stride), with a free-walk Thoroughbred default.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Clayton HM (1995) Comparison of the stride kinematics of the collected, medium, and extended walks in horses. Am J Vet Res 56:849-852 (PMID 7574149)
Back W, Clayton HM (eds) Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (Saunders Elsevier 2013), walk chapter

findings.title: Fetlocks barely sink under load at walk and trot, and the trot sinks almost no more than the walk
findings.observed: Standing fore pastern: 33° from vertical. Maximum in stance: 43° at walk (+10°) and 45° at trot (+12°). The hind goes 30° → 38° (walk) and 40° (trot). Lowest fore fetlock height: 0.194 m at walk and 0.191 m at trot, against 0.209 m standing, a drop of only 15-18 mm. The sag parameters are walk 10°/8° and trot 12°/10°, a ratio of 1.2, so the distal limb looks almost rigid.
findings.expected: Fetlock (MCP) extension is close to linear in vertical force (McGuigan & Wilson 2003), and the distal 'leg spring' shortens by ~127 mm at the gallop. Peak forelimb vertical force is about 0.6 BW at walk and about 1.0-1.1 BW at a working trot (Witte et al. 2004, from duty factor). So the trot fetlock should extend roughly 1.6-1.9 times as much as the walk's, about 20-30° beyond standing at a working trot. The fetlock should visibly drop several centimetres, a hallmark of the trotting stance.
findings.evidence: index.html:224-225, 240-241 (sag values); index.html:1390 (a = A.pastern + P.sag*load - tip); index.html:552-553 (rest pastern angles); measurements.json walk/trot stance pastern angle and fetlock y

fixOptions.label: Increase sag per gait
fixOptions.approach: Fore sag: walk ~14°, trot ~22-25°. Hind sag about 80% of the fore value.
fixOptions.risk: Low to medium. Check that the pastern and hoof do not clip the ground and that the IK still reaches (the leg shortens by a few more cm).

fixOptions.label: Derive sag from load
fixOptions.approach: Compute the peak load from duty, Fpk ∝ 1/duty (Witte 2004), with a fore/hind weight split of about 57/43. Map it to MCP extension with a single stiffness constant, so walk, trot, canter, race and custom running styles stay consistent.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Gallop and race also get much deeper fetlocks, which is anatomically right but changes their look.

references: McGuigan MP, Wilson AM (2003) The effect of gait and digital flexor muscle activation on limb compliance in the forelimb of the horse. J Exp Biol 206:1325-1336 (PMID 12624168)
Witte TH, Knill K, Wilson AM (2004) Determination of peak vertical ground reaction force from duty factor in the horse. J Exp Biol 207:3639-3648

findings.title: Grazing 'stand' pose sinks the forehand about 24 cm, folding the elbows, while the hooves stay square
findings.observed: BODY.graze lowers the spine 0.12 m, pitches the spine -3° and pitches the chest a further -12° about (0.3, 1.3). Worked through the rig, this moves the shoulder joint (0.72, 1.22) to about (0.69, 0.98), a 24 cm drop, and the brisket from 0.90 m to about 0.71 m. The fore hooves stay at their square rest spots (GAITS.stand fore xc 0.56) and the knee is straight, so the IK closes the elbow from about 138° to about 84°. The humerus ends up nearly horizontal (pointing back) and the elbow moves about 15 cm back, while the chest floor hangs about 20 cm below the elbows. The hips drop about 9 cm, so the hocks and stifles flex too. No sheet tile shows this pose: sheet 00's 'stand' body matches the walk at g = 0, so this is computed from the code.
findings.expected: The serratus sling suspends the thorax between the forelimbs, which stay straight (stay apparatus, locked carpus and elbow) while grazing. The withers drop only a few cm. Most of the reach comes from neck and poll flexion, and horses typically adopt a staggered grazing stance with one fore well protracted and the other retracted (or base-wide). This stance is common enough to cause uneven feet in foals (van Heel et al. 2006).
findings.evidence: index.html:1643-1653 (BODY.graze); index.html:244-248 (GAITS.stand square xc); index.html:1379 (stand footPath: every hoof at rest); index.html:701-703, 1196 (scapula is a child of the chest bone); index.html:748 (trunk x > 0.45 fully skinned to the chest)

fixOptions.label: Keep the forelimbs straight
fixOptions.approach: Reduce the graze spine drop to ~0.02-0.04 m and the chest pitch to ~-3°. Get the muzzle to the grass with neck1/neck2/head flexion alone (raise neck1 flexion or extend the neck).
fixOptions.risk: Low. The muzzle may no longer reach 2-10 cm above the grass, so re-check the head and neck angles.

fixOptions.label: Add a grazing stance
fixOptions.approach: Give the stand gait per-leg xc offsets: one fore protracted about 0.25-0.35 m and the other retracted. Alternate the side per horse via the phase offset o.
fixOptions.risk: Low to medium. GAITS.stand uses one xc per limb pair today, so a per-leg override is needed in footPath.

fixOptions.label: Rest and graze variants
fixOptions.approach: Split stand into 'graze' (staggered fores, low head) and 'rest' (square, or one hind cocked on the toe), and pick randomly per background horse.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: van Heel MCV, Kroekenstoel AM, van Dierendonck MC, van Weeren PR, Back W (2006) Uneven feet in a foal may develop as a consequence of lateral grazing behaviour induced by conformational traits. Equine Vet J 38:646-651
Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S, Anatomy of the Horse, 6th ed. (2011): stay apparatus and thoracic sling

findings.title: Standing pose: the hind legs stand under the body, well ahead of the point-of-buttock plumb line
findings.observed: Standing: point of buttock at x = -0.858 m, hock joint at -0.614 m, hind cannon about vertical at x ≈ -0.62 to -0.63, hind toe at -0.491 m. The hind cannon sits about 23-24 cm ahead of the vertical through the point of buttock (still about 15 cm even allowing for the calcaneal tuber behind the joint centre). Fore toe to hind toe is only 1.12 m, 0.69 × the 1.62 m withers height. In sheet 00 (left side, right side and 3/4 tiles) the rump overhangs the hocks and the horse looks 'camped under' behind.
findings.expected: Viewed from the side, a vertical dropped from the tuber ischii (point of buttock) should touch the point of the hock and run down the back of the cannon to the heel bulbs (standard conformation plumb line). Hind cannons set clearly in front of that line are the fault 'camped under/standing under behind'.
findings.evidence: index.html:553 (HIND ho [-0.62, 0.56], co [-0.56, COFFIN_Y]); index.html:247 (GAITS.stand hind xc -0.56); index.html:508 (TRUNK rear row x -0.86); measurements.json static.standing buttock/RH; sheet 00-stand tiles 'left side', 'right side', 'hindleg, right side'

fixOptions.label: Move the standing hind hooves back
fixOptions.approach: Set the stand hind xc and HIND.co x to about -0.66 to -0.70, with the hock at about -0.72, so the cannon is close to the buttock plumb line.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. The hock opens and the stifle extends, so re-check the standing hock angle (now 146°) and the walk/trot hind xc, which are centred on the old rest geometry.

fixOptions.label: Shorten the rear overhang instead
fixOptions.approach: Pull the TRUNK rows behind x = -0.68 (buttock, tail head) forward by ~0.08-0.1 m so the buttock line meets the existing hocks.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. Changes body length (shoulder-to-buttock is 1.58 m now, 0.97 × height) and the tail and tack positions. Coordinate with the proportions lens.

references: Baxter GM (ed) Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses, 6th ed. (Wiley-Blackwell 2011), ch. 2 Conformation: lateral plumb lines
Ross MW, Dyson SJ, Diagnosis and Management of Lameness in the Horse, 2nd ed. (2011), conformation chapter

findings.title: Standing pasterns are upright, especially behind
findings.observed: Standing hoof-pastern axis: fore 57° from the horizontal (FORE.pastern 33° from vertical), hind 60° (HIND.pastern 30°).
findings.expected: Normal hoof-pastern axes are about 50-55° in front and 53-57° behind. Thoroughbreds tend toward the lower end in front (often 48-52°). A 60° hind pastern reads as upright, a conformation fault linked to concussion.
findings.evidence: index.html:552-553 (FORE.pastern 33*DEG, HIND.pastern 30*DEG); measurements.json static.standing fore/hind pastern angles

fixOptions.label: Slope the pasterns
fixOptions.approach: Set FORE.pastern to ~36-38° and HIND.pastern to ~34-35° from vertical, and keep the hoof wall angle parallel so the axis is unbroken.
fixOptions.risk: Low to medium. The fetlock height and fetlock-toe offset change, so every gait's stance geometry and breakover shift slightly. Re-check hoof/pastern alignment with the hoof lens.

fixOptions.label: Per-horse pastern control
fixOptions.approach: Expose pastern slope in look.conf (alongside the new hoof control) with the Thoroughbred default above.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses, 6th ed. (2011): hoof-pastern axis
Ross & Dyson, Diagnosis and Management of Lameness in the Horse, 2nd ed. (2011)

findings.title: Trot diagonals are perfectly synchronous; real horses land the hind slightly before the diagonal fore
findings.observed: GAITS.trot land: LF 0.0 = RH 0.0, RF 0.5 = LH 0.5. Both diagonal partners also lift off on the same frame, since duty is equal fore and hind. In sheet 02-trot the diagonal pairs move in exact lockstep.
findings.expected: Riding horses at the trot show positive diagonal advanced placement: the hind touches down first, by +29.8 ± 7.6 ms in Swedish Warmbloods (Holmström 1994), about 4% of a 0.72 s stride. The fore usually stays down slightly longer than its diagonal hind.
findings.evidence: index.html:223 (land), index.html:222 (single duty for fore and hind)

fixOptions.label: Small hind-first offset
fixOptions.approach: Set land RH: -0.03 (0.97) and LH: 0.47, keeping the fore landings at 0 and 0.5.
fixOptions.risk: Very low.

fixOptions.label: Separate fore and hind duty
fixOptions.approach: Allow fore.duty and hind.duty (e.g. 0.42 and 0.39) so the diagonal also dissociates at lift-off.
fixOptions.risk: Low. footPath reads G.duty and G.stanceLen globally, so it would need a per-limb duty.

references: Holmström M, Fredricson I, Drevemo S (1994) Biokinematic analysis of the Swedish Warmblood riding horse at trot. Equine Vet J 26:235-240 (PMID 8542845)
Clayton HM (1997) Classification of collected trot, passage and piaffe based on temporal variables. Equine Vet J Suppl 23 (PMID 9354290)

findings.title: Walk footfalls are metronomically even (exactly 25%); most real walks are slightly lateral
findings.observed: GAITS.walk land: LH 0, LF 0.25, RH 0.5, RF 0.75, so the hind-to-same-side-fore interval equals the fore-to-opposite-hind interval exactly. Fore and hind share one duty factor, 0.6.
findings.expected: In Clayton's walk study only 1 of 6 horses showed equal lateral and diagonal intervals. Horses commonly walk with a limb phase a little under 0.25 (the fore follows its same-side hind sooner than the opposite hind follows the fore). Griffin et al. show that a limb phase below 25% is what produces the visible twice-per-stride rise and fall of the centre of mass. Forelimb stance is usually slightly longer than hindlimb stance.
findings.evidence: index.html:236-238

fixOptions.label: Lateral couplet offset
fixOptions.approach: Set LF to 0.22 and RF to 0.72 (limb phase about 0.22), keeping the hinds at 0 and 0.5.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Check that the hind does not land while the same-side fore is still planted on the same spot (fore lift-off at u = 0.6 must come before the hind's arrival).

fixOptions.label: Expose walk 'lateralness' as a quirk
fixOptions.approach: Add a running-style parameter for limb phase (0.18-0.27). Pacy, lateral walkers are a recognisable individual trait.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Clayton HM (1995) Am J Vet Res 56:849-852
Hildebrand M (1965) Symmetrical gaits of horses. Science 150:701-708
Griffin, Main & Farley (2004) J Exp Biol 207:3545-3558

findings.title: Trot foreleg action is high and showy for a Thoroughbred (forearm to 48°, toe to 32 cm)
findings.observed: In the trot swing the forearm reaches 48° from vertical, the carpus flexes 87°, and the fore toe rises to 0.32 m with the fetlock at 0.43 m, close to knee height (0.50 m standing). Fore toe clearance is 1.7 times the hind's (0.19 m). In sheet 02-trot, tiles g = 1/8 and 5/8, the near fore folds with the forearm close to horizontal.
findings.expected: Thoroughbreds are known for a long, low, 'daisy-cutter' trot. Forearm elevation and fore hoof flight are modest compared with high-action breeds, and hoof clearance at a working trot is in the order of 15-20 cm. Hackney- or Saddlebred-style knee action, with the forearm near horizontal, is a breed trait, not Thoroughbred. Carpal flexion near 85-90° is itself plausible; the excess comes from the 0.22 m fetlock lift.
findings.evidence: index.html:224 (trot fore lift 0.22, flex 88°); index.html:1407 (lift profile); index.html:256-264 (tuneGait kneeAction now scales this per horse); measurements.json trot LF swing toe max 0.322, fetlock max 0.429, forearm max 48.3°

fixOptions.label: Lower the default lift
fixOptions.approach: Trot fore lift ~0.14-0.16 and flex ~75-80°, so the toe peaks around 0.18-0.22 m.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Toe clearance in early swing must stay above the ground during breakover fade.

fixOptions.label: Use the new kneeAction control
fixOptions.approach: Keep the GAITS values but give the default Thoroughbred running style kneeAction ≈ 0.7-0.8 for the trot, reserving higher values for horses known for a high action.
fixOptions.risk: Low. tuneGait applies kneeAction to every gait, so a trot-only factor may be wanted.

references: Back W, Schamhardt HC, Barneveld A et al. (1995) Kinematic differences between the distal portions of the forelimbs and hind limbs at the trot. Am J Vet Res 56:1522-1528
Back & Clayton (eds) Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013), trot chapter
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, trotting plates

findings.title: Walk hoof flight paths are flat-topped plateaus instead of an early peak followed by a low glide
findings.observed: Hind toe height in the walk swing: 0.05 → 0.10 → 0.11 → 0.11 → 0.11 → 0.11 → 0.11 → 0.09 → 0.07 → 0.04 m, a plateau of about 11 cm for about 40% of the swing. The fore toe holds 0.13-0.15 m from s ≈ 0.25 to 0.6. The shape comes from a symmetric smoothstep rise (0-0.3) and fall (0.6-1) on the fetlock lift, so the feet look carried or marching rather than swung.
findings.expected: At walk and trot the hoof peaks early in the swing, as the distal joints fold just after breakover. It then travels forward low over the ground and descends gently into contact. The forelimb arc is often described as bimodal (a large early peak and a smaller one before landing) and the hind arc as single-peaked. Clearance at walk is small, a few to about 10 cm.
findings.evidence: index.html:1407 (fy = fy0 + P.lift*smoothstep(0,P.rise,s)*(1-smoothstep(P.fall,1,s))); index.html:240-241 (walk lift 0.14/0.12, rise 0.3, fall 0.6); measurements.json walk swing toeY series

fixOptions.label: Skewed lift profile
fixOptions.approach: Use an asymmetric bump for walk and trot: peak at s ≈ 0.25-0.3, then a long decay (e.g. fall start 0.35-0.4 with a soft tail), and lower the walk lift to ~0.09-0.1 m.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Watch for toe-drag in mid-swing on uneven ground (paddock and parade-ring paths).

fixOptions.label: Data-driven arc
fixOptions.approach: Tabulate a normalised hoof-height curve per gait (fore bimodal, hind unimodal) and scale it by lift.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Back & Clayton (eds) Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013), hoof flight arc
Clayton HM, The Dynamic Horse (Sport Horse Publications 2004)

findings.title: Hock hyperextends past straight (192-193°) at race push-off and locks at 180° in early swing
findings.observed: Hock dorsal angle (stifle-hock-fetlock) from measurements.json: race RH k=6 = 192°, LH k=9 = 193°, which means the cannon bends backward past the line of the gaskin. RH k=7-9 and LH k=10-12 stay at 179-180° (fully straight). In tile 05-race g=2/8 the trailing RH (white sock) is a straight rod about 56° behind vertical. The same lock-out happens without hockPush: canter LH k=21-24 is 179-180° (03-canter g=6/8), and the walk RH pops from 150° to 162° at lift-off (k=4). While the race hock is straight the stifle is flexed (128-129°).
findings.expected: The tarsocrural joint never reaches 180°. At gallop push-off it peaks at roughly 160-170°, and at rest it sits at 148-160° (jumping Thoroughbreds 148°, Morna racehorses 160.4°, per Ahmad et al. 2025). Because of the reciprocal apparatus (peroneus tertius and SDFT), the hock cannot extend while the stifle is flexed. A hock that extends with a flexed stifle is the classic clinical sign of a ruptured peroneus tertius.
findings.evidence: index.html:215 (race hockPush 40°, which opens the hock past rest); index.html:1357-1360 (stance push = hockPush*smoothstep(0.45,1,sp), giving eta = 34°-8°+12°*load-40°, about -14°, so the hock is about 194°); index.html:1371 (the push is held into early swing); index.html:1442-1447 (femur-clamp fallback re-solves tibia+cannon as a free 2-bone chain, which straightens to 180° when the target is out of reach); tiles 05-race g=2/8, 03-canter g=6/8, 01-walk g=1/8

fixOptions.label: Hard cap on hock extension
fixOptions.approach: Clamp eta (cannon minus tibia) to at least about 12° (hock at most about 168°) in both branches. In footPath, limit hockRest+hockOpen+flex. In the femur-clamp fallback, if the free solve gives aCan-aTib < 12°, re-solve with eta fixed at 12° and accept a small target miss, or let the femur pass its clamp slightly.
fixOptions.risk: At race push-off the leg loses about 3-5 cm of reach, so the toe may lift slightly early or slide unless the fetlock/hip compensate.

fixOptions.label: Replace hockPush with hip extension plus fetlock
fixOptions.approach: Reduce hockPush to about 10-15° and get the late-stance leg length from hip extension instead: allow the femur to retract to about -15° in stance only, and add more fetlock extension.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the race silhouette and needs retuning of hind xc and stride so the 7 m stride still fits.

fixOptions.label: Shorten the race stance reach
fixOptions.approach: Move the race hind stance window (xc) or the duty so the planted toe never needs more than about 168° of hock to stay planted.
fixOptions.risk: Stance length then no longer matches the published ~7 m stride and 0.2 duty, or the hooves slip.

references: Dyce KM, Sack WO, Wensing CJG. Textbook of Veterinary Anatomy, 4th ed. (2010), hindlimb chapter: reciprocal apparatus (peroneus tertius + SDFT)
Ahmad I et al. (2025) Evaluating forelimb and hindlimb joint conformation of Morna racehorses. Vet Sci 12(1):20 (hock 160.4°; jumping Thoroughbreds 148°)
Back W, Clayton HM (eds). Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013)
Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses (Baxter ed.), peroneus tertius rupture

findings.title: Stifle and hock are decoupled: the stifle takes nearly all the stance compression and snaps open alone (reciprocal apparatus violated)
findings.observed: Stance flexion from touchdown to minimum: race stifle 168° to 90° (-78°) while the hock goes 154° to 142° (-12°). Gallop stifle 133° to 107° (-26°), hock 152° to 142° (-10°). Trot stifle 142° to 110° (-32°), hock 150° to 142° (-8°). Before touchdown in race (k=29 to 31) the stifle opens 127° to 168° while the hock stays fixed at 154°. In walk swing the stifle reaches 79° with the hock at 131-140°. Overall hock/stifle regression slope is 0.54-0.79 (walk r=0.69).
findings.expected: In the horse, the peroneus tertius (cranial) and SDFT (caudal) make the stifle and hock flex and extend together, close to 1:1. In stance both flex under load and then extend for push-off; the tarsus is a main shock absorber. Walk ROMs are similar: stifle about 39-43° and tarsus about 37-39° (Egenvall et al. 2023; Douglas et al. 2026). The tarsus flexes in early stance and generates positive work in late stance at trot (Dutto et al. 2006).
findings.evidence: index.html:1436-1440 (hind IK: hock angle eta comes from a schedule (hockRest + hockOpen + f.flex) and the 2-bone solve puts every remaining change of hip-to-fetlock distance into femur and stifle); GAITS hockSag 6-12° at index.html:205,215,223,231,239; tiles 05-race g=0/8 to g=1/8 (stifle buckles), 02-trot g=0/8 to g=1/8

fixOptions.label: Coupled 3-segment IK
fixOptions.approach: Make hock flexion a function of stifle flexion (delta-hock about 0.8-1.0 x delta-stifle from rest, plus a small per-gait offset). Solve the femur-tibia-cannon chain by a 1-D bisection/Newton search on the stifle angle so the fetlock still hits its target.
fixOptions.risk: Some swing targets become unreachable and need a fallback. The IK costs a few more iterations per hind leg (negligible).

fixOptions.label: Distance-driven hock
fixOptions.approach: Keep the 2-bone solve but compute eta from the current hip-to-fetlock distance, using a table built at rig time from the coupled relation, so a compressed leg flexes the hock as well as the stifle.
fixOptions.risk: The table depends on horse scale and pitch, so the edge cases need care.

fixOptions.label: Quick retune
fixOptions.approach: Raise hockSag (trot about 18°, gallop about 25°, race about 30°) and reduce the stance body drop so the stifle needs less flexion.
fixOptions.risk: Only partial: the swing-phase decoupling and the touchdown snap stay.

references: Dyce, Sack & Wensing, Textbook of Veterinary Anatomy (2010): reciprocal apparatus
Egenvall A, Clayton HM, Byström A (2023) PeerJ 11:e16373 (walk: hip ROM 16.7-20.6°, stifle 39.0-43.1°, tarsus about 37-39°)
Douglas L et al. (2026) Animals 16(13):1938 (walk tarsal ROM 38.0 ± 3.6°)
Dutto DJ, Hoyt DF, Clayton HM, Cogger EA, Wickler SJ (2006) J Exp Biol 209:3990-3999

findings.title: Femur swings to horizontal: hip ROM 3-5x too large and the stifle rises 20-30 cm into the barrel
findings.observed: Femur angle from vertical in late swing: race 86-89° (stifle y 1.06-1.09 m, level with the hip joint at 1.08), gallop 79-83° (stifle 1.08-1.11), canter 77-81°, trot 74-76° (stifle 1.06-1.07), walk 67° (stifle 1.04). The belly line at that x is about 0.80-0.89 m, so the stifle sits 0.2-0.3 m inside the trunk. Femur range relative to the croup-buttock line: walk 67°, trot 77°, gallop 76°, race 116°. Minimum stifle angle: race 26-30°, gallop 50°, canter 55-65°, trot 69°. Visually the hind leg seems to sprout from mid-belly (05-race g=5/8-6/8, 04-gallop g=6/8-7/8, 01-walk g=3/8).
findings.expected: Hip ROM at walk is about 17-21° (Egenvall et al. 2023) and remains modest at trot, so most of the reach comes from coupled stifle and hock flexion. Even at full gallop, the stifle comes forward under the flank at about the belly line, never up level with the hip joint (Muybridge 1887 gallop plates). Stifle flexion in fast gaits bottoms out around 80-100°. A stifle angle near 30° would put the gaskin flat against the thigh.
findings.evidence: index.html:1395 (FEMUR_RANGE [0,76°], applied in the hips-bone frame, so hips 'gather' rotation of up to 11° (index.html:1512) plus spine pitch lets the world angle reach 89°); index.html:1441-1447; index.html:537 (short femur, see the proportions finding); tiles 05-race g=5/8,6/8; 04-gallop g=6/8,7/8; 02-trot g=6/8; 01-walk g=3/8

fixOptions.label: Tighter femur limit
fixOptions.approach: Lower FEMUR_RANGE max to about 45-55° measured in the world/pelvis frame (subtract the hips rotation). Let the coupled stifle and hock fold to bring the hoof forward (depends on the reciprocal-coupling fix).
fixOptions.risk: Without the coupling, the hoof may not reach its landing spot; the swing may need more hock flex or less lift.

fixOptions.label: Phase-scheduled hip
fixOptions.approach: Drive the femur from a smooth per-gait hip-angle curve (e.g. walk ±10°, trot ±15°, gallop ±25° about a forward mean) and solve only the coupled stifle/hock to the fetlock target. In stance keep the full IK so the hooves stay planted.
fixOptions.risk: Significant rework of solveLeg; the swing hoof path will deviate from footPath and needs tuning.

fixOptions.label: Fix proportions first
fixOptions.approach: Lengthen the femur (see the proportions finding) so normal hip angles reach the targets without hyperflexion.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the hindquarter silhouette, thigh mesh and gear placement.

references: Egenvall A, Clayton HM, Byström A (2023) Pilot study of locomotor asymmetry in horses walking in circles with and without a rider. PeerJ 11:e16373
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, gallop plates; Muybridge (1878) The Horse in Motion
Back W, Clayton HM, Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013)

findings.title: Femur dwells, whips and snaps: pinned at its limits through the swing, then the stifle straightens to 168° at touchdown and buckles
findings.observed: Race RH: the femur stays at -7..+15° for the first ~40% of swing (k=7-15) while the leg folds backward from the stifle (tibia goes past horizontal to -104°, hock 3-13 cm above the stifle at k=12-17). It then whips 15° to 78° in 5 samples (about 0.07 s), pins at 86-89°, and just before touchdown drops 87° to 41° (k=28-30) while the stifle snaps 97° to 168°. In early stance the femur then re-protracts 56° to 69° and the stifle collapses 168° to 90°. Peak angular speeds: race femur 2044°/s and stifle 3051°/s at k=29; gallop 801°/s and 1273°/s. Relative to the croup-buttock line the hip flexes 8-12° in early stance at trot, canter and race.
findings.expected: Hip protraction starts at lift-off and is a smooth, roughly sinusoidal swing, with at most a small terminal retraction (about 5-10°) before contact. In stance the hip extends steadily (the hip does positive propulsive work; Dutto et al. 2006). At contact the stifle and hock are already moderately flexed (not near straight) and yield together.
findings.evidence: index.html:1442-1447 (hard clamp: aFem = clamp(...) with no smoothing; the same pose sits at the limit, so the angle saturates and then jumps when the target moves away from the limit); index.html:1369 (swingX flick/retract with hind xc puts the landing toe 0.72 m ahead of the hip in race); tiles 05-race g=2/8-3/8 (femur vertical, leg folded back), g=7/8 to g=0/8 (snap)

fixOptions.label: Soft limits
fixOptions.approach: Replace clamp() with a smooth saturation (e.g. a tanh-style or blended limit over about 10°) and low-pass the femur angle within the swing.
fixOptions.risk: Small fetlock target errors near the limits; swing toe height may change slightly.

fixOptions.label: Reshape the swing path
fixOptions.approach: Tune swingX (flick, retract) and the lift/fall timing for the hind so the hoof comes forward early in the swing (femur leads) and the terminal retraction is small, keeping the landing reach achievable without straightening the stifle.
fixOptions.risk: Needs per-gait tuning; risk of hind-fore interference at gallop.

fixOptions.label: Scheduled femur
fixOptions.approach: Use the phase-scheduled hip curve described in the femur over-rotation finding, so femur motion is smooth by construction.
fixOptions.risk: Same as that finding: solveLeg rework.

references: Dutto DJ et al. (2006) Joint work and power for both the forelimb and hindlimb during trotting in the horse. J Exp Biol 209:3990-3999
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion
Back W, Clayton HM, Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013)

findings.title: Missing hamstring mass / second thigh: the rear outline breaks between buttock and gaskin, and the hind legs look 'split up behind'
findings.observed: The trunk's rear rings end as a rounded barrel: bottoms at 1.13 m (x=-0.86), 0.99 (x=-0.80) and 0.85 (x=-0.68), so the belly continues back under the hindquarters. The gaskin's back line runs from (-0.52, 0.97) to (-0.57, 0.83) to (-0.61, 0.67), which is 0.11-0.25 m in front of where the thigh's back contour should be. The femur mesh lies almost entirely inside the trunk. Result: a notch behind the leg and a thin stick-like gaskin emerging under the flank (00-stand 'right side' and 'hindleg, right side' close-up). From behind, the legs hang as separate thin columns from under an oval rump with a gap right up to the trunk (00-stand 'rear'; 05-race and 04-gallop rear tiles).
findings.expected: The hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) run from the tuber ischii down to the tibia and calcaneus. In profile the posterior contour is a continuous line from the point of buttock down the thigh and gaskin to the point of hock. From behind, the hindquarters are widest at the stifles/thighs and the inner thighs meet nearly down to the gaskins. A gap there ('split up behind') is a conformation fault.
findings.evidence: index.html:491-494 (TRUNK rear rings: [-0.86,1.45,1.13,...], [-0.8,1.535,0.99,...], [-0.68,1.59,0.85,...]); index.html:1186 (femur sections, back up to 0.22, inside the trunk); index.html:1187 (tibia sections, back 0.17 to 0.06); tiles 00-stand right side, hindleg right side, rear, 3/4 rear-left

fixOptions.label: Rigid second-thigh mesh on the tibia
fixOptions.approach: Add a muscle bulge to the tibia bone covering t of about 0 to 0.5, reaching back about 0.2 m toward the buttock plumb line and inward so the inner thighs nearly meet under the tail. It then follows the leg in motion.
fixOptions.risk: At extreme hip angles the rigid bulge intersects the trunk or tail; the shape needs care at push-off.

fixOptions.label: Skinned hamstring curtain
fixOptions.approach: Loft a surface from the point of buttock to the upper tibia and calcaneus, skin-weighted between the hips bone and the tibia bone (add the tibia nodes to the body skeleton before mergeRigid).
fixOptions.risk: Skinning artifacts at large joint angles; touches the merge/skinning pipeline.

fixOptions.label: Reshape the trunk rear rings
fixOptions.approach: Raise and narrow the rear-bottom of the TRUNK rings (x -0.68..-0.86) so the barrel ends higher, and let the enlarged thigh and gaskin meshes form the lower outline.
fixOptions.risk: Static only; the trunk does not follow the leg, so it still looks wrong in motion unless combined with the rigid-mesh option.

references: Dyce, Sack & Wensing, Textbook of Veterinary Anatomy (2010): pelvic limb musculature (hamstring group)
Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses: conformation, hind limbs viewed from behind ('split up behind')
Ross MW, Dyson SJ, Diagnosis and Management of Lameness in the Horse (2011): conformation chapter

findings.title: Hind legs stand under the body: the point-of-buttock plumb line falls 16-19 cm behind the hock
findings.observed: Standing: point of buttock x=-0.858. Hock joint x=-0.614, with the point-of-hock mesh at about -0.70 (cannon back extent 0.085). Back of the fetlock about -0.69, heel about -0.60. A vertical from the buttock therefore passes about 0.16 m behind the point of hock and about 0.17 m behind the back of the fetlock. The hock joint is only 0.10 m behind the hip joint (-0.515) while the buttock is 0.34 m behind it. The 00-stand side tiles show the rump overhanging well behind the hind cannon.
findings.expected: Classic side-view conformation: a plumb line from the point of buttock touches the point of hock and runs down the back of the cannon to just behind the heel. Hind cannons standing forward of that line are 'camped under' or 'standing under'.
findings.evidence: index.html:537 (HIND ho [-0.62,0.56], co [-0.56,...]); index.html:245 (stand hind xc -0.56); index.html:491-493 (TRUNK rear rings at x=-0.86/-0.8); measurements.json static.standing buttock vs RH hock/fetlock; tiles 00-stand left side, right side, hindleg close-up

fixOptions.label: Move hock and hoof back
fixOptions.approach: Shift HIND.ho and HIND.co back by about 0.12-0.15 m (cannon stays vertical) and move the stand and gait hind xc back by the same amount.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the fore-hind spacing, the walk overtracking claim and hoofprint placement; the tibia becomes more sloped (re-check the rest hock angle).

fixOptions.label: Shorten the rump overhang
fixOptions.approach: Move the rear TRUNK rings and the tail root forward by about 0.08-0.10 m so the buttock sits over the hock.
fixOptions.risk: Changes body length and the croup silhouette (other lenses) plus the tail and saddle-cloth placement.

fixOptions.label: Split the difference
fixOptions.approach: Move the hock/hoof back about 7 cm and the buttock forward about 7 cm.
fixOptions.risk: Combines smaller versions of both risks.

references: Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses (Baxter ed., 2011): conformation, plumb lines of the hind limb
Ross MW, Dyson SJ, Diagnosis and Management of Lameness in the Horse (2011): conformation
Weller R, Pfau T, May SA, Wilson AM (2006) Variation in conformation in a cohort of National Hunt racehorses. Equine Vet J 38:616-621

findings.title: Femur too short and gaskin too long (femur:tibia = 0.69), with a high stifle and over-angled rest joints
findings.observed: Joint-centre lengths: hip to stifle 0.306 m, stifle to hock 0.444 m, hock to fetlock 0.347 m. Femur/tibia = 0.69. Rest angles: femur 33° forward of vertical, tibia 37° back; stifle angle 110°, hock 146°. The stifle sits 4 cm above the belly line at 0.915 m, only 0.26 m below the hip joint. Because the femur is short, the IK needs extreme hip and stifle angles to reach targets (see the femur over-rotation finding).
findings.expected: In the horse the femur and tibia are of similar functional length (femur about 1.0-1.1 x tibia, roughly 0.38-0.42 m vs 0.36-0.40 m joint-to-joint in a 160-165 cm Thoroughbred). The long femur is what lets a modest hip ROM move the stifle a long way. Published standing angles: jumping Thoroughbreds stifle 114°, hock 148°; Morna racehorses stifle 128.6 ± 4.1°, hock 160.4 ± 3.9° (Ahmad et al. 2025, same hip-stifle-hock-fetlock joint-centre definition). The model's 110°/146° is at or beyond the angled end of that range.
findings.evidence: index.html:537 (HIND hip [-0.52,1.18], st [-0.36,0.92], ho [-0.62,0.56]); index.html:1193-1195 (rest angles and lengths); measurements.json static.standing RH

fixOptions.label: Lower and advance the stifle
fixOptions.approach: Move HIND.st to about (-0.31, 0.84). This gives a femur of about 0.38 m and a tibia of about 0.38-0.40 m with the hip, hock and hoof unchanged; rest stifle becomes about 120° and hock about 150°. Re-check the thigh/tibia mesh sections.
fixOptions.risk: The stifle sits lower, at the belly line; the stifle/flank fold and the thigh mesh shape need a visual pass. All gait poses change.

fixOptions.label: Raise the hip joint
fixOptions.approach: Raise and move back HIND.hip (about (-0.55, 1.24)) to lengthen the femur without moving the stifle.
fixOptions.risk: The hip pivot moves relative to the croup and the trunk skin; the thigh mesh may poke through the croup at protraction.

fixOptions.label: Keep proportions, compensate in motion
fixOptions.approach: Leave the rest pose and rely on the motion fixes (soft limits, coupled IK).
fixOptions.risk: The silhouette stays slightly 'long gaskin / short thigh'; extreme poses remain harder to avoid.

references: Ahmad I et al. (2025) Vet Sci 12(1):20 (stifle 128.6°, hock 160.4°, hind fetlock 155.5°; jumping Thoroughbreds 114°/148°/157°)
Getty R (ed.) Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 5th ed. (1975): equine femur and tibia
Buchner HHF, Savelberg HHCM, Schamhardt HC, Barneveld A (1997) Inertial properties of Dutch Warmblood horses. J Biomech 30:653-658 (segment lengths)
Weller R et al. (2006) Equine Vet J 38:616-621

findings.title: Point of hock sits at the joint, not above it, and there is no calcanean tendon line
findings.observed: The hind cannon mesh reaches its largest back extent (0.085 m) at t=-0.02, about 7 mm above the tarsocrural joint (y about 0.567). At t=-0.12 (4 cm above) it shrinks to 0.05, and the tibia mesh tapers to 0.06 at t=0.8 and 0.045 at the hock. The hock reads as a soft lump at joint level with a concave back above it (00-stand hindleg close-up). There is no straight 'Achilles' line from the gaskin to the point of hock.
findings.expected: The tuber calcanei (point of hock) projects about 8-12 cm above and about 8-10 cm behind the tarsocrural joint, at roughly 0.62-0.66 m in a 163 cm horse. It is the lever arm of the gastrocnemius and SDFT. From it the taut common calcanean tendon runs straight up to the gaskin muscles, with a visible hollow in front of it. The calcaneus moves with the tarsus and cannon, not the tibia.
findings.evidence: index.html:1188 (hind cannon sections [-0.12,0.04,0.05,..], [-0.02,0.045,0.085,..]); index.html:1187 (tibia back extents 0.125 to 0.06 to 0.045 toward the hock); tile 00-stand 'hindleg, right side'

fixOptions.label: Calcaneus block on the cannon
fixOptions.approach: Extend the cannon mesh upward (t of about -0.3..-0.1) with a back extent of about 0.09-0.10 m so the point of hock peaks about 8 cm above the joint. It then rotates correctly with the cannon when the hock flexes.
fixOptions.risk: Low; check intersection with the tibia mesh at maximum hock flexion (about 80°).

fixOptions.label: Tendon line on the tibia
fixOptions.approach: Thicken the tibia's back extent over t of about 0.55-1.0 to a straight line (about 0.07-0.08) so the gaskin runs into the point of hock as a tendon.
fixOptions.risk: Low; slightly heavier-looking gaskin.

fixOptions.label: Both, with a gaskin hollow
fixOptions.approach: Combine the two and keep a small front-to-back gap between the tibia's bone line and the tendon, so the hollow reads in the flat shading.
fixOptions.risk: Low; more triangles per hind leg.

references: Dyce, Sack & Wensing, Textbook of Veterinary Anatomy (2010): tarsus, calcaneus, common calcanean tendon
König HE, Liebich H-G, Veterinary Anatomy of Domestic Mammals (7th ed., 2020): pelvic limb

findings.title: Hind hoof too tall and too upright, with a broken-forward hoof-pastern axis
findings.observed: hoofGeo (hind): the top ring's front is at co.x+0.035 at y=0.104 and the toe at co.x+0.069 at y=0.002. That gives a dorsal wall at about 72° to the ground and a toe-coronet height of about 10.4 cm, with the coffin joint at 9.2 cm. The rest pastern is 30° from vertical (60° to the ground), so the hoof is about 12° steeper than the pastern: a broken-forward axis (boxy/club look in 00-stand hindleg close-up). The fore hoof uses the same construction (about 73°).
findings.expected: A Thoroughbred hind hoof has a dorsal wall of about 50-57° and a hoof-pastern axis that is straight (hoof and pastern parallel). The hind pastern is about 53-57° to the ground. Toe height (coronet at the toe) is about 6.5-7.5 cm, and the coffin joint lies about 2-3 cm below the coronet.
findings.evidence: index.html:487-488 (HOOF_H 0.09, COFFIN_Y, HOOF_TOE 0.069); index.html:1122-1128 (HOOF_SHAPE hind top [0.039,..], bot [0.058,..], top ring at co.y+0.012); index.html:537 (HIND.pastern 30°); tile 00-stand hindleg close-up

fixOptions.label: Reshape the capsule only
fixOptions.approach: Move the top ring back and down (front edge at about co.x+0.01, top at about 0.08) so the dorsal wall is about 55°, keeping sole/toe positions (no IK change).
fixOptions.risk: A gap or step can appear at the coronet / pastern junction; check the hoof flip in swing.

fixOptions.label: Align pastern and hoof
fixOptions.approach: Also set HIND.pastern to about 34-36° from vertical (54-56° to the ground) to match the new wall angle.
fixOptions.risk: Rest fetlock height drops about 1 cm and all stance targets shift slightly.

fixOptions.label: Shorter hoof overall
fixOptions.approach: Lower HOOF_H/COFFIN_Y to about 0.07 so the coffin joint sits inside the capsule.
fixOptions.risk: Touches every foot computation (plantedFetlock, prints, white-marking heights), fore and hind.

references: O'Grady SE, Poupard DA (2003) Proper physiologic horseshoeing. Vet Clin North Am Equine Pract 19:333-351 (straight hoof-pastern axis)
Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses (2011): hoof angles, fore about 50-54°, hind about 53-57°
Kummer M et al. (2006) Evaluation of a standardised radiographic technique for assessment of the equine distal limb / hoof conformation (Equine Vet J)

findings.title: Hind fetlock barely sinks at mid-stance; peak extension comes late, from the cannon tipping back
findings.observed: Fetlock height under load drops only from 0.213 m (rest) to 0.19 m (race), 0.20 (gallop, trot, walk). At mid-stance the pastern is at most 45° from vertical in race (rest 30° + sag 15°), 42° gallop, 40° trot. The race fetlock dorsal angle is 229° at mid-stance (k=3) and peaks at 246° only at about 78% of stance (k=5), when the cannon has tipped 43° back. The 05-race stance tiles (g=1/8, RH) show an upright pastern.
findings.expected: Hind fetlock hyperextension peaks around mid-stance, at peak vertical load. At racing speed (12-17 m/s) the hind fetlock hyperextends strongly (Symons et al. 2014) and the pastern approaches about 20-30° to the ground, so the fetlock sinks visibly toward the track. At trot, hind fetlock extension rises roughly 20-30° above standing.
findings.evidence: index.html:1351-1353 (load = sin²(πsp); a = pastern + sag*load - tip); GAITS hind sag 8-15° at index.html:205,215,223,231,239; tile 05-race g=1/8

fixOptions.label: Larger, earlier sag
fixOptions.approach: Raise the hind sag (walk about 12°, trot about 20°, canter/gallop about 25°, race about 30-35°) and skew the load curve so it peaks at about 40-50% of stance.
fixOptions.risk: At race the ergot/fetlock may come too close to the ground or the pastern mesh may intersect the hoof; check the visuals.

fixOptions.label: Single compression scalar
fixOptions.approach: Drive fetlock drop, hock flexion and stifle flexion from one per-gait 'limb compression' curve so they peak together.
fixOptions.risk: Needs the coupled-IK work; more tuning.

references: Symons JE, Garcia TC, Stover SM (2014) Distal hindlimb kinematics of galloping Thoroughbred racehorses on dirt and synthetic racetrack surfaces. Equine Vet J 46:227-232
Back W, Schamhardt HC et al. (1995) Kinematic differences between the distal portions of the forelimbs and hind limbs of horses at the trot. Am J Vet Res 56:1522-1528
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion

findings.title: No push-off extension at trot and gallop: the hind leg leaves the ground still flexed, with the stance sitting forward of the hip
findings.observed: At lift-off the gallop stifle is 102° (its stance minimum is 99-107°) and the hock 152°. The hoof leaves only 0.28-0.30 m behind the hip after landing 0.58 m in front of it. The trot stifle flexes 142° to 110° and stays at 105-107° to lift-off (no re-extension), and the stance runs +0.61 m to -0.50 m about the hip. In race, the push-off length comes only from the impossible hock hyperextension (see the hyperextension finding). In 04-gallop g=2/8 the lifting RH is still under the buttock.
findings.expected: In late stance the hip, stifle and hock extend together to propel the body (the hip and tarsus do positive work in late stance at trot; Dutto et al. 2006). The hind hoof leaves the ground well behind the hip, with the limb angled back. Stance is biased caudally (less protraction at contact than retraction at lift-off), as Muybridge's trot and gallop plates show.
findings.evidence: GAITS hind xc and duty at index.html:205,223 (gallop xc -0.45, trot -0.5); index.html:1357-1360 (no late-stance extension term except race hockPush); measurements gallop RH k=0-11, trot RH k=0-12; tile 04-gallop g=2/8

fixOptions.label: Late-stance extension term
fixOptions.approach: In stance after about 55%, drive the coupled stifle/hock toward about 150°/160° (bounded by the hock cap) while the femur retracts, instead of only scheduling hock sag.
fixOptions.risk: Leg-length budget: the toe may leave the ground early unless the stance window moves back or the fetlock extends.

fixOptions.label: Shift the hind stance window back
fixOptions.approach: Move the hind xc for trot/gallop back by about 0.1-0.15 m so contact is nearer the hip vertical and lift-off further behind it.
fixOptions.risk: Changes hind/fore print spacing, the walk/trot tracking-up look and the hoofprint trail; possible change in fore-hind clearance.

references: Dutto DJ et al. (2006) J Exp Biol 209:3990-3999
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion (trot, canter, gallop plates)
Back W, Clayton HM, Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013)

findings.title: Hind track never narrows: the hooves stay 0.35 m apart at every speed and the limbs hang as parallel columns
findings.observed: Every hind joint and hoof stays at z = ±0.173-0.177 in every gait and phase (measurements.json), so the hoof centres are 0.35 m apart standing and at 16.8 m/s. In the rear tiles (01-05 'rear g=1/4, 3/4') the hind legs are vertical, parallel and wide, like table legs, with no convergence toward the midline. The limb also shows no outward stifle / inward hock set.
findings.expected: Standing square, the hind hooves are roughly one hoof-width apart (centres about 0.2-0.25 m). As speed rises, horses place the hooves closer to the midline, and at the gallop the hind prints fall close to the line of travel. From behind, the stifles sit slightly outside the hips and the hocks and cannons come in under the body.
findings.evidence: index.html:537 (HIND.z 0.175); index.html:1333-1336 and 1404-1408 (abduction only used for body roll and curved paths, never for a per-gait track width); tiles 05-race rear g=1/4, 3/4; 04-gallop rear

fixOptions.label: Per-gait track width
fixOptions.approach: Add a hind track half-width per gait (e.g. walk 0.11, trot 0.09, canter/gallop 0.06, race 0.05) and feed it through the existing abductedZ path for every gait, not only on curves.
fixOptions.risk: Legs may cross or interfere at gallop; needs a minimum clearance and a check of the front/rear views.

fixOptions.label: Narrower rest stance
fixOptions.approach: Reduce HIND.z for the hooves (about 0.12-0.13) while keeping the hip joints wide, so the leg angles in slightly from hip to hoof.
fixOptions.risk: The inner thigh meshes may overlap at the midline; changes the rear silhouette.

references: Back W, Clayton HM, Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013): limb placement and track width vs speed
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, rear and oblique gallop views

findings.title: Hind cannon is round in section (7.2 cm wide x 7.4 cm deep) instead of flat
findings.observed: Hind cannon sections at t=0.25-0.85: front 0.030-0.031, back 0.043, half-width 0.034-0.036. That gives a near-circular 7.2 x 7.4 cm section with no flat side-to-side profile and no separate tendon edge at the back.
findings.expected: A good Thoroughbred cannon is 'flat': narrower side-to-side (about 5-5.5 cm) than front-to-back (about 6.5-7 cm). The suspensory ligament and the flexor tendons form a distinct, straight plantar edge behind the bone.

fixOptions.label: Flatten the section
fixOptions.approach: Reduce the half-width to about 0.026-0.028 and raise the back extent to about 0.045-0.048 over t=0.25-0.85, keeping the circumference.
fixOptions.risk: Low; check white-marking edges and bandage meshes (index.html:1191) still wrap the leg.

references: Adams & Stashak's Lameness in Horses (2011): conformation of the metatarsal region
König HE, Liebich H-G, Veterinary Anatomy of Domestic Mammals: metatarsus and plantar tendons

findings.title: Racing gallop footfalls bunched in pairs: limb lags about half of real, overlap 3x too long, aerial phase 43% of the stride
findings.observed: land RH 0, LH 0.09, RF 0.27, LF 0.37 with duty 0.2 and T 0.43 s. That gives lags of 39 ms (RH to LH), 77 ms (LH to RF) and 43 ms (RF to LF). Stances overlap for 0.23 of the stride (~99 ms): RH/LH 0.11, LH/RF 0.02, RF/LF 0.10. Suspension runs from LF lift-off at 0.57 to RH contact at 1.0, i.e. 0.43 of the stride (185 ms). measurements.json agrees: toe-contact strings show 13/32 airborne samples (0.41). On sheet 05-race, 4 of the 8 side tiles (g=4/8 to 7/8) are fully airborne, both hinds are down together at g=1/8 and both fores at g=3/8. The rhythm reads as two doublets and a long float, not four evenly spaced beats.
findings.expected: Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006, Thoroughbreds at 17 m/s: aerial phase 119 ms (~27-29% of a 415 ms stride; about 27% at every speed from 9 to 17 m/s), total limb overlap only 35 ms, fore stance 77 ms, hind stance 94 ms. Under those constraints the three inter-limb lags add up to ~219 ms, ~70-75 ms each (~0.17-0.18 of the stride). The racing gallop is a nearly sequential 4-beat 'drum roll' with a shorter gathered suspension.
findings.evidence: index.html:211-216 (GAITS.race land/duty); index.html:1345-1348 (footPath uses one G.duty, stance starts at G.land); index.html:1505-1530 (BODY.race phases 0.8-0.97 are keyed to the current long aerial phase); measurements.json gaits.race toe-contact strings; sheet 05-race tiles g=1/8, 3/8, 4/8-7/8

fixOptions.label: Retime land table
fixOptions.approach: Spread the beats to roughly land {RH 0, LH 0.17, RF 0.36, LF 0.53} (keep duty ~0.2). LF then lifts at ~0.73, giving ~27% aerial and ~0.08 overlap. Shift the BODY.race cyc() phases (height peak 0.82, pitch 0.8, gather 0.9, neck 0.86-0.97) by about +0.12 so they stay keyed to the new aerial phase.
fixOptions.risk: Changes which legs are loaded at the same time, so the body-height dip and the jockey/rein timing need retuning. Mirrored right-lead tables follow automatically via RIGHT_LEAD.

fixOptions.label: Lag parameters
fixOptions.approach: Replace absolute land phases with hindLag, diagLag and foreLag (s or stride fraction) plus fore/hind duty, and compute land and the aerial fraction from them. Expose them as per-horse running-style knobs (e.g. a 'tight-paired' vs 'evenly drummed' gallop), which also serves the customisation request.
fixOptions.risk: Needs a guard so the lags plus the LF stance never exceed one stride and the suspension does not vanish.

references: Witte TH, Hirst CV, Wilson AM (2006) Effect of speed on stride parameters in racehorses at gallop in field conditions. J Exp Biol 209:4389-4397, doi:10.1242/jeb.02518
Muybridge E (1899) Animals in Motion - gallop plates

findings.title: Trunk pitch at gallop and race is far too small, and the rocking pivots about the croup instead of the trunk's centre
findings.observed: Race: the croup-to-withers line pitches 7.6 deg peak to peak (-2.4 to +5.3). The cranial thorax (spine->withers, girth->brisket) pitches only 3.0-3.2 deg, because chest.rotation (-1 deg - 3 deg x gather) cancels spine.rotation.z (2.5 deg). Gallop (6.2 m/s): 7.0 deg body, 4.2 deg thorax. Croup height range is only 0.5 cm in the gallop and 3.0 cm in the race, against 11.7 / 12.6 cm at the withers: the trunk see-saws about a nearly fixed croup. Pitch is a pure cosine (max nose-up g=0.84), so it keeps rotating at speed through most of the flight.
findings.expected: Pfau, Witte & Wilson 2006 (withers-mounted IMU, Thoroughbreds at 7-17 m/s): trunk pitch range rises with speed from 11.2 deg (10.0-12.4) at 7 m/s to 19.0 deg (18.3-19.7) at 17 m/s. The pitch curve has a broad maximum with near-zero pitch velocity through the aerial phase (40-60% of stride after lead-fore contact). With ~19 deg about a pivot near the girth, the croup and withers move ~0.15-0.3 m relative to each other, and the hindquarters visibly rise and fall in antiphase with the forehand.
findings.evidence: index.html:1508-1513 (BODY.race spine.position/rotation.z 2.5 deg, chest -3 deg x gather); index.html:1476-1481 (BODY.gallop 3 deg, chest -2 deg); measurements.json: race thorax pitch 3.0 deg, body 7.6 deg, croup y 1.496-1.526; gallop croup y 1.567-1.572; sheet 05-race g=0/8 vs g=4/8 (the back line barely changes angle)

fixOptions.label: Bigger pitch, no chest cancel
fixOptions.approach: Raise spine.rotation.z to ~+/-9 deg (race) and ~+/-5.5 deg (gallop). Drop or reverse the chest counter-rotation so the thorax carries the pitch. Add a horizontal/vertical spine offset so the rotation pivots near the girth (x ~ +0.15) rather than the croup.
fixOptions.risk: Shoulder and hip heights then swing by ~+/-0.1 m, so stance legs may over-reach or crumple at the extremes (the IK clamps at l1+l2). The jockey pivot already removes 70% of back pitch from the rider, so check the reins.

fixOptions.label: Stance-driven pitch curve
fixOptions.approach: Replace the cosine with a piecewise C1 curve: nose-down rotation while the hinds are loaded, nose-up while the fores are loaded, and a held plateau (constant angle) through the aerial phase. Key it off the land/duty table so it follows any retiming.
fixOptions.risk: Must stay periodic and C1 for the seamless loop and the 0.6 s gait blend.

fixOptions.label: Physics-lite pitch from leg loads
fixOptions.approach: Integrate a pitch angular velocity from the summed load (sin^2 stance profile) of hind vs fore legs times their lever arms about the COM, with zero torque in flight, then normalise to a target range per gait (11 deg slow gallop -> 19 deg race).
fixOptions.risk: Drift and periodicity need a correction step. Harder to art-direct.

references: Pfau T, Witte TH, Wilson AM (2006) Centre of mass movement and mechanical energy fluctuation during gallop locomotion in the Thoroughbred racehorse. J Exp Biol 209:3742-3757, doi:10.1242/jeb.02439

findings.title: Fetlock barely drops in stance at speed; the stance compression happens at the elbow/shoulder instead
findings.observed: Race forelimb: the pastern goes from 33 deg to only 50 deg from vertical (sag 17 deg). The fetlock sinks from 0.209 to 0.182 m (2.7 cm) and carpus-to-toe shortens only 16 mm. Meanwhile scapTop-to-fetlock shortens 153-156 mm in stance: elbow 128 -> 105 deg and shoulder 112 -> 77 deg (interior), because the body is lowered 8.5 cm (spine offset -0.085) and the IK bends the upper limb. Hind: fetlock 0.213 -> 0.191 m, while the stifle folds 137 -> 90 deg. Canter and gallop fore drops are 2.0-2.1 cm. Sag barely scales with speed (13/14/17 deg canter/gallop/race). At touchdown the fetlock is straight or slightly flexed (175-179 deg interior; the pastern keeps a fixed world angle while the cannon slopes forward). On sheet 05-race g=1/8 and g=3/8 the stance pasterns stay at ~45 deg.
findings.expected: McGuigan & Wilson 2003: at the gallop the distal passive leg spring (fetlock/digit) shortens by 127 mm (106-128 mm), the proximal spring by only 12 mm (9-15 mm), and MCP angle is linear in limb force. Witte et al. 2006: peak fore force rises from 16.8 N/kg at 9 m/s to 24.7 N/kg at 17 m/s, so the drop should grow with speed. At racing speed the pastern approaches horizontal and the fetlock nearly touches the track. Ratzlaff et al. 1993: the fetlock is already extended at hoof contact in the gallop (199-206 deg, i.e. ~20-26 deg past straight) and peaks at mid-stance with peak heel force. The forelimb above the fetlock acts as a near-rigid strut.
findings.evidence: index.html:204, 214, 230 (fore/hind sag per gait); index.html:1351-1353 (a = A.pastern + P.sag*load - tip); index.html:1314-1318 (plantedFetlock, PASTERN 0.14 at index.html:487); index.html:1508 (race spine lowered -0.085, which forces elbow/shoulder flexion through IK); measurements.json race RF stance fetlock y 0.209->0.182, elbow 128->105, shoulder 112->77

fixOptions.label: Raise sag, scale with speed
fixOptions.approach: Set fore sag to ~40-45 deg (race), ~28-32 deg (gallop), ~22 deg (canter), and hind about 70% of the fore value. Add a touchdown pre-extension: pastern angle = cannon angle + ~20 deg at u=0 instead of the fixed A.pastern. Reduce the race spine lowering so the drop comes from the fetlock, not the elbow.
fixOptions.risk: With PASTERN=0.14 the fetlock can only drop ~0.117 m before the pastern is horizontal, so the hoof/pastern mesh may clip the ground and the ergot area needs checking. The body height curve must be re-tuned.

fixOptions.label: Strut-and-spring stance
fixOptions.approach: Solve stance height from a near-constant proximal limb length (scapTop->fetlock within ~1-2 cm, elbow/shoulder change reciprocally) plus a fetlock spring whose drop follows a force profile scaled by gait speed. Expose 'fetlock drop' as a per-horse trait for low, sinking runners (e.g. an Oguri Cap-style low gallop).
fixOptions.risk: Touches footPath, solveLeg and BODY heights together, so loop seams and gait blends need re-checking.

references: McGuigan MP, Wilson AM (2003) The effect of gait and digital flexor muscle activation on limb compliance in the forelimb of the horse Equus caballus. J Exp Biol 206:1325-1336, doi:10.1242/jeb.00254
Witte TH, Hirst CV, Wilson AM (2006) J Exp Biol 209:4389-4397
Ratzlaff MH et al. (1993) Relationship between locomotor forces, hoof position and joint motion during the support phase of the stride of galloping horses. Acta Anat 146:200-204
Butcher MT, Ashley-Ross MA (2002) Fetlock joint kinematics differ with age in Thoroughbred racehorses. J Biomech 35:563-571

findings.title: 'Gallop' uses trot-length strides at a racing stride rate: 2.6 m at 2.38 Hz (6.2 m/s), shorter than the canter and quicker than the race
findings.observed: GAITS.gallop T 0.42 s, stride 2.6 m, giving 2.38 strides/s and 6.19 m/s. Its stride is shorter than the canter's (2.96 m), equal to the trot's (2.6 m), and its stride rate is higher than the racing gallop's (2.33 Hz at 16.8 m/s). Duty is 0.35 for every leg. Speed nearly triples from gallop to race while stride frequency falls slightly, so the gallop looks like a scurrying, short-stepping bound.
findings.expected: Witte et al. 2006: stride frequency rises modestly with speed, from 2.02 Hz at 9 m/s (stride ~4.45 m) to 2.41 Hz at 17 m/s (~7.05 m), roughly f = 1.58 + 0.049*v. Duty at 9 m/s is fore 0.27 / hind 0.29, aerial ~27%. A horse moving at 6 m/s is normally cantering at ~1.7-1.9 Hz with ~3.3 m strides. A gallop should never have a shorter stride than the canter.
findings.evidence: index.html:201-206 (GAITS.gallop T/stride/duty); index.html:211-212 (race T 0.43); measurements.json gaits.gallop.meta speedMs 6.19, strideM 2.6; gaits.canter strideM 2.955

fixOptions.label: Make it a 9-10 m/s gallop
fixOptions.approach: T ~0.49 s (2.05 Hz), stride ~4.5-4.8 m, duty fore ~0.27 / hind ~0.29, land re-spaced for ~27% aerial. Give BODY.gallop part of the race's reach aids (lower body, scapSwing ~14 deg).
fixOptions.risk: A ~1.25 m stance may exceed the legs' reach at the current gallop body height (the reason race needed BODY.race). Scenes using the gallop will scroll ~50% faster.

fixOptions.label: Keep 6.2 m/s, slow the cadence
fixOptions.approach: T ~0.53 s (1.9 Hz) with stride ~3.3 m. This is effectively a fast 4-beat 'hand gallop' between canter and race.
fixOptions.risk: Little visual difference from the canter. The footfall table still needs more aerial time.

fixOptions.label: Speed-driven cadence
fixOptions.approach: Derive T from a target speed via f = 1.58 + 0.049*v (Witte endpoints), and stride = v/f, with a per-horse stride-length/frequency bias (a 'pitch' runner vs a long 'stride' runner) as a customisation trait.
fixOptions.risk: makeGait's whole-strides-per-loop rounding changes stride by up to ~7%, so either accept it or adjust T to match.

references: Witte TH, Hirst CV, Wilson AM (2006) J Exp Biol 209:4389-4397, doi:10.1242/jeb.02518
Pfau T, Witte TH, Wilson AM (2006) J Exp Biol 209:3742-3757 (gallop studied from 7 m/s up)

findings.title: Forelimb swing fold is anatomically impossible: the humerus is parked near horizontal and the elbow folds to ~31-45 deg, and in the race the hoof lifts into the belly
findings.observed: Race RF at g~0.75-0.97: the humerus sits on the ARM_RANGE floor (-76 deg, -78 deg in world with pitch: nearly horizontal behind the point of shoulder, so the elbow is hoisted towards shoulder height). Meanwhile the forearm swings forward to +65 deg and the elbow interior angle closes to 36-45 deg (minimum 31 deg on LF). The humerus only protracts afterwards (g 0.0-0.19, -79 -> 0 deg), so the forearm reaches forward before the elbow comes forward. Earlier, at g~0.69, the cannon flips to -139 deg from vertical and the RF toe peaks at 0.95 m, level with the elbow (0.945 m) and 10-17 cm above the belly line there (girth bottom ~0.79 m), so the hoof passes inside the barrel (sheet 05-race g=5/8 and 6/8: the near forefoot disappears into the chest/belly). Slow gallop: elbow minimum 39-48 deg, fore toe up to 0.72 m.
findings.expected: In a real gallop swing the humerus protracts with the forearm: the elbow is drawn forward and down under the shoulder while the carpus and fetlock fold. The elbow is a hinge that cannot close to ~35 deg (the forearm would lie along the humerus; the olecranon blocks it). Its working range in locomotion is roughly 90-150 deg, with the tightest fold in the early swing. In Muybridge's gallop plates the folded forefoot stays below the belly line, roughly at the opposite knee to elbow height, tucked behind the forearm, never inside the trunk silhouette.
findings.evidence: index.html:1394 (ARM_RANGE [-76 deg, 2 deg]); index.html:1426-1432 (clamp, then forearm/cannon re-solve); index.html:214 (race fore lift 0.44, flex 125 deg); index.html:1370-1371 (swing lift/flex humps); measurements.json race RF k=22 toe y 0.952 vs elbow 0.945, k=24-31 humerus -75..-78 deg, elbow 36-99 deg; sheet 05-race g=5/8, 6/8, 7/8; 04-gallop g=0/8, 7/8

fixOptions.label: Tighten limits, lower lift
fixOptions.approach: Raise the ARM_RANGE floor to ~-60 deg and add an elbow minimum (~75 deg interior) that hands the excess fold to the carpus and pastern curl. Reduce race fore lift (0.44 -> ~0.30) and gallop lift so the toe stays under the belly.
fixOptions.risk: With a less-folded upper arm, the hoof may drag or swing forward too early in the swing. flexPeak/flexEnd may need retiming.

fixOptions.label: Scripted humerus, IK below
fixOptions.approach: In the swing, drive the humerus angle by a curve (from about -55 deg at lift-off to ~0 deg at full reach, protracting through mid-swing) and solve only forearm and cannon (knee) for the hoof target. This mirrors real proximal-first protraction.
fixOptions.risk: Must match the stance IK pose at lift-off and touchdown (C1) to avoid pops. It changes the look of every gait's swing.

fixOptions.label: Belly clearance constraint
fixOptions.approach: Clamp the swing fetlock/toe target below the TRUNK loft's bottom at its x (minus a margin, accounting for z), letting the carpus fold more instead.
fixOptions.risk: Treats the symptom only. The elbow angle stays wrong unless combined with option 1 or 2.

references: Muybridge E (1899) Animals in Motion - galloping horse plates (e.g. 'Annie G.', 'Sallie Gardner')
Back W, Clayton HM (eds) Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed. (2013) - forelimb joint ranges in swing

findings.title: Vertical bounce scales the wrong way with speed: the canter and slow gallop are too flat and the race bounces the most
findings.observed: Peak-to-peak spine (approx. COM) height: canter 7.0 cm (withers 8.3), gallop 8.0 cm (withers 11.7, croup 0.5), race 10.0 cm (withers 12.6, croup 3.0). Each is a single cosine. In the canter, the cosine's peak vertical acceleration is only 3.8 m/s^2 (0.035 m amplitude at T 0.6 s), so the body floats instead of falling during the 72 ms suspension.
findings.expected: Pfau et al. 2006: COM dorsoventral displacement falls with speed, from 185 mm (170-200) at 7 m/s to 83 mm (75-91) at 17 m/s. Dunbar et al. 2008, canter: withers vertical displacement 18 +/- 5 cm, ear 23 +/- 5 cm. In any aerial phase the trunk follows a ballistic arc (-9.81 m/s^2).
findings.evidence: index.html:1559 (canter spine.position amplitude 0.035); index.html:1476 (gallop 0.04); index.html:1508 (race 0.05); measurements.json withers/croup/spine y ranges

fixOptions.label: Retune amplitudes
fixOptions.approach: Spine height amplitude ~0.08-0.09 m (canter), ~0.09 m (gallop at 7-9 m/s), ~0.04 m (race), with withers/croup motion following from the corrected pitch (see the trunk-pitch finding).
fixOptions.risk: At the top of the bounce the stance legs may hit the IK reach limit (l1+l2). xc and lift may need small changes.

fixOptions.label: Ballistic flight + stance dip
fixOptions.approach: Build height from the footfall table: a parabola with -g during the aerial phase (height set by the flight time) and a smooth spring-mass dip across the stance. The bounce then scales automatically when lags or duty change.
fixOptions.risk: Must stay periodic and C1 for loop seams and the 0.6 s gait blend.
