findings.title: Canter rocking is about half the real range in trunk pitch, pelvis pitch, head pitch and head height
findings.observed: Canter: croup-to-withers pitch 5.7 deg (thorax segment 3.6-3.7 deg; chest counter-rotates -1.5 deg x gather). Pelvis (buttock->croup) pitch 10.7 deg. Head-in-space pitch 4.4 deg. Poll vertical 11.9 cm, withers 8.3 cm. The rocking-horse motion described in the comment is barely visible on sheet 03-canter (back line g=0/8 vs g=4/8).
findings.expected: Dunbar et al. 2008, overground canter: trunk pitch 8 +/- 1 deg, head pitch 10 +/- 4 deg, neck pitch 8 +/- 3 deg, ear vertical 23 +/- 5 cm, withers vertical 18 +/- 5 cm. Egenvall, Engstrom & Bystrom 2023: pelvic pitch ROM in canter 15-16 deg, thoracolumbar flexion-extension ROM 9 deg.
findings.evidence: index.html:1559-1567 (BODY.canter: spine.rotation.z 2.5 deg, chest -1.5 deg, hips 3 deg, head -4 deg, height 0.035); measurements.json canter pitch -1.67..4.08 deg, poll y 1.783-1.902; sheet 03-canter

fixOptions.label: Scale the canter curves
fixOptions.approach: spine.rotation.z ~4 deg, remove most of the chest counter-rotation, hips gather ~4-5 deg (pelvis ~15 deg in space), head amplitude ~5 deg, height amplitude ~0.08 m.
fixOptions.risk: The hind IK may run short at the forehand-up / haunch-down extreme. Check the trailing-hind touchdown pose.

fixOptions.label: Shared stance-driven body model
fixOptions.approach: Use the same stance-driven pitch/height generator proposed for the gallop, with canter-specific gains, so the canter, gallop and race share one consistent mechanism.
fixOptions.risk: Broader refactor of BODY.*.

findings.title: Canter head/neck nod is about 0.3-0.4 of a stride out of phase: highest during the leading-fore stance instead of lowest
findings.observed: BODY.canter neck1 = -1 deg + 4 deg cos(2pi(g-0.62)). Measured neck-to-thorax angle peaks (most raised) at g=0.62, in the middle of the leading-fore stance (LF 0.5-0.88), and is lowest at g=0.12 during the trailing-hind stance. The poll is highest at g=0.75 and lowest at g=0.25. The model's gallop and race do the opposite (neck lowest at ~0.37-0.39, right at lead-fore touchdown; highest ~0.87-0.89 in flight), so the canter is the inconsistent one.
findings.expected: Dunbar et al. 2008, canter: neck lowering (protraction: neck ventroflexion, head dorsiflexion) begins late in the airborne phase and continues into the forelimb support. Raising (retraction) begins at touchdown of the leading forelimb and continues into the early airborne phase. So the neck is lowest at about leading-fore touchdown (g~0.5 here) and highest early in the suspension (g~0.9-0.95).
findings.evidence: index.html:1565-1567 (canter neck1 phase 0.62, neck2 0.68, head 0.72); compare index.html:1514-1516 (race 0.86/0.92/0.97) and 1483-1485 (gallop 0.88/0.94/0.97); measurements.json canter neck-to-thorax first harmonic peak at g=0.62

fixOptions.label: Shift the phases
fixOptions.approach: Move canter neck1/neck2/head phases by about +0.3 (to ~0.92/0.98/0.02), keeping head-on-neck counter-rotation as now.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Re-check the rein/jockey hand follow (it tracks the bit) and the mane wave phases.

fixOptions.label: Key nod to lead-fore touchdown
fixOptions.approach: Compute the neck/head phase for every leaded gait from G.land of the lead fore (neck minimum at its touchdown), so retimed footfalls or a per-horse 'head-pump' style stay consistent.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Needs a right-lead check (land table mirrored).

references: Dunbar DC, Macpherson JM, Simmons RW, Zarcades A (2008) J Exp Biol 211:3889-3907, doi:10.1242/jeb.020578

findings.title: Racing gallop gives fore and hind legs the same duty and stance length; hinds should stay down longer and sweep further
findings.observed: One G.duty for all legs: race duty 0.2 for fore and hind, stance 86 ms, stance length 1.44 m each (7.22 m x 0.2). Gallop 0.35 / canter 0.38 for all four legs likewise.
findings.expected: Witte et al. 2006 at 17 m/s: fore duty 0.18 (77 ms, stance length 1.31 m) vs hind 0.22 (94 ms, 1.58 m). At 9 m/s: fore 0.27 (131 ms, 1.18 m) vs hind 0.29 (143 ms, 1.28 m). Hind stance is consistently longer and covers more ground.
findings.evidence: index.html:1345 (const DUTY = G.duty used for every leg); index.html:258 (stanceLen = stride*duty); index.html:212, 202

fixOptions.label: Per-limb duty
fixOptions.approach: Allow G.fore.duty / G.hind.duty (falling back to G.duty) in footPath and makeGait, e.g. race 0.185 / 0.225, gallop (at 9 m/s) 0.27 / 0.29.
fixOptions.risk: The longer hind stance (~1.6 m) can exceed hind reach. hockPush and xc may need retuning, and the aerial fraction changes, so retime land at the same time.

references: Witte TH, Hirst CV, Wilson AM (2006) J Exp Biol 209:4389-4397, doi:10.1242/jeb.02518

findings.title: Hooves land flat, pinned at the toe, instead of heel-first at the gallop
findings.observed: The hoof's sole tilt reaches 0.0 deg one or two samples before touchdown in canter, gallop and race (race RF: 8.2, 3.9, 0.7, 0.0 deg toe-up over k=5-8). The stance starts with the toe pinned and the hoof flat, so there is no heel-first contact.
findings.expected: Ratzlaff et al. 1993 (galloping horses): hoof angle at heel contact is 6-7 deg from horizontal (toe up, heel strikes first), rising to 28-31 deg at peak toe force during breakover.
findings.evidence: index.html:1347-1353 (toe pinned from u=0, tip=0 at touchdown); index.html:1368 and 1372 (breakover fade and curl reach 0 before landing); measurements.json sole-tilt series

fixOptions.label: Heel-first landing window
fixOptions.approach: For the first ~10-15% of stance, pin the heel rather than the toe, with the hoof 6-7 deg toe-up, and let it rotate flat onto the toe-pinned stance. In the swing, keep ~6 deg toe-up at touchdown.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the stance pin point, so a small heel-to-toe slip must be avoided by rotating about the heel until flat. Barely visible at racing speed.

references: Ratzlaff MH et al. (1993) Acta Anat 146:200-204

findings.title: Canter diagonal pair lands and lifts at exactly the same instant
findings.observed: LH and RF both land at 0.27 and lift at 0.65 (toe-contact strings for LH and RF in measurements.json are identical). The middle beat is perfectly fused, a mechanical-looking 3-beat.
findings.expected: In ridden and unridden canters the diagonal pair is usually slightly dissociated, with the hind generally landing first, and the dissociation grows as the canter lengthens towards a 4-beat gallop. Burns & Clayton 1997 report large diagonal dissociation (0.164 s) in collected canter pirouettes, and Clayton's canter work treats diagonal dissociation as a measured, variable trait. Exact working-canter values vary by horse.
findings.evidence: index.html:229 (canter land LH 0.27, RF 0.27); measurements.json gaits.canter toe-contact strings LH == RF

fixOptions.label: Small dissociation knob
fixOptions.approach: Land LH ~0.25 and RF ~0.29 (about 15-25 ms apart). Expose 'diagonal dissociation' as a per-horse running-style parameter, since it is a real individual trait.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The canter body curves are keyed to footfalls only loosely.

findings.title: The withers are hidden under the root of the neck, so the topline has no withers peak
findings.observed: The trunk's withers row peaks at x=0.46, y=1.625 (measurements: withers (0.457, 1.622)). NECK row 0 starts its crest at (0.40, 1.63), 6 cm BEHIND that peak, and row 1 is at (0.60, 1.73) after stretch(). At the withers' own x the neck's dorsal surface is about 1.66 m, 3.6 cm above the withers. The outline therefore climbs without a break from the back's low point (x=0, 1.53) through the withers and up the crest (~27 deg) to the poll: there is no local maximum and no change of angle at the withers. The first mane blade (t=0.35, x≈0.47) also sits right over the peak, on the chest bone. Seen in 00-stand 'stand: right side', 'stand: left side' and '3/4 front-right': the back runs straight into the neck with no withers bump. The race tiles (05, g=0..7/8) read the same.
findings.expected: In a Thoroughbred the withers are high and distinct: a long ridge of thoracic spinous processes (about T3-T9, highest near T5-T6) that forms the topline's local high point. The crest of the neck starts IN FRONT of the withers, because the funicular nuchal ligament inserts on those spines. At normal head carriage the base of the crest lies at or slightly below the withers, often with a small dip, and the mane stops at the front of the withers. Behind the peak the back drops about 9 cm to its lowest point (Matsuura et al. 2024, mostly TBs: 159.9 cm at the withers, 150.8 cm at the lowest point of the back). The model gets the 9 cm dip right but hides the peak in front of it.
findings.evidence: index.html:504 (TRUNK row x=0.46, top 1.625); index.html:512-513 (NECK rows 0-1: crest (0.4,1.63), (0.58,1.72)); index.html:664-671 (stretch() lengthens the neck forward but leaves row 0 behind the withers); index.html:1069 and 1079 (mane starts at t=0.35, mounted on the chest bone over the withers); 00-stand tiles 'stand: right side', 'stand: left side', 'stand: 3/4 front-right'; measurements.json static.standing.withers

fixOptions.label: Move the neck root forward and down
fixOptions.approach: Move NECK row 0's crest to about (0.52-0.55, 1.58-1.60) and pull row 1's crest down slightly, so the crest meets the trunk about 6-10 cm in front of the withers peak and below it. Start the mane at t≈0.55 so it ends at the front of the withers. Mane positions are derived from NECK_ROWS and follow automatically.
fixOptions.risk: The neck skin weights use fixed points nA/nB (index.html:720) and the neck1 bone sits at (0.56,1.44); check for creasing when the neck pumps in race and graze. The front edge of the saddle cloth (C1=0.45) is right at the withers.

fixOptions.label: Withers ridge parameter on the trunk loft
fixOptions.approach: Add a per-row 'ridge' value that raises only the top vertex ([0,1] of PROF.trunk) for rows x≈0.28-0.56, e.g. +3 to +5 cm at x=0.40-0.46, to form a narrow fin. Expose it as look.conf.withers (high/'shark-fin' TB withers vs flat or mutton withers) for roster variety.
fixOptions.risk: rowAt() for the saddle, rug and jockey reads TRUNK tops. A raised ridge must reach rowAt too, or the saddle cloth will cut into the fin.

fixOptions.label: Lower the neck carriage at rest
fixOptions.approach: Keep the tables but rotate neck1 down a few degrees in the stand pose so the crest drops below the withers. This only works for poses with the head down.
fixOptions.risk: Changes head carriage everywhere and misses the root cause: the crest still starts behind the withers.

references: Matsuura A, Torii S, Ojima Y, Kiku Y. 3D imaging and body measurement of riding horses using four scanners simultaneously. J Equine Sci 2024;35(1) (PMC10955269): height at withers 159.9, height at back 150.8, height at croup 159.2 cm

Thomas HS. The Horse Conformation Handbook. Storey 2005 (withers and the neck tie-in)

findings.title: The hindquarters are narrow and peaked over the croup, with no points of hip and a single central rump cone
findings.observed: The whole trunk uses one 12-point profile (PROF.trunk) with a ridge vertex at [0.52,0.9] and widest at mid-height. Over the quarters the upper width factor is only 0.78-0.82. At the level of the points of hip (y≈1.45, ~15 cm below the croup top) the croup is only 36 cm wide (half-width 0.178-0.180 at x=-0.40..-0.52). It is 23 cm wide 5 cm below the top and 41-42 cm at y=1.40. The widest part of the quarters is the thigh mesh at y≈1.1-1.2 (≈53 cm). The rear row (x=-0.86, half-width 0.11) closes in one central cone at (-0.91,1.27), so there is a single 'point of buttock' on the midline. In 00 'stand: rear' and 05 'race rear g=3/4' the quarters read as a pear/lemon with a roof ridge where the tail comes out, pointed again at the crotch. 00 'stand: top' shows a smooth cigar outline with no hip angles. The loin has the same A-frame top: about 22 cm wide 3.5 cm below the spine at x=-0.36.
findings.expected: Seen from behind, a Thoroughbred's hindquarters are 'square'. The points of hip (tuber coxae) are the widest point near the top: 52.2 cm across the tubera coxae vs 50.6 cm between the hip joints (Matsuura et al. 2024, mainly TBs at 160 cm; ≈53 and ≈52 cm scaled to 163 cm). The croup top is broad and rounded by the gluteus medius over the loin and croup. The tubera coxae show as angular bumps at the front corners of the croup. The two points of buttock (tuber ischii) are separate rounded prominences on either side of a midline groove under the tail.
findings.evidence: index.html:396 (PROF.trunk single profile, ridge vertex [0.52,0.9]); index.html:492-496 (TRUNK rows x=-0.86..-0.36, wu 0.7-0.82); index.html:701-704 (trunkRings); 00-stand 'stand: rear', 'stand: top', 'stand: 3/4 rear-left'; 05-race 'race rear g=3/4' and 'g=1/4'; 04-gallop rear tiles

fixOptions.label: Square up the profile over the quarters
fixOptions.approach: For rows x=-0.68..-0.36, raise wu to ~0.95-1.05 and flatten the top: per row, blend the ridge vertex from [0.52,0.9] toward [0.75,0.93], so the croup is ≈50-53 cm across at y≈1.45 and gently rounded on top. Expose the multiplier as look.conf.hips (croup width) for roster variety.
fixOptions.risk: drape() for the saddle cloth and rug and shell() for the tack call ringAt with PROF.trunk. If the profile becomes per-row, those calls need the same per-row profile or the rug will clip.

fixOptions.label: Add point-of-hip and twin-buttock masses on the hips bone
fixOptions.approach: Add small jittered icosahedra/wedges skinned 100% to `hips`: tuber coxae at ≈(-0.42, 1.46, ±0.25), plus two rounded buttock masses at ≈(-0.86, 1.25, ±0.09) with a shallow groove between them. This is the same pattern as the triceps blob at index.html:1169, merged into the rigid set.
fixOptions.risk: Rigid lumps may show seams when the hips bone flexes 11 deg in race. Keep them small or blend them into the skinned trunk.

fixOptions.label: Per-region cross-sections
fixOptions.approach: Replace the single trunk profile with a 16-18 point profile and per-row shape weights: withers keel, oval barrel, square croup with tuber-coxae corners, and twin buttocks with a perineal groove.
fixOptions.risk: Touches the saddle, rug and jockey code that reads the profile, and costs extra faces under the dapple subdivide (16x).

references: Matsuura A et al. J Equine Sci 2024;35(1) (PMC10955269): hip width (between hip joints) 50.6 cm, waist width (between tubera coxae) 52.2 cm, mostly Thoroughbreds
Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (tuber coxae, tuber sacrale, tuber ischii surface anatomy)
Stashak TS. Adams' Lameness in Horses, 5th ed. Lippincott 2002, ch.1 Conformation (hindquarters viewed from behind)

findings.title: The shoulder blades stand vertical and stick out of the sides of the withers like epaulettes
findings.observed: FORE.sc and FORE.sh share the leg plane z=0.165, so the scapula is vertical in the frontal plane: its top is as far from the midline as the shoulder joint. The scapula mesh (half-width 0.022-0.04) ends at y≈1.52-1.54 and spans z≈0.14-0.19 there, but the trunk at x≈0.47-0.5 is only 0.07-0.10 half-width at y=1.50-1.55. The blade's upper end therefore stands 5-10 cm proud of the side of the withers, and is still ~6 cm proud at mid-blade (y≈1.42). In 00 'stand: front' and 'stand: chest + forelegs, front' two vertical slabs flank the base of the neck with a gap between them and the withers. '3/4 front-right' shows a ridge above the shoulder.
findings.expected: The scapula lies flat on the narrow, laterally compressed cranial thorax, held only by muscle (the thoracic-limb synsarcosis: serratus ventralis, rhomboideus, trapezius). Its dorsal border and scapular cartilage sit against the withers beside the spinous processes, just a few cm from the midline. The blade slopes outward and down to the shoulder joint. From the front the two shoulders form a V that converges at the withers, and the withers are the narrowest part of the forehand's top.
findings.evidence: index.html:536 (FORE: z 0.165 shared by sc [0.5,1.5] and sh [0.72,1.22]); index.html:1152 and 1156 (P() puts every fore joint at the same z); index.html:1164 (scapula limb sections); index.html:504-505 (TRUNK rows 0.46/0.58 with wu 0.42/0.5); 00-stand 'stand: front', 'stand: chest + forelegs, front', 'stand: 3/4 front-right'

fixOptions.label: Tilt only the scapula mesh inward
fixOptions.approach: Build the scapula limb from V(sc.x, sc.y, side*0.07-0.08) to sh at z=0.165, leaving the joints and IK unchanged, so the blade leans on the chest wall with its top beside the withers. Thin its half-width slightly at the top.
fixOptions.risk: The blade rotates about the scap joint (still at z=0.165) during scapSwing and the abduction in solveLeg (index.html:1407), so its top moves a little off the wall at extreme swing. Small.

fixOptions.label: Lean the whole forelimb plane at rest
fixOptions.approach: Put the scap joint at z≈0.08 with a rest rotation.x so the limb plane leans out to the shoulder joint and the limb below hangs vertical. Update solveLeg/abductedZ to use the tilted plane.
fixOptions.risk: Rework of the abduction and foot-tracking math (index.html:1333-1336, 1404-1408); risk of foot slide in the stance phase.

fixOptions.label: Bury the blade by widening the upper chest
fixOptions.approach: Raise wu for rows x=0.46-0.58 so the trunk covers the blade's top edge.
fixOptions.risk: Makes the withers broad and mutton-like: wrong for a TB and fights the withers finding.

Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (scapular cartilage beside the withers)
Stashak TS. Adams' Lameness in Horses, 5th ed. 2002, ch.1 (front view of the forehand)

findings.title: The forehand is about 25% too wide across the arms, with the forelegs set far apart under a box-like chest
findings.observed: Measured across the outer surfaces of the arms the chest is 2×(0.165 + 0.078 humerus half-width) ≈ 48.6 cm, with the triceps blob reaching z≈0.22. The trunk alone is 46 cm wide at the point-of-shoulder level (x=0.5, y=1.2, half-width 0.231). The fore hooves stand at ±0.165: 33 cm centre-to-centre and 22 cm clear between hooves 11 cm wide. The inner gap between the knees is ≈23 cm. In 00 'stand: front' and 'stand: chest + forelegs, front' the chest reads as a broad box with the forearms dropping from its outer corners.
findings.expected: Chest width measured across the outer sides of the humeri is 38.6 cm in TB riding horses 160 cm at the withers (Matsuura et al. 2024), ≈39-40 cm scaled to 163 cm. Thoroughbreds are comparatively narrow-chested. Standing square, the front feet are roughly one hoof-width apart (≈10-14 cm clear), with the limb under the point of shoulder (Stashak plumb-line rule).

fixOptions.label: Narrow the forehand
fixOptions.approach: FORE.z 0.165 → ~0.14; humerus/triceps half-widths −15-20%; TRUNK half-widths for x=0.46-0.76 −10% (0.24→0.215, 0.235→0.21, 0.215→0.19). Target an outer arm width of ≈40-42 cm.

fixOptions.label: Chest-width customization
fixOptions.approach: Add look.conf.chest that scales FORE.z, the front TRUNK rows' half-widths and the arm/triceps widths together. Narrow-chested TBs and broad sprinters can then differ, which is the per-horse customization the owner asked for.

findings.title: The belly line stays flat and then drops between the hind legs, leaving a box-corner ledge over the gaskin
findings.observed: TRUNK bottom heights run 0.83 (x 0.18) → 0.855 (0) → 0.89 (-0.19) → 0.875 (-0.36) → 0.845 (-0.52) → 0.85 (-0.68). The belly line rises only 6 cm, then drops again behind the stifle (stifle at 0.92) to 7 cm below it. The trunk's rear-bottom corner at about (-0.68, 0.85) sticks ~10 cm out behind the back edge of the gaskin (tibia rear surface ≈(-0.58, 0.83)). The 'hamstring' mass is part of the static trunk, not the leg. In 00 'stand: hindleg, right side' a flat dark underside runs back to the quarters and the gaskin comes out from under a box corner. 'stand: right side' shows a straight underline from the elbow to the hind leg with no flank tuck or stifle fold. In race tiles 05 g=2/8 and g=4/8 the rump stays a fixed ball while the leg swings under it.
findings.expected: In a fit racing Thoroughbred the underline rises from the girth (deepest just behind the elbow) back to the flank and the stifle fold, giving the 'tucked-up', long underline. There is no belly wall behind the stifle. The rear outline runs from the point of buttock down the hamstrings (semitendinosus and biceps femoris, the 'second thigh') smoothly into the gaskin and the point of hock, and those muscles move with the limb.
findings.evidence: index.html:493-499 (TRUNK bottoms for x=-0.8..0.18); index.html:537 (HIND stifle [-0.36,0.92]); index.html:1186-1187 (femur/tibia sections: the back bulge of the thigh is the only hamstring); 00-stand 'stand: hindleg, right side', 'stand: right side'; 05-race 'g=2/8', 'g=4/8'

fixOptions.label: Raise the rear underline
fixOptions.approach: Raise TRUNK bottoms behind the girth so the belly rises into the flank and the trunk ends above the stifle: x=-0.19 → ~0.92, -0.36 → ~0.96, -0.52 → ~1.00, -0.68 → ~1.03, -0.8 → ~1.08. Let the thigh and gaskin meshes form the lower rear outline. A conf.tuck parameter (fit vs grass-belly) could drive this.
fixOptions.risk: A gap may open between the thigh and the trunk at full protraction or retraction. The rug hem (74% of barrel depth) and saddle cloth follow rowAt automatically.

fixOptions.label: Hamstring / second-thigh mass on the leg
fixOptions.approach: Add a rigid hamstring loft on L.fem (or split between L.fem and L.tib) running from near the point of buttock to the back of the gaskin, so the rear outline follows the leg in every gait.
fixOptions.risk: Must not poke through the static rump at extreme extension (race hockPush 40 deg).

fixOptions.label: Skin the flank to the femur
fixOptions.approach: Give the lower rear trunk vertices (x<-0.3, y<1.05) partial weights to the femur bones, so the flank and stifle fold stretch as the stifle advances.
fixOptions.risk: The femur nodes are rigid bones outside body.skeleton today; needs a skeleton rework (mergeRigid) and per-side weights.

Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (hamstring group: semitendinosus, biceps femoris, semimembranosus)
Matsuura A et al. J Equine Sci 2024;35(1) (PMC10955269): chest depth 76.6 cm measured just behind the elbow, the deepest part of the trunk

findings.title: The elbow, upper forearm and stifle sink into the barrel during the stride
findings.observed: From measurements.json, mapped into the chest frame and the hip frame and compared with the trunk loft's surface. In race the elbow joint rises to y=1.17 and moves back to x=0.29-0.42 (rest 0.48, 0.96), ending 7.4 cm INSIDE the chest wall. Worst depth per gait: walk 4.0, trot 6.9, canter 6.9, gallop 7.4, race 7.4 cm. The humerus reaches 76-80 deg from vertical, pinned at ARM_RANGE -76 deg. The shoulder joint moves through x=0.62-0.80 while the breast surface stays fixed, so the point of shoulder vanishes into the breast and pulls back out. The stifle reaches (-0.22, 1.11) and sits 3.8-6.3 cm inside the belly wall in every gait (femur up to FEMUR_RANGE 76 deg). In 05 'race g=0/8' and 03 'canter g=1/8' the near fore comes out of the middle of the barrel with no elbow visible. In 05 'g=5/8' the near hind thigh merges into the belly.
findings.expected: The elbow and triceps ride along the outside of the chest wall: the olecranon stays visible behind the top of the forearm all through the stride, and the limb moves mostly fore and aft against the ribs. The pectorals and brachiocephalicus stretch over the moving point of shoulder. At the stifle, the flank fold lifts with the stifle instead of the stifle passing into the abdomen.
findings.evidence: index.html:1394-1395 (ARM_RANGE [-76,2] deg, FEMUR_RANGE [0,76] deg); index.html:1426-1432 and 1442-1448 (swing clamps); index.html:1167-1171 (humerus, triceps, forearm meshes at z 0.165); index.html:499-506 (TRUNK half-widths 0.24-0.28 around the elbow); measurements.json gaits.*.samples (elbow/stifle vs withers+neck1 and buttock+hip frames); 05-race 'g=0/8', 'g=5/8'; 03-canter 'g=1/8'

fixOptions.label: Tighten the humerus and femur swing ranges
fixOptions.approach: Raise ARM_RANGE's lower bound from -76 deg to about -55/-60 deg and FEMUR_RANGE's upper bound from 76 deg to about 60 deg, so the swing fold comes from the knee and hock instead of driving the elbow and stifle up into the trunk.
fixOptions.risk: Changes swing reach and hoof clearance in race and gallop; may need retuned flex/lift values. Re-check that the IK still reaches the touchdown spots.

fixOptions.label: Narrow the trunk under the arm
fixOptions.approach: Shrink the trunk half-width around the elbow (x 0.3-0.55, y 0.9-1.15) to ribcage width, so the humerus/triceps meshes, which move with the limb, form the outer surface there.
fixOptions.risk: A visible seam or gap between the arm and the chest at rest unless the triceps mesh is enlarged to cover it.

fixOptions.label: Skin the body wall to the limbs
fixOptions.approach: Give trunk vertices near the elbow partial weights to the humerus, and flank vertices partial weights to the femur, so the skin moves with the limb.
fixOptions.risk: Requires the limb nodes to be bones of the body skeleton (mergeRigid restructuring); possible candy-wrapper artefacts.

references: Dyce KM, Sack WO, Wensing CJG. Textbook of Veterinary Anatomy, 4th ed. 2010 (thoracic limb attachment, extrinsic muscles)
Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (stifle fold / plica lateralis)
Muybridge E. Animals in Motion (1899; Dover reprint 1957), gallop plates: elbow and triceps visible against the chest through the stride

findings.title: The pelvis landmarks are misplaced: the croup peak sits right over the hip joint, the hip joint is far ahead of the point of buttock, and the femur is short
findings.observed: The croup's highest point (TRUNK x=-0.52, 1.605; measurements croup (-0.525, 1.593)) lies directly over the hip joint (HIND.hip (-0.52, 1.18)). The hip joint is 34 cm (horizontal) ahead of the point of buttock (-0.858, 1.27). The femur from hip to stifle is only 0.305 m long, 31.6 deg from vertical, with the stifle 16 cm ahead of the hip. The back from the withers peak to the croup peak is 0.98 m, while the croup peak to the point of buttock is only 0.33 m horizontally. There is no point of hip anywhere on the surface, so the croup reads short and the back long.
findings.expected: The croup's highest point (tuber sacrale) and the points of hip lie roughly 25-30 cm cranial to the hip joint. The acetabulum sits about 55-60% of the pelvis length back from the point of hip and below the line to the point of buttock. Pelvis length from point of hip to point of buttock is 52.9 ± 1.5 cm in sound Thoroughbreds (Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020), which puts the hip joint ≈20 cm ahead of the point of buttock. The TB femur is ≈0.40-0.45 m long, and the same study reports a thigh length of 49.8 cm and a back length of 93.1 cm.
findings.evidence: index.html:495 (TRUNK croup row x=-0.52); index.html:537 (HIND hip [-0.52,1.18], st [-0.36,0.92]); index.html:1186 (femur loft hip→stifle); measurements.json static.standing croup/buttock/RH.hip/RH.stifle; 00-stand 'stand: right side', 'stand: hindleg, right side'

fixOptions.label: Re-seat the hip joint and croup
fixOptions.approach: Move HIND.hip back and up to about (-0.64, 1.25) with the stifle and hock unchanged (femur ≈0.43 m). Move the croup's highest row forward to x≈-0.42 and let the tops from -0.52 to -0.8 slope ~20-25 deg to the tail head. Move the hips bone pivot to the lumbosacral joint (see the lumbosacral finding).
fixOptions.risk: Hind gait parameters (xc, FEMUR_RANGE, hockPush, flick) were tuned to the current geometry. IK reach and stance clearance must be revalidated against measurements in all gaits.

fixOptions.label: Fix the surface landmarks only
fixOptions.approach: Keep the hip joint, but move the croup peak forward (TRUNK rows) and add a visible point of hip at ≈(-0.42, 1.46). The quarters then read right from the side without touching the IK.
fixOptions.risk: The femur stays short and the hip joint stays too far forward. A purely cosmetic fix.

references: Mostafa MB, Elemmawy YM. Relationships between morphometric measurements and musculoskeletal disorders in jumping Thoroughbred horses. J Equine Sci 2020 (PMC7316700): pelvis 52.9 ± 1.5 cm, thigh 49.8 cm, back 93.1 cm in sound horses
Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (pelvis: tuber coxae, tuber sacrale, acetabulum, tuber ischii)
Anderson TM, McIlwraith CW. Longitudinal development of equine conformation from weanling to age 3 years in the Thoroughbred. Equine Vet J 2004;36:563-570

findings.title: The hind legs hang as straight vertical posts 35 cm apart, with no stifles-out, hocks-in shape from behind
findings.observed: Standing, the RH hip, stifle, hock and toe are at z = 0.169 / 0.170 / 0.173 / 0.176: one vertical column at ±0.175, giving hind hooves 35 cm apart centre-to-centre. The thigh mesh is even shifted 2 cm INWARD toward the midline. The stifles are therefore no wider than the hocks or feet, and the widest part of the lower quarters is just the thigh mesh at y≈1.15. In 00 'stand: rear' and the rear tiles of 01-05 the hind legs read as two parallel posts at the corners of the rump, with a wide gap down to the ground.
findings.expected: Seen from behind, the limb runs out from the hip joint to the stifle and gaskin (the widest part of the lower quarters), then in toward the hocks. A plumb line dropped from the point of buttock, roughly 10-12 cm from the midline, should bisect the hock, cannon, fetlock and hoof (Stashak). That puts the hind feet about 20-26 cm apart centre-to-centre.
findings.evidence: index.html:537 (HIND.z 0.175 for every hind joint); index.html:1185-1186 (inward offset −0.02 on the thigh mesh); measurements.json static.standing RH/LH z; 00-stand 'stand: rear'; 01-walk to 05-race 'rear' tiles

fixOptions.label: Mesh-only frontal shaping
fixOptions.approach: Keep the IK plane, but offset the femur/stifle mesh OUTWARD (+0.03 to +0.05) instead of inward and taper the gaskin mesh inward toward the hock. Optionally narrow HIND.z to ~0.15 so the feet land about 30 cm apart.
fixOptions.risk: The visual leg no longer matches the planar IK line exactly. Small at these offsets.

fixOptions.label: Lean the hind limb plane inward
fixOptions.approach: Give each hind limb a rest abduction (femur rotation.x) so it leans from the hip at ±0.18 to feet at about ±0.12. Update abductedZ and the stance-tracking math to use the leaned plane.
fixOptions.risk: IK foot-tracking changes; risk of hooves crossing in the gallop if the lateral spacing gets too small.

references: Stashak TS. Adams' Lameness in Horses, 5th ed. 2002, ch.1 Conformation (rear view: plumb line from the point of buttock bisects hock, cannon, fetlock and foot)
Ross MW, Dyson SJ. Diagnosis and Management of Lameness in the Horse, 2nd ed. Elsevier 2011, ch. Conformation and lameness
Matsuura A et al. J Equine Sci 2024 (PMC10955269): width between the hip joints 50.6 cm

findings.title: The lumbosacral bend happens mid-loin, 22 cm in front of the croup
findings.observed: The `hips` bone pivots at (-0.3, 1.42), 22 cm in front of the croup peak (x=-0.52). The trunk skin weights blend hips → spine across x=-0.55..-0.12 (a 43 cm band), so the race lumbosacral flexion (hips 2 deg + 9 deg·gather, about -7 to +11 deg) and the gallop/canter flexion bend the whole loin gradually instead of hinging at the front of the croup. The tack weights copy the same keys.
findings.expected: Flexion and extension of the caudal back are concentrated at the lumbosacral junction, which lies on the line between the two points of hip under the front of the croup. Faber et al. (2001) found the largest flexion-extension at canter between L5 and S3 (up to 8.6 deg per joint, 15.8 deg maximum overall), with the lumbar segments in front comparatively stiff.
findings.evidence: index.html:677 (hips bone V(-0.3,1.42)); index.html:711 and 740 (skin keys [-0.55→hips], [-0.12→spine]); index.html:1480, 1512, 1563 (hips.rotation.z in gallop/race/canter); 05-race g=4/8-6/8

fixOptions.label: Move the pivot and tighten the weights
fixOptions.approach: Put `hips` at the LS joint, ≈V(-0.42, 1.45) (or wherever the croup peak moves to), and change the skin keys to about [-0.50→hips], [-0.32→spine] in both index.html:711 and the tack copy at 740.
fixOptions.risk: A sharper crease at the LS when race flexes 11 deg. The hind limbs (children of hips) shift slightly in their arcs; recheck stance foot slip.

fixOptions.label: Add a lumbar bone
fixOptions.approach: Insert a lumbar bone between spine and hips that takes ~25% of the flexion, with the LS taking ~75%, so the loin curves slightly while most of the bend stays at the croup.
fixOptions.risk: Adds a bone to the body skeleton, its weights, and blending in pose(); every BODY.* needs a value.

references: Faber M, Johnston C, Schamhardt HC, van Weeren PR, Roepstorff L, Barneveld A. Three-dimensional kinematics of the equine spine during canter. Equine Vet J Suppl 2001;(33):145-149
Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (lumbosacral junction under the line between the tubera coxae)

findings.title: From the front the breast is a flat-bottomed box, with no pectoral masses or inverted V between the forelegs
findings.observed: The chest floor between the forearms (rows x=0.46-0.58) is a flat keel about 22 cm wide at y≈0.90-0.94. The profile's single bottom vertex gives no midline groove, and the forearm tops attach at the keel's outer corners. In 00 'stand: chest + forelegs, front' and 'stand: front' the breast reads as one slab with a level underside between the legs.
findings.expected: The descending and transverse pectorals form two rounded masses with a shallow central groove. Between the forearms they meet the chest floor in an inverted V roughly at elbow height, and the forearms emerge from the sides of the pectoral mass. In a lean TB the V is narrow.
findings.evidence: index.html:396 (PROF.trunk bottom [0.52,-0.88],[0,-1]); index.html:504-508 (front TRUNK rows, wd 0.86-0.92); 00-stand 'stand: chest + forelegs, front', 'stand: front'

fixOptions.label: Pectoral blobs plus a midline groove
fixOptions.approach: Add two flattened icosahedra on the chest bone at ≈(0.66, 1.0, ±0.07), merged like the triceps blob, and pull the front rows' bottom-centre vertex up 2-3 cm to make the groove and V.
fixOptions.risk: Must not intersect the forearm tops when the leg protracts. Minor.

fixOptions.label: Dedicated breast loft
fixOptions.approach: Give rows x≥0.58 their own bottom profile (two lobes with a central notch) as part of a per-region trunk profile.
fixOptions.risk: Shared with the per-row profile work in the croup finding.

references: Budras KD, Sack WO, Röck S. Anatomy of the Horse, 5th ed. 2009 (pectoral muscles, surface anatomy of the breast)
Thomas HS. The Horse Conformation Handbook. Storey 2005 (front view: chest and 'inverted V' between the forelegs)

findings.title: Trot head nod is inverted: poll and withers are highest at diagonal mid-stance and lowest at lift-off/suspension
findings.observed: measurements.json, trot: LF+RH are planted from g=0 to 0.44. The poll peaks at 1.867 m at g=0.16-0.19, which is 36-43% of that stance. It bottoms at 1.797 m at g=0.41-0.44, which is 92-99% of stance, i.e. at lift-off and into the suspension. The withers follow the same timing (max g=0.156, min g=0.406). The amplitudes are fine (head range 70 mm, withers 48 mm); only the phase is wrong, by exactly half a step. Sheet 02-trot: the head is high at g=1/8-2/8 while the diagonal pair carries the weight, and low at g=3/8 as the pair leaves the ground.
findings.expected: Rhodin et al. 2022 (head, withers and pelvis timing across gaits and breeds), at trot: head minima at 39-46% of forelimb stance and maxima at 92-97%; withers minima at 39-42% and maxima at 91-98%. Head, withers and croup rise and fall together twice per stride. Head range 60-78 mm, withers 47-92 mm. The trunk is a spring-mass system: lowest at mid-stance, highest in suspension. This is the head nod vets read for lameness.
findings.evidence: index.html:1572 BODY.trot spine.position 0.022*cyc(g,2,0.32) (peaks at g=0.16/0.66); neck1/neck2/head ride on it with cyc phases 0.36/0.40/0.42 (lines 1577-1579; current file, BODY.trot 1570-1590). measurements.json gaits.trot samples (poll/withers y vs LF/RH toe contact). 02-trot tiles g=1/8, 2/8 (high) vs 3/8 (low).

fixOptions.label: Re-phase the trot bob
fixOptions.approach: Change cyc(g,2,0.32) to about cyc(g,2,0.86) in spine.position (minimum near 42% of stance). Shift the neck1/neck2/head, spine.rotation, hips and chest phases by the same ~0.27 of a stride.
fixOptions.risk: The trunk/withers lens shares this term, so coordinate. The legs will be most compressed at mid-stance, which is correct, but re-check the IK reach margins.

fixOptions.label: Derive the bob from the stance legs
fixOptions.approach: Compute trunk height from the stance fraction s of the loaded leg pair (lowest at s~0.45, highest in suspension) instead of a hand-phased cosine, so the bob follows `land`/`duty` whenever a gait is retuned.
fixOptions.risk: New coupling between leg timing and body motion. The loop must stay seamless, and blending between gaits needs testing.

fixOptions.label: Add an automated phase check
fixOptions.approach: Extend the measurement script so it asserts the poll/withers minima fall within Rhodin's % of forelimb stance for walk and trot, and fails on regressions.
fixOptions.risk: None at runtime. Only guards against future drift.

references: Rhodin M, Smit IH, Persson-Sjodin E, et al. (2022) Timing of vertical head, withers and pelvis movements relative to the footfalls in different equine gaits and breeds. Animals (Basel). PMC9657284
Buchner HHF, Savelberg HHCM, Schamhardt HC, Barneveld A (1996) Head and trunk movement adaptations in horses with experimentally induced fore- or hindlimb lameness. Equine Vet J 28:71-76

findings.title: Eyes float 1-3.6 cm outside the skull; the head narrows at eye level and has no orbit rim or brow
findings.observed: The eye is an octahedron centred at head-space (0.225, 0.02, +/-0.106) with a half-depth of 0.013, so it spans z 0.093-0.119. From the HEAD rows and PROF.head, the head surface at that spot is only z = 0.080-0.086. The whole eye therefore sits 1.0-3.6 cm out from the cheek. In 00-stand 'stand: head, front' the eyes are dark diamonds sticking out past the head outline like pins. The cross-section is also inverted: the head is widest (22.3 cm) at x=0.15, y=-0.02, on the cheek 4 cm below the eye. At eye height it is 16.6 cm wide and the flat forehead is about 12 cm wide, so the section is a 'roof' that narrows upward. The eye is a 6 x 3.8 cm diamond facing straight sideways, with no lid or brow ridge above it.
findings.expected: The equine eye sits in a complete bony orbit closed behind by the supraorbital (zygomatic) process of the frontal bone. The skull is widest across the orbits and zygomatic arches; the forehead is broad and flat between the eyes, with a prominent brow ridge and the supraorbital fossa above each eye. The large globe (~4-5 cm) bulges only slightly past the orbit rim, and the lid opening is almond-shaped, facing laterally and somewhat forward.
findings.evidence: index.html:984-986 (OctahedronGeometry(0.024) scale(1.25,0.8,0.55) translate(0.225,0.02,s*0.106)); HEAD rows 536-545; head ring wUp=w*0.78 / wDown=w*0.7 at 971; PROF.head (~398). Tiles 00-stand 'stand: head, front' and 'stand: head, right side'. Computed surface half-widths: 0.083 at (0.225, 0.02); max full width 0.223 at x=0.15, y=-0.019.

fixOptions.label: Seat the eye and add a brow
fixOptions.approach: Move the eye in to z~0.08-0.085 so it sits half-sunk in the cheek. Add a small coat-coloured wedge above and behind it as the supraorbital rim.
fixOptions.risk: The hood eye holes (hole() around EYE) and the blinker cups use EYE/z 0.13, so check they still line up.

fixOptions.label: Give the head an orbital width
fixOptions.approach: For rows x 0.1-0.3, raise the upper width factor (wUp ~0.95 instead of 0.78) and move the profile's widest point to u~0.5-0.6 (eye height). This gives a broad flat forehead with the eye set into it, and the face narrows below.
fixOptions.risk: Face markings, hood, bridle and bit read rowAt/ringX and follow automatically, but need a visual pass. The front silhouette changes noticeably.

fixOptions.label: Almond eye with a lid
fixOptions.approach: Replace the octahedron with a 6-8-vertex almond (longer than tall), add an upper-lid lip in coat colour, and angle it ~15-20 deg forward of straight lateral.
fixOptions.risk: Negligible polygon cost. The hood and blinker fit should be re-checked.

references: Budras KD, Sack WO, Roeck S. Anatomy of the Horse (Schluetersche), head/skull plates: orbit, supraorbital process, zygomatic arch
Koenig HE, Liebich H-G. Veterinary Anatomy of Domestic Animals: skull of the horse (orbit, facial crest)
Evans KE, McGreevy PD (2006) Conformation of the equine skull: a morphometric study. Anat Histol Embryol 35:221-227 (zygomatic width as a primary head measure)

findings.title: Walk head nod moves in phase with the withers; a real head is ~25% of a stride out of phase (lowest at fore mid-stance, highest in fore double support)
findings.observed: The poll bottoms at 1.721 m at g=0.31 and 0.81. That is only 10% into the LF/RF stance (LF lands 0.25, RF lifts 0.34), i.e. during forelimb double support. The poll peaks at 1.837 m at g=0.06 and 0.56, about 52% of fore stance, during hind double support. The withers' minimum and maximum fall on the same samples (0.313 / 0.063), so head and withers move in phase. The amplitudes are right (head range 116 mm, withers 34 mm, head pitch 11 deg, nose-down when low). The code comment states the intent: 'lowest just after each fore touchdown'.
findings.expected: Rhodin et al. 2022, walk: head minima at 46-48% of forelimb stance and maxima at 86-88% (reached in dual hind and dual fore support respectively); withers minima at 4.6-13% and maxima at 42-48%. The withers are about 25% of a stride out of phase with the head; head range 79-117 mm, withers 27-36 mm. Loscher et al. 2016: head and withers phase shift 25.0 +/- 2.5% of the stride, with the head highest during forelimb double support (it unloads the forelimbs during the costly double-support collision). Dunbar et al. 2008: at walk, head pitch is in phase with head height (the model already does this).
findings.evidence: index.html:1619-1641 BODY.walk: spine.position cyc(g,2,0.1) at 1622; neck1 -7 deg + 2.4 deg*cyc(g,2,0.1) at 1628; neck2 cyc(g,2,0.16); head cyc(g,2,0.22) at 1630. measurements.json gaits.walk (poll and withers min both at sample 10). 01-walk tiles g=2/8 and 6/8 (head lowest, right after the fore touchdowns).

fixOptions.label: Shift and enlarge the neck nod
fixOptions.approach: Move the neck1/neck2/head phases by ~+0.23 of a stride (cyc(g,2,0.1) to ~cyc(g,2,0.55), 0.16 to ~0.6, 0.22 to ~0.66). Raise the neck1 amplitude from 2.4 deg to ~4-5 deg so the neck nod outweighs the 3.4 cm in-phase trunk bob. Keep the withers bob as it is, since it is already correct.
fixOptions.risk: The jockey hand slide and rein running mean react to head motion. Re-check the walk-to-trot blend.

fixOptions.label: Head-mass pendulum
fixOptions.approach: Drive neck pitch from the trunk's vertical acceleration with a lag (neck = -k * a_trunk(g - d)). The antiphase then emerges in walk, and the same mechanism is reusable for the bounding gaits.
fixOptions.risk: Needs tuning per gait, and the result can overshoot at high speeds.

fixOptions.label: Validate against Rhodin percentages
fixOptions.approach: Add walk head and withers phase targets (% of fore stance) to the measurement script.
fixOptions.risk: None.

references: Rhodin M, Smit IH, Persson-Sjodin E, et al. (2022) Animals (Basel), PMC9657284
Loscher DM, Meyer F, Kracht K, Nyakatura JA (2016) Timing of head movements is consistent with energy minimization in walking ungulates. Proc R Soc B 283:20161908
Dunbar DC, Macpherson JM, Simmons RW, Zarcades A (2008) Stabilization and mobility of the head, neck and trunk in horses during overground locomotion. J Exp Biol 211:3889-3907

findings.title: Canter head bob is half the real amplitude, and neck flexion timing runs ~0.4 of a stride early
findings.observed: measurements.json, canter: the poll travels only 11.9 cm (1.783-1.902 m) and head pitch in space is 4.4 deg. Relative to the trunk, the neck is lowest at g~0.06 (start of the trailing-hind stance) and highest at g~0.59, just after the leading fore lands (LF lands 0.5). Head-vs-neck is most extended at g=0.25 and most flexed at 0.75. The poll is highest at g=0.75, in mid leading-fore stance. On sheet 03-canter the head height barely changes across g=0/8-7/8.
findings.expected: Dunbar et al. 2008, canter: the ear travels 23 +/- 5 cm vertically; head pitch 10 +/- 4 deg, neck pitch 8 +/- 3 deg; mean head-to-neck angle 109 deg. Neck-to-trunk lowering (protraction) starts late in the airborne phase and continues into forelimb support. Neck raising (retraction) starts at touchdown of the leading forelimb and continues into the early airborne phase. The head counter-rotates on the neck (nose up relative to the neck while the neck drops). So the neck should be lowest on the trunk around leading-fore touchdown (g~0.5) and highest early in the suspension (g~0.9-0.95).
findings.evidence: index.html:1593-1617 BODY.canter: spine.position 0.035*cyc(g,1,0.82) at 1596; neck1 -1 deg + 4 deg*cyc(g,1,0.62) at 1602; neck2 2.5 deg*cyc(g,1,0.68); head -4 deg*cyc(g,1,0.72) at 1604. measurements.json gaits.canter. 03-canter tiles g=0/8-7/8.

fixOptions.label: Re-phase and enlarge the canter neck
fixOptions.approach: Move the neck1/neck2 phases to ~0.95 (lowest at ~0.45-0.5) and the head term to ~cyc(g,1,0.97) so it is most extended near g~0.47. Raise the neck1 amplitude to ~6-7 deg and the head to ~5 deg so the ear travels ~20 cm.
fixOptions.risk: The gallop<->canter blend and the jockey's rein hand slide (capped at 6 cm) must be re-checked.

fixOptions.label: Couple neck pitch to trunk pitch
fixOptions.approach: neck_rel = -alpha * trunkPitch(g - delta), shared by the canter, gallop and race bodies, so all bounding gaits keep a consistent head-neck pendulum.
fixOptions.risk: The gallop and race already look plausible (their neck-to-trunk minimum is near LF touchdown and maximum in suspension), so this must not regress them.

fixOptions.label: Expose per-gait nod gain
fixOptions.approach: Let run.neckPump default above 1 for canter (e.g., 1.8), so the existing pump scaling raises the amplitude without retuning the phases.
fixOptions.risk: Fixes amplitude only, not timing.

references: Dunbar DC, Macpherson JM, Simmons RW, Zarcades A (2008) J Exp Biol 211:3889-3907 (PMC2768006)
Back W, Clayton HM (eds) Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013: canter and gallop chapters

findings.title: Ears are base-widest diamond pyramids with no forward-facing opening, and they can only tilt, never swivel
findings.observed: Each ear is ConeGeometry(0.036, 0.15, 4) scaled (0.62, 1, 1): a 4-sided pyramid that is widest at its base (7.2 cm side-to-side, 4.5 cm front-to-back) and tapers straight to the tip. A diamond corner, i.e. a ridge, faces forward instead of a concave opening. It is one colour apart from a dark tip, with no pale inner hair. Animation (idleEars and the gallop/race/canter ear lines) only changes rotation.z (tilt back) and rotation.x (lean sideways). There is no rotation about the ear's own long axis, and a symmetric pyramid would not show one anyway. In 00-stand 'head, front' they read as cat or fox ears; in 'head, right side' and the race front tiles they read as thin spikes. earSet and earTilt (new) move the base and the rest tilt only.
findings.expected: The equine pinna (auricular cartilage) is lanceolate. Its base is narrow and partly tube-shaped on the scutiform cartilage, it is widest around its middle third, and it ends in a pointed tip, often slightly turned in. It is rolled into a funnel whose opening (concha) faces forward and outward when the horse is attentive, lined with pale hair. Each ear moves independently: forward, adduct, flatten back, rotate the opening sideways or backward, and droop (EquiFACS ear action descriptors EAD101-EAD105). Rotating the opening is the main expressive ear motion; a racehorse often has one ear forward and one back toward the jockey.
findings.evidence: index.html:990-1001 (earGeo; mount rotation including earSet/earTilt); idleEars 1664-1670 (rotation.z/x only); BODY.gallop/race/canter ear loops (around 1524, 1555, 1605); hood ear covers sized to the cone (~1056). Tiles 00 'stand: head, front', 'stand: head, right side'; 05-race front tiles.

fixOptions.label: Leaf-shaped ear with a concha
fixOptions.approach: Loft the ear from 3-4 small rings: a narrow base, widest at ~40% of its length, then the tip. Push the forward face's centre vertices inward to form a shallow concave opening and paint it pale.
fixOptions.risk: The hood ear covers (cones at ~1056) must be rebuilt to fit. Slightly more vertices.

fixOptions.label: Add an ear-swivel joint
fixOptions.approach: Insert an Object3D between the mount and the mesh that rotates about the ear's long axis. Drive it independently per ear in idleEars (forward to sideways to back), and let earsAtSpeed rotate plus flatten rather than only tilt.
fixOptions.risk: Only reads once the ear has a visible opening (option 1 or 3).

fixOptions.label: Cheap shape fix
fixOptions.approach: Use a 3-sided cone with one flat face forward, pinch the base ring to ~60% so it is no longer widest at the bottom, and paint the forward face pale.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Still no real concavity.

references: Wathan J, Burrows AM, Waller BM, McComb K (2015) EquiFACS: The Equine Facial Action Coding System. PLoS ONE 10(8):e0131738
Budras KD, Sack WO, Roeck S. Anatomy of the Horse: auricular and scutiform cartilages, auricular muscles

findings.title: Nostrils are small, nearly flush and almost invisible, and never flare at speed
findings.observed: Each nostril is an octahedron of radius 0.018, scaled (1.4, 0.9, 0.5), at head-space (0.6, -0.012, +/-0.066). The surface there is z~0.068, so only ~0.7 cm pokes out, showing a ~3.9 x 2.5 cm near-black diamond that faces straight sideways. It sits on the muzzle, which is already painted dark (pal.muzzle for x>0.55), so there is little contrast. Nostrils cannot be seen in 00 'stand: head, front' and are barely visible in 'stand: head, right side' or the 06 jockey close-ups. Their size is identical at rest and at 16.8 m/s.
findings.expected: Nostrils are large, comma-shaped openings framed by the alar cartilages, with the alar fold (false nostril) above. They sit on the front corners of the muzzle facing forward and outward, so they are clearly visible from the front. Horses are obligate nasal breathers. At canter and gallop they breathe once per stride (Bramble & Carrier 1983), and the nostrils open wide and round (EquiFACS AD38 nostril dilator); flared nostrils are a hallmark of race photographs.
findings.evidence: index.html:987-989 (nostril); muzzle colour 979; breath puffs already coupled 1:1 with the stride (breath code ~2960: 'At a canter or gallop horses breathe once per stride'). Tiles 00 'stand: head, front' and 'stand: head, right side'; 06 'jockey close'.

fixOptions.label: Bigger, forward-facing nostrils
fixOptions.approach: Radius ~0.024, scale ~(1.6, 1.1, 0.5), rotated ~25-30 deg toward forward-lateral and seated on the surface. Use a colour clearly darker than pal.muzzle, or a pinkish inner tone for white muzzles.
fixOptions.risk: Keep clear of the noseband (x 0.425-0.455) and the bit ring (x 0.555).

fixOptions.label: Flare with breathing
fixOptions.approach: Store rig.nostrils and scale them each frame: 1.0 at rest, ~1.4-1.6 at canter/gallop/race, pulsing once per stride in phase with the existing breath puff.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The gait blend needs the scale interpolated too.

fixOptions.label: Real opening in the muzzle loft
fixOptions.approach: Split the muzzle rings and inset vertices to cut a true opening that can deepen when dilated.
fixOptions.risk: Face-marking paint (snip, bald) and gear rowAt need adjusting.

references: Bramble DM, Carrier DR (1983) Running and breathing in mammals. Science 219:251-256
Wathan J et al. (2015) EquiFACS. PLoS ONE 10(8):e0131738 (AD38 nostril dilator)
Budras KD, Sack WO, Roeck S. Anatomy of the Horse: nasal vestibule, alar cartilages, nasal diverticulum

findings.title: Neck crest starts behind the withers summit and rides over it, so the topline shows no withers
findings.observed: NECK row 0 puts the crest at (0.40, 1.63), behind the withers summit (TRUNK x=0.46, top 1.625; measured withers (0.457, 1.622)). Between rows 0 and 1, the neck topline is ~1.66 m at x=0.457 and ~1.69 m at x=0.52, against the trunk's 1.625 and 1.59 m. The visible topline therefore rises straight from the back into the crest with no withers bump (00-stand 'left side', 'right side'). The new conf.withers (+1 adds a 3 cm bump centred on x=0.46) still leaves the summit under the neck. A measuring stick on the visible withers would read ~166 cm, not 163.
findings.expected: In a Thoroughbred the withers (spinous processes of ~T3-T9) are a high, well-defined summit behind the neck. The crest ties in in front of and slightly below the summit, often with a slight dip where the mane ends. Height is measured at the withers summit, so the summit must be the topline's high point at the shoulder.
findings.evidence: index.html:527-534 (NECK row 0 [0.4, 1.63, 0.74, 1.14, 0.19]); TRUNK rows 516-521; withers control at 734 (withersH*0.03*bell(x, 0.46, 0.14)); measurements.json static.standing.withers. Tiles 00 'stand: left side' and 'stand: right side'.

fixOptions.label: Tie the neck in lower and further forward
fixOptions.approach: Move NECK row 0's crest to about [0.5, 1.58] and adjust row 1, so the crest starts ~4-6 cm below and in front of the withers summit and the trunk's withers stand clear.
fixOptions.risk: Mane blade placement follows NECK_ROWS (fine). Check the neck-root seam while neck1 swings, and the saddle cloth/jockey reach.

fixOptions.label: Taller, longer withers in the trunk
fixOptions.approach: Raise the TRUNK top for rows x 0.34-0.58 by 3-5 cm, with the peak at ~0.42-0.46 and a longer slope back. Keep 163 cm by rescaling.
fixOptions.risk: The saddle, cloth and jockey read rowAt, and the height scale factor shifts.

fixOptions.label: Let conf.withers lower the neck root
fixOptions.approach: Have withersH also drop NECK row 0's crest y by ~0.03*withersH, so 'high, prominent withers' actually shows.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Budras KD, Sack WO, Roeck S. Anatomy of the Horse: thoracic spinous processes and the nuchal ligament
Thomas HS (2005) The Horse Conformation Handbook. Storey: withers and neck tie-in

findings.title: At racing speed the head is more flexed than at rest, and the 'very low (Oguri Cap)' carriage tucks the nose further
findings.observed: Race: the face line (poll to muzzle) runs from -47 to -59 deg (mean -53), against -44.6 deg standing. The head-to-neck angle stays at 114-123 deg (standing 120) while the neck drops to nearly level (withers-to-poll 2-15 deg). In 05-race g=3/8 and 7/8 the head looks tucked under an arched crest rather than stretched forward. The new applyRun maps headCarriage -1 ('very low, neck stretched (Oguri Cap)') to neck1 -10 deg, neck2 -4 deg and head +7 deg. In space the face ends up ~7 deg further nose-down (mean ~-60 deg): lowered and curled, not stretched. The code comment says 'a lowered neck pokes the nose out'.
findings.expected: Galloping racehorses extend at the poll as speed rises. The head is pushed forward with the face well in front of the vertical and the head-to-neck angle opens; jockeys 'give the horse its head', because poll flexion raises upper-airway impedance during hard exercise (Petsche et al. 1995). Low-headed runners such as Oguri Cap carry the poll low with the neck and head stretched out and the face nearer horizontal, not tucked.
findings.evidence: index.html:1542-1568 BODY.race (neck1 -9 deg + 6 deg*cyc at 1551, neck2 -4 deg, head 6 deg - 7 deg*cyc at 1553); applyRun 1709-1720 (neck1 +hc*10 deg at 1713, head -hc*7 deg at 1715); RUN_CONTROLS headCarriage at 3278. measurements.json gaits.race (face angle and head-neck angle per sample). Tiles 05-race g=3/8 and 7/8; 06 jockey close.

fixOptions.label: Open the race poll
fixOptions.approach: Raise BODY.race's head.rotation.z offset by ~+8 to 12 deg, so the face averages about -40 to -45 deg and the head-to-neck angle opens to ~125-135 deg at full stretch.
fixOptions.risk: The bit, reins and jockey hand slide re-centre via the running mean. Check the hood and bridle visually.

fixOptions.label: Make low carriage poke the nose out
fixOptions.approach: In applyRun, make the head counter-rotation larger than the neck drop (e.g., head -hc*20 deg against neck1+neck2 +hc*14 deg), and optionally add a separate 'pollFlexion' run control.
fixOptions.risk: Large values can overextend the head and stretch the throat skin near the poll, so check the neck/head seam.

fixOptions.label: Author carriage as target angles
fixOptions.approach: Describe each gait and style as world-space targets (neck inclination, face angle) and solve the bone rotations from them, so a preset like Oguri Cap reads as 'neck ~0 deg, face ~-35 deg'.
fixOptions.risk: Refactors BODY.* and bodyMean. Every gait must be re-verified.

references: Petsche VM, Derksen FJ, Berney CE, Robinson NE (1995) Effect of head position on upper airway function in exercising horses. Equine Vet J 27:18-22
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, gallop plates (extended head and neck)
Back W, Clayton HM (eds) Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013: the gallop

findings.title: Forelock sticks out from the forehead like a horn and lifts further at speed
findings.observed: The forelock cones are mounted at the poll with rotation HEAD_TILT-72 deg, so they point 24 deg below horizontal while the face slopes at -42 to -45 deg. The lock leaves the forehead at ~18 deg, and its 0.17 m tip ends 5 cm above the face (head-space tip (0.16, 0.14) vs a forehead top of 0.085). In the race, the mane wave (amp 0.5, +0.115 to 0.305 rad) lifts it further, to 25-36 deg off the forehead. It shows as a black spike in front of the ears in 00 'stand: head, right side' and across the gait sheets.
findings.expected: The forelock (cirrus capitis) grows from the poll and falls under gravity flat on the forehead toward the eyes. In a headwind it streams back over the poll; it does not project forward and up.
findings.evidence: index.html:1087-1099 (mount.rotation.set(..., HEAD_TILT - 72*DEG); rig.mane.push amp 0.5); mane wave loops in BODY.race/gallop. Tile 00 'stand: head, right side'.

fixOptions.label: Lay it on the face
fixOptions.approach: Rest rotation of about HEAD_TILT-88 deg with a small lift, so it follows the forehead line, and cut its mane-wave amplitude to ~0.15.
fixOptions.risk: Low. It may clip the browband or blinkers (gear) and needs a check.

fixOptions.label: Gravity-hung forelock
fixOptions.approach: Each frame, set its angle from the head's world pitch so it always hangs down the face, plus a small backward stream at speed.
fixOptions.risk: Adds per-frame work, which is small.

fixOptions.label: Fanned shards on the surface
fixOptions.approach: Build 3-4 thin shards that follow the HEADP top line from x=0 to ~0.2.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Budras KD, Sack WO, Roeck S. Anatomy of the Horse: hair tracts of the head (forelock)

findings.title: Muzzle ends in one tapered cap: no upper lip, chin, chin groove or mouth line
findings.observed: The head loft ends at a point cap (0.66, -0.035) after a last ring 10.5 cm deep (x=0.63), so the upper lip and the chin merge into one blunt cone. The lower line runs smoothly from jowl to cap with no chin bulge and no chin (curb) groove. The bit ring floats at x=0.555 on an unbroken cheek with no mouth commissure behind it. The 00 'stand: head, right side' tile shows a beak-like tip.
findings.expected: In profile the muzzle is squarish. A full, mobile upper lip sits in front; the lower lip and rounded chin sit below and slightly behind it, with a shallow chin groove behind the chin. The corners of the mouth lie ~8-10 cm behind the lips, where the bit rests in the gap between the incisors and cheek teeth.
findings.evidence: index.html:543-544 (HEAD rows 0.58 and 0.63); loft caps at 972; bit ring at ~1072 (x=0.555). Tile 00 'stand: head, right side'.

fixOptions.label: Square the muzzle
fixOptions.approach: Replace the point cap with 1-2 extra rows (x ~0.645 and 0.66) that keep the depth and give a flat front. Add a chin bulge (bottom +1 cm at x~0.6) and a slight groove at x~0.55.
fixOptions.risk: Face markings (snip, bald) and gear rowAt follow the rows. Check the muzzle colour band.

fixOptions.label: Paint a mouth line
fixOptions.approach: Add a dark strip from the commissure (x~0.55, y~-0.05) to the lips.
fixOptions.risk: Cosmetic only.

fixOptions.label: Separate lower jaw
fixOptions.approach: Split the chin/lower lip into its own mesh on a jaw pivot, enabling an open mouth at speed or chewing while grazing.
fixOptions.risk: Needs a bridle and bit re-fit.

references: Budras KD, Sack WO, Roeck S. Anatomy of the Horse: lips, chin and mental region
Manfredi J, Clayton HM, Rosenstein D (2005) Radiographic study of bit position within the horse's oral cavity. Equine Comp Exerc Physiol 2:195-201

findings.title: conf.head scales the whole head uniformly, ears and eyes included; no separate head length/width, jowl, eye, nostril, neck-set or throatlatch controls
findings.observed: head.scale.setScalar(headSize) scales head length, depth and width, plus the eyes, nostrils, ears and forelock mounted on the head, all together. A 'big head' therefore also gets bigger ears, mixing ear size into head size. The neck has only length (0.85-1.2) and crest (0.6-1.6). There is no high- or low-set neck, no throatlatch thickness, and no long-narrow vs short-broad head. Profile moves only the top line.
findings.expected: Famous horses differ on independent head and neck traits: long narrow vs short broad heads (Evans & McGreevy found breed differences in skull length, width and mandibular depth indices), heavy vs clean jowls, large eyes, large nostrils, high-set vs low-set necks, thick vs clean throatlatches. Ear size varies independently of head size, which matters for the requested small- and big-ear quirks.
findings.evidence: index.html:675-684 (conf parsing); head.scale.setScalar(headSize) (around 772); CONF_CONTROLS 3259-3276.

fixOptions.label: Split the head scale
fixOptions.approach: Add conf.headLength (scale head-space x), headWidth (scale z), jowl (multiply the bottom depth of rows x<=0.25), eyeSize and nostrilSize. Divide the ear/eye/nostril mount scales by headSize so their own controls stay independent.
fixOptions.risk: Gear (hood, bridle, blinkers) uses rowAt and ringX and mostly follows, but blinker and bit offsets are absolute and need scaling.

fixOptions.label: Neck set-on control
fixOptions.approach: Add conf.neckSet to shift NECK rows 0-1 (crest and throat y, +/-4 cm) and the neck1 bone, giving high-set vs low-set necks.
fixOptions.risk: Watch the chest/neck seam and the saddle cloth front edge.

fixOptions.label: Throatlatch control
fixOptions.approach: Add conf.throatlatch to scale the depth of NECK rows 4-5 and the bottom of HEAD rows x<=0.05.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

references: Evans KE, McGreevy PD (2006) Conformation of the equine skull: a morphometric study. Anat Histol Embryol 35:221-227
Thomas HS (2005) The Horse Conformation Handbook: head, throatlatch and neck set

findings.title: In mid and late swing the humerus swings back almost to horizontal and the elbow closes to 31-58°, pushing the elbow joint 13-20 cm up into the barrel and holding the forearm up like a hackney's
findings.observed: In swing the humerus sits at -72° to -79° from vertical, i.e. only 11-18° below horizontal and pointing backward, for 6-8 of the 32 samples in the gallop and race. The elbow interior angle closes to 39-45° in the gallop, 31-38° in the race, 58° in the canter and 73° in the trot (rest 137.6°). In the trunk frame the elbow joint starts 3.8 cm below the chest's lateral lower surface at rest and ends up above it: by 13 cm in the trot, 17 cm in the canter, 18 cm in the gallop and 20 cm in the race (race RF k=0: elbow at body-frame (0.40, 1.17) against a surface at 0.97). The top of the forearm vanishes into the ribcage, and the forearm sticks out of mid-chest at 60-70° in front of vertical while the knee is still bent 65-110° (race RF k=26-31: actual knee flexion 93-110° against a planned 64-105°, because the humerus hit ARM_RANGE[0] and the fallback solve folds the knee further). The fetlock target causes this. It holds the full lift (fetlock 0.63-0.65 m) from about 25% to 55% of the swing while knee flexion fades after flexPeak, so the target sits too close to the shoulder and the bend -1 IK can only reach it by folding the elbow. Visible in tiles 04-gallop g=0/8 and 7/8, 05-race g=0/8 and 7/8, and 03-canter g=0/8 and 7/8.
findings.expected: The humerus is bound to the chest wall by the pectoral and triceps muscles, so the elbow stays tucked low against the thorax with the olecranon near the floor of the chest in every phase. It never rises into the barrel, and the humerus never lies near horizontal. The forearm is brought forward by scapular protraction and shoulder extension; the carpus (knee) does the folding. Back et al. (1995) give smooth trot curves in which the elbow keeps a moderate range (roughly 90-150°), and at the walk the elbow reaches peak flexion late in the swing (84% of stride, Hodson et al. 2000). Elbow angles below about 70° do not appear in equine kinematics, and at 31-45° the forearm flexors would pass through the triceps mass. In Muybridge's gallop plates the forearm is near vertical at peak carpal flexion, with the hoof tucked under the elbow; the carpus then opens as the forearm reaches forward. A Thoroughbred's action is long and low (a 'daisy-cutter'), not high-kneed.
findings.evidence: index.html:1394 ARM_RANGE = [-76°, +2°] (allows a near-horizontal humerus); index.html:1420-1431 (solve2 with bend -1, then the clamp fallback that re-solves the forearm and cannon); index.html:1370-1371 (swing lift plateau and flex hump); GAITS fore lift/rise/fall/flexPeak/flexEnd at index.html:204, 214, 222, 230. Measurements from my node scripts: elbow minimum per gait; humerus < -70° samples; the elbow-vs-trunk-surface check (trot +0.130, canter +0.171, gallop +0.181, race +0.200 m); race RF planned vs actual knee flexion k=26-31. Sheets: 04-gallop g=0/8 and g=7/8, 05-race g=0/8 and g=7/8, 03-canter g=0/8 and g=7/8.

fixOptions.label: Reshape the fore swing path
fixOptions.approach: Make the fetlock peak early, at or just after flexPeak (about 0.25-0.35 of the swing), placed under or behind the elbow, then let it descend and move forward as the carpus opens (start 'fall' around 0.4). Keep the shoulder-to-fetlock distance at or above about 0.75 m so the IK never has to fold the elbow, and tune lift per gait (lower overall for a Thoroughbred).
fixOptions.risk: Changes the look of every gait. Hoof clearance, the trot fore/hind overlap and the touchdown position need re-checking.

fixOptions.label: Tighten the arm limits
fixOptions.approach: Raise ARM_RANGE[0] to about -55..-60°, add an elbow-flexion floor (interior angle ≥ about 80°) and apply the humerus limit in stance as well. Let the carpus take the excess through the existing fallback at index.html:1426-1431.
fixOptions.risk: When the limits bind, the fetlock misses its planned target and the hoof path can jump. Best combined with the first option.

fixOptions.label: Joint-angle-driven swing
fixOptions.approach: Drive the fore swing by forward kinematics: scapula, shoulder, elbow, carpus and fetlock angle-vs-time curves per gait, digitised from Back et al. 1995, Hodson et al. 2000 and Muybridge. Use IK only in stance and in the last ~15% of the swing to land on the planned spot. This also makes knee action a per-horse 'running style' parameter (low daisy-cutter vs high knee).
fixOptions.risk: Needs blending at lift-off and touchdown, plus angle data for 5 gaits. Largest rewrite of solveLeg.

Hodson E, Clayton HM, Lanovaz JL. The forelimb in walking horses: 1. Kinematics and ground reaction forces. Equine Vet J 2000;32:287-294 (PMID 10952376)
Muybridge E. Animals in Motion (1899; Dover 1957), gallop plates (Annie G., Sallie Gardner)
Getty R (ed). Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 5th ed., 1975: equine thoracic limb and its muscular attachment to the trunk
Clayton HM, Back W (eds). Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013

findings.title: The forelimb runs out of reach. The elbow snaps fully straight (164-178°) just after lift-off, and before touchdown the leg locks straight with the elbow in front of the breast
findings.observed: In the early swing of the race the fetlock target runs about 34 cm further behind the lift-off spot because the swingX flick keeps it moving at ground speed. The leg cannot reach it: the target is missed by 4-16 cm from w=0.04 to w=0.31 (race RF k=16-23). The elbow opens to 177°/172°/164° (RF k=16-18) and 178°/173°/165° (LF k=19-21). The canter LF reaches 174° at k=29. Late in the race swing (w=0.90-0.97, RF k=6-8) the target is 1.42 m forward and missed by 6-9 cm. There the humerus is pinned at the ARM_RANGE[1] limit (humerus +0.2° to +0.5°, vertical) and the leg is a straight pole. In the body frame the elbow sits at x=0.80-0.82 at y≈0.95, beside and in front of the breast (trunk front x=0.81; rest point of shoulder x=0.72), 2 cm ahead of the moved shoulder joint. Tile 05-race g=2/8 shows the near foreleg growing out of the base of the neck.
findings.expected: The equine elbow is a hinge whose extension is stopped by the anconeal process of the ulna engaging the olecranon fossa. Its maximum extension in life is roughly 150-160°, never 175-180°. At toe-off the elbow begins to flex at once as the limb folds. At touchdown the humerus still slopes down and back, so the elbow stays behind the point of the shoulder and under the chest; the reach comes from scapular protraction plus the extended elbow, carpus and fetlock, not from the arm swinging out in front of the breast.
findings.evidence: index.html:1369 swingX(..., P.flick ?? 0.4, P.retract ?? 0.2) (fore uses the default 0.4 flick; race has no fore.flick); index.html:1386 solve2 clamps d to l1+l2 (straight limb when out of reach); index.html:1394 ARM_RANGE[1] = +2°; index.html:1412-1417 scapula swing about scapTop (scapSwing 18° in race, index.html:214). Measurements: my re-implementation of footPath compared with the measured fetlock (race RF errors 0.041-0.162 m at k=16-23 and 0.026-0.086 m at k=6-8); elbow interior angles above 155° at race RF k=16-18, LF k=19-22 and canter LF k=29-30; most forward elbow x=0.822 at race k=11 LF. Sheet 05-race g=2/8 and 3/8.

fixOptions.label: Keep the targets reachable
fixOptions.approach: Give the forelimbs their own small flick (fore.flick about 0.1, or 0 in race), so the hoof leaves the ground and folds up rather than sliding back, and clamp the fetlock target to at most about 0.95 × (arm + forearm + cannon) from the shoulder so the limb always keeps a bend.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The fore may look like it 'picks up' sooner, which is closer to the real thing.

fixOptions.label: Hard joint limits
fixOptions.approach: In solveLeg, cap the elbow interior angle at about 155° and the humerus at about 15-20° behind vertical (instead of +2°), then solve the remaining distance with the carpus and fetlock.
fixOptions.risk: When a limit binds, the planned target is missed, so the hoof can land short of toeDown unless the stance start is moved to match (see the stance-placement finding).

fixOptions.label: Reduce reach demand at racing speed
fixOptions.approach: Let the scapula translate forward along the thorax (it has no clavicle) as well as rotate, and/or pull fore.xc and the touchdown spot back so the 1.44 m stance fits inside the limb's comfortable arc.
fixOptions.risk: Changes how the race stride reads and interacts with the hind placement (overreach).

references: Getty R (ed). Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 1975: elbow joint, extension limited by the anconeal process
König HE, Liebich HG. Veterinary Anatomy of Domestic Mammals: elbow joint as a ginglymus with locked extension
Back W et al. Equine Vet J 1995;27:31-38 (forelimb angle-time curves)
Muybridge E. Animals in Motion (gallop plates)

findings.title: The fetlock barely sinks under load: the stance drop is 1.5-2.7 cm, and at the gallop the joint never extends past its standing angle
findings.observed: Lowest fetlock height in stance vs 0.209 m standing: walk 0.194, trot 0.191, canter 0.189, gallop 0.188, race 0.182 (a drop of only 1.5/1.8/2.0/2.1/2.7 cm). Peak fetlock dorsiflexion (pastern relative to cannon) in stance: walk 44.5°, trot 42.9°, canter 44-48°, race 48-50°, and in the gallop only 34-37° against 33° standing, so the fetlock does not 'give' at all at the gallop. The pastern never passes 50° from vertical. Elbow-to-toe shortening in stance is 2.7-5.9 cm. The cause: sag (10-17°) is added to the pastern's angle in world space and peaks at the time midpoint of stance, while the cannon is still tilted 12-35° forward, so the relative joint angle cancels out. Touchdown in the race even lands with the fetlock 5° flexed (race RF k=9). In 05-race g=3/8 and 4/8 the planted fetlocks stay high with steep pasterns.
findings.expected: The fetlock is the forelimb's main spring. Back et al. (1995): 'The fetlock joint acts as an elastic spring, thereby conserving energy'. McGuigan and Wilson (2003) measured the distal leg spring shortening by 127 mm (range 106-128) at the gallop, mostly through fetlock dorsiflexion. At racing speed the pastern goes nearly horizontal and the ergot almost touches the ground (Muybridge's plates; Butcher and Ashley-Ross 2002 measured fast fetlock dorsiflexion after impact at 14 m/s). Peak extension should come near mid-stance, when the cannon is vertical. The non-lead fore carries more load than the lead (15.2 vs 12.8 N/kg peak vertical force) and should sink more.
findings.evidence: index.html:1351-1353 (load = sin²(π·sp), a = A.pastern + P.sag·load - tip, world-frame); index.html:1454 aPas = f.pastern - pitch (not relative to the cannon); GAITS fore.sag 10-17° at index.html:204, 214, 222, 230, 238; COFFIN_Y = 0.092 and PASTERN = 0.14 at index.html:487. Measurements: summary2.js stance fetlock minimum per gait; per-phase table (fetExt column) for gallop RF k=10-21 and race RF k=9-15.

fixOptions.label: Bigger, cannon-relative sag
fixOptions.approach: Define the stance pastern angle relative to the cannon (aPas = aCan + rest + sag·load) and raise fore sag to about 20° walk, 30° trot, 40° canter, 50-55° gallop and race. Peak the load when the cannon is vertical rather than at sp=0.5.
fixOptions.risk: The fetlock ball (r=0.047) can clip the ground near a horizontal pastern. Clamp the fetlock height to ≥ about 0.07 m. Body height in stance drops slightly.

fixOptions.label: Lower the coffin joint, lengthen the pastern
fixOptions.approach: Bring COFFIN_Y down to about 0.06-0.065 m (see the hoof finding) and lengthen PASTERN, so a near-horizontal pastern gives a realistic 10-12 cm fetlock drop at the gallop.
fixOptions.risk: Touches plantedFetlock, HOOF_TOE and every hoof/pastern mesh; all gaits need re-tuning.

fixOptions.label: Per-horse and per-leg compliance
fixOptions.approach: Scale sag by speed, body mass and lead/non-lead (non-lead fore about 15% more), and expose it as a customization trait (e.g. a 'soft pasterns' or 'springy' runner).
fixOptions.risk: Low. Needs sane limits so extreme horses don't hit the ground with the fetlock.
