findings.title: Fore hoof capsule is a tall, upright 'boot': dorsal wall 72.6°, level coronet (heels 10 cm tall), heel wall leaning forward, hoof-pastern axis broken forward by about 16°
findings.observed: From HOOF_SHAPE.fore and hoofGeo, the coronet ring is level at y=0.104 m, front edge at co.x+0.037, back at co.x-0.041. The sole ring runs from co.x+0.069 (toe) to co.x-0.031 (heel). So the dorsal wall rises 10.2 cm over 3.2 cm, about 72.6° to the ground. The pastern at rest is 57° (33° from vertical), so the hoof-pastern axis is broken forward by about 16°, the look of a club foot. The heel is as tall as the toe (10.2 cm) and its ground edge sits 1 cm ahead of its coronet edge, so the heel wall leans past vertical. The ground surface is 10.0 cm long by 11.2 cm wide, and the coffin joint sits 9.2 cm above the ground. In tile 00-stand 'foreleg, right side' the hoof reads as a tall block steeper than the pastern.
findings.expected: A Thoroughbred fore hoof has a dorsal wall of about 50° (around 47-55°). Mata et al. 2024 associate a DHWA of about 50° with soundness; Kane et al. 1998 measured toe and heel angles in racehorses and found larger toe-heel angle differences to be a risk factor, so the heel should roughly parallel the toe. The dorsal wall should be parallel to the pastern (straight hoof-pastern axis); Anderson and McIlwraith 2004 found pastern and hoof angles correlated. The coronet slopes down from about 6-7 cm at the toe to about 3-4 cm at the heels, and the ground surface is about 12-13 cm long and wide, wider at the ground than at the coronet in every direction.
findings.evidence: index.html:1122 HOOF_SHAPE.fore top [0.041,0.037,0.044] bot [0.057,0.043,0.056]; index.html:1123-1128 hoofGeo (top ring at co.y+0.012, level; sole ring centred at co.x+HOOF_TOE-bu); index.html:487-488 HOOF_H=0.09, HOOF_TOE=0.069; FORE.pastern 33° at index.html:536. Sheet 00-stand tile 'stand: foreleg, right side' (r2c2).

fixOptions.label: Re-author the capsule
fixOptions.approach: Tilt the coronet ring (toe edge about 6.5 cm, heel edge about 3.5 cm above the sole). Move the top ring's front edge back so the toe wall is about 50-55° and parallel to the pastern. Put the heel's ground edge behind its coronet edge, with a heel angle within about 5° of the toe. Widen and lengthen the sole ring to about 12-13 cm.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The racing plate (ring at the sole) and the pale-horn colouring follow the new rings; breakover pivots must still sit on the toe.

fixOptions.label: Lower the coffin joint
fixOptions.approach: Reduce HOOF_H to about 0.06-0.065 and lengthen PASTERN to keep the fetlock height. Update HOOF_TOE, plantedFetlock and the leg-marking heights (LEG_WHITE) accordingly.
fixOptions.risk: Every gait's fetlock path shifts by about 3 cm and needs a re-check. Leg markings move.

fixOptions.label: Parametric hoof angle
fixOptions.approach: Expose dorsal-wall angle and hoof size per horse (upright/club, flat-footed, small or big feet) and derive the rings from it, which also serves the customization goal.
fixOptions.risk: Needs limits so the hoof-pastern axis stays plausible; extra UI and data plumbing.

references: Kane AJ, Stover SM, Gardner IA, et al. Hoof size, shape, and balance as possible risk factors for catastrophic musculoskeletal injury of Thoroughbred racehorses. Am J Vet Res 1998;59:1545-1552 (PMID 9858404)
Mata F et al. Investigating associations between horse hoof conformation and presence of lameness. Animals 2024 (PMID 39335286)

findings.title: Fore stance is shifted forward: the limb lands steeply protracted and lifts off barely retracted (at the gallop it never passes vertical)
findings.observed: Cannon angle from vertical at touchdown / lift-off: walk +27.9° / -10.3°, trot +30.2° / -6..-12°, canter +31.6° / -20°, gallop +35.5° / ≈0° (RF -0.2°, LF +1.8°), race +38.6° / -25.1°. The cannon passes vertical at 56% (walk), 64% (trot), 62% (canter), 61% (race) and never in the gallop. Measured as a straight line from the top of the scapula to the toe, the limb lands at +25..+33° and lifts at only -3..-21°. Stance centres sit ahead of the standing toe (0.629) by +8 cm walk, +12 trot, +8 canter, +20 gallop and +6 race. So the forelegs work almost entirely in front of the body and never push back under it.
findings.expected: Hodson et al. (2000): at the walk the metacarpus is vertical at 28% of the stride, about 45% of the stance; the change from braking to propulsion follows at 34% of the stride. The stance is roughly balanced about the vertical, with clear retraction before lift-off. In Muybridge's trot and gallop plates the fore leaves the ground with the cannon well behind vertical, the heel up and the toe last, behind the elbow line.
findings.evidence: GAITS fore.xc at index.html:204 (gallop 0.76), 214 (race 0.62), 222 (trot 0.68), 230 (canter 0.64), 238 (walk 0.64); index.html:1347 toeDown = P.xc + STANCE_LEN/2 + HOOF_TOE. Measurements: summary.js touchdown/lift-off cannon and limb-axis angles; cannon-vertical timing script; gallop RF/LF per-phase tables (canV goes from 35.5 to 0.0 over k=10-21).

fixOptions.label: Move the stance back
fixOptions.approach: Lower fore.xc per gait so the cannon is vertical at about 45-50% of stance, e.g. gallop about 0.60-0.62, trot about 0.60, walk/canter about 0.58.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the fore/hind spacing (check overreach and the trot overlap) and the body's pitch balance.

fixOptions.label: Angle-based placement
fixOptions.approach: Specify touchdown and lift-off limb angles per gait (e.g. gallop +20° / -30°) and derive toeDown and the stance length from them and the horse's leg length, so it holds for any size.
fixOptions.risk: The stride and duty already set the stance length; the two must be reconciled or the hoof slides.

fixOptions.label: Lean the trunk over the stance
fixOptions.approach: Add a small forward chest translation over the fore stance (the thoracic sling lets the trunk move relative to the scapulae), so the limb rotates behind vertical without changing xc much.
fixOptions.risk: Interacts with the BODY.* motion and the jockey.

references: Hodson E, Clayton HM, Lanovaz JL. The forelimb in walking horses: 1. Equine Vet J 2000;32:287-294 (PMID 10952376)
Muybridge E. Animals in Motion (walk, trot and gallop plates)
Clayton HM, Back W (eds). Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013

findings.title: At the trot the departing fore hoof is still on the ground line when the same-side hind lands, so the two hooves intersect (forging)
findings.observed: Trot RF lifts off at about g=0.9 and RH lands at g=1.0. At k=30 the RF toe is only 2.4 cm off the ground and at k=31 7.3 cm, still moving backward (default fore flick 0.4, curl ramping over smoothstep(0, 0.28)). The RH toe arrives at (0.125, 0.010). The RF toe at (0.117, 0.073) is 3.3 cm from the RH hoof's coffin-toe axis at almost the same z (0.167 vs 0.176), less than the hoof half-widths (4.9-5.6 cm), so the meshes overlap. The same happens for LF/LH at k=15. Tile 02-trot g=0/8 shows the RF hoof sitting on the RH's dorsal wall; g=4/8 is the same on the left.
findings.expected: At the trot the hind tracks up into or just behind the fore print, but only after the fore has folded away. Within about 70 ms of toe-off the fore hoof is flexed up behind the knee and moving forward, so the hooves clear by many centimetres. A hind toe striking the departing fore foot is the gait fault called forging. It is a defect, not normal Thoroughbred movement.
findings.evidence: index.html:1369 (fore swing uses the default flick 0.4); index.html:1372 (curl = smoothstep(0, 0.28, s)...); index.html:221-223 trot land/duty/fore; HIND.z 0.175 vs FORE.z 0.165 at index.html:536-537. Measurements: clear.js closest approach of 0.033 m (trot RF/RH k=31, LF/LH k=15); raw positions for k=28-2. Sheet 02-trot g=0/8 (zoomed) and g=4/8.

fixOptions.label: Faster fore pick-up
fixOptions.approach: For the forelimbs, use a smaller flick (about 0.1-0.15), start the curl immediately (e.g. smoothstep(0, 0.12)) and raise the fetlock sooner (rise about 0.2), so the toe is above about 10 cm within about 15% of the swing.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Re-check that the other gaits keep a smooth lift-off.

fixOptions.label: Retime the trot
fixOptions.approach: Lift the fore slightly earlier than the diagonal hind lands (e.g. fore duty 0.37-0.38 vs hind 0.4), as in real trotting.
fixOptions.risk: Shortens the fore stance; fetlock and sag tuning may need adjusting.

fixOptions.label: Collision guard
fixOptions.approach: Add a simple same-side check that lifts or advances the fore hoof target when the hind toe comes within a hoof radius. This also protects custom stride and size combinations.
fixOptions.risk: A procedural correction can introduce small pops; it needs smoothing.

references: Stashak TS (ed). Adams' Lameness in Horses, 5th ed., 2002: gait faults (forging, overreaching)
Clayton HM, Back W (eds). Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013: trot timing and tracking up
Back W, Schamhardt HC, Hartman W, Barneveld A. Kinematic differences between the distal portions of the forelimbs and hind limbs of horses at the trot. Am J Vet Res 1995;56:1522-1528 (PMID 8585667)

findings.title: Forelimbs swing in fixed vertical planes 33 cm apart at every speed: no adduction toward the midline and no frontal-plane lean at the gallop
findings.observed: Fore toe, knee and elbow z stay at ±0.164-0.166 m in all five gaits (summary2.js), so the two fore hoof tracks are a constant 33 cm apart centre to centre and the legs stay vertical in the front views (05-race front g=0 and g=1/2, 04-gallop front, 02-trot front). On a straight, footPath returns no fz, so solveLeg always targets L.z. abductedZ only acts on curved path mode.
findings.expected: As speed rises, horses place the forefeet progressively closer to the midline, and in the gallop the limbs lean inward in the frontal plane. Parkes et al. 2020 measured whole-limb frontal-plane inclination of about 1-10° on the straight in galloping Thoroughbreds. Over a limb about 1.5 m long that moves the hoof roughly 3-25 cm toward the midline. Race front views of real horses show the forefeet landing nearly in one track.
findings.evidence: index.html:536 FORE.z = 0.165; index.html:1401 _t.set(f.fx, f.fy, f.fz ?? L.z); index.html:1333-1336 abductedZ (used only when G.path). Measurements: z ranges per gait (summary2.js). Sheets: 05-race front g=0 and g=1/2, 04-gallop front, 02-trot front.

fixOptions.label: Per-gait track width
fixOptions.approach: Add fore.track (fraction of FORE.z) per gait, e.g. walk 0.9, trot 0.6, canter/gallop 0.4, race 0.25. Feed toeZ = L.z·track through the existing abductedZ in stance and swing.
fixOptions.risk: LF and RF hooves pass closer together; check fore-fore interference in the swing and the scapula abduction look.

fixOptions.label: Lean tied to speed and lead
fixOptions.approach: Lean the limb plane (scap.rotation.x) by a speed-dependent angle, slightly more on the lead leg, as Parkes et al. found for the inside/lead fore.
fixOptions.risk: Interacts with body roll (spine.rotation.x); needs a curve-running check.

references: Parkes RSV, Pfau T, Weller R, Witte TH. The effect of curve running on distal limb kinematics in the Thoroughbred racehorse. PLoS One 2020;15:e0244105 (PMID 33373408)
Clayton HM, Back W (eds). Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013

findings.title: Breakover and lift-off: the hoof rotates only 34° before toe-off, then rolls back toward flat in the air, and in the race the fetlock stays over-extended after lift-off
findings.observed: The heel starts rising at 62% of stance and reaches only BREAKOVER = 34° at toe-off. After toe-off that tip fades over the first 30% of the swing while the curl is still ramping in, so the hoof sole turns back toward flat for 2-3 samples before flipping up: race RF hoof axis 3.5° → 7.1° → 13.3° (k=15-17), gallop LF 4.0° → 6.1° → 15.9° → 16.8° (k=24-27). In the race the fetlock is still dorsiflexed 45.6° in the air at k=16-17, more than standing (33°).
findings.expected: Toe-off is the end of a continuous roll over the toe. The fetlock and coffin joints then flex in a single cycle through the swing, with no re-extension right after lift-off (Hodson et al. 2000: one flexion cycle, fetlock peak at 81% and coffin at 84% of stride at the walk). In Muybridge's trot and gallop plates the hoof leaves the ground steeply rotated, with the sole facing backward.
findings.evidence: index.html:193-194 BREAKOVER 34°, BREAKOVER_START 0.62; index.html:1366-1370 and 1379 (lift-off tip faded by 'fade' over s=0..0.3); index.html:1372 curl ramp; index.html:1454-1455 hoof/pastern lerp. Measurements: per-phase table hoofTip and fetExt columns (race RF k=15-19, gallop LF k=24-28).

fixOptions.label: Monotonic hoof roll
fixOptions.approach: Hand the breakover tip straight into the curl (aHoof = max(tip pose, curl pose) or blend from the lift-off angle) so the hoof angle never reverses after toe-off.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

fixOptions.label: Gait-dependent breakover
fixOptions.approach: Make BREAKOVER and BREAKOVER_START per gait (e.g. larger roll, starting later in stance, at the gallop and race) and start fetlock flexion at toe-off.
fixOptions.risk: A larger roll lifts the coffin earlier; check the IK reach at lift-off (see the out-of-reach finding).

references: Hodson E, Clayton HM, Lanovaz JL. Equine Vet J 2000;32:287-294 (PMID 10952376)
Muybridge E. Animals in Motion (trot and gallop plates)
Back W et al. Am J Vet Res 1995;56:1522-1528 (PMID 8585667)

findings.title: The shoulder blades stand out beside the base of the neck as two vertical slabs in the front view
findings.observed: The scapula limb (half-width 0.022-0.04 m, front/back 0.12) is lofted parallel to the midline at z=±0.165 from scapTop (0.50, 1.50). Near the withers the trunk is narrow (TRUNK row x=0.46 has a top width factor of 0.42), so the blade's outer face, at about z 0.19-0.20, sits outside the body. The front tiles (00-stand 'front', 'chest + forelegs, front'; 05-race front) show two flat-topped vertical slabs on either side of the neck, separated from it by dark gaps, like epaulettes.
findings.expected: The cranial thorax is laterally compressed, so the scapulae converge dorsally, their cartilages lying against the withers under the trapezius and rhomboideus. In a front view the shoulders form a smooth wedge widening from the base of the neck to the point of the shoulder, with no proud plates.
findings.evidence: index.html:1164 scapula limb(sc, sh, ...) sections; index.html:536 FORE.z 0.165 (same z for sc and sh); TRUNK rows at index.html:503-506. Sheets: 00-stand r0c2 ('stand: front'), r2c1 ('chest + forelegs, front', zoomed); 05-race r2c0.

fixOptions.label: Angle the blade inward
fixOptions.approach: Give the scapula top a smaller |z| (about 0.09-0.11) than the shoulder joint (0.165), so the blade follows the ribcage, and keep the abduction pivot at the new scapTop.
fixOptions.risk: The scap joint's frame changes; check the limb-plane abduction (rotation.x) and the arm mesh fit.

fixOptions.label: Thin and sink the blade
fixOptions.approach: Reduce the blade's lateral half-width near its top and let the trunk/neck loft cover it, keeping only the shoulder's lower half as a surface feature.
fixOptions.risk: The shoulder slope may read less clearly from the side.

references: Getty R (ed). Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 1975: scapula and the thoracic sling (serratus ventralis, rhomboideus, trapezius)
König HE, Liebich HG. Veterinary Anatomy of Domestic Mammals

findings.title: The scapula pivots about its top, so at full protraction the shoulder joint rides about 9 cm up and 8 cm forward
findings.observed: L.scap.rotation.z swings the whole blade about scapTop (±18° in the race, ±7-10° in the other gaits). In the race the shoulder joint moves from its rest point (0.72, 1.222) to (0.804, 1.309) in the body frame, 8.4 cm forward and 8.7 cm up, while the top of the scapula does not move. This lifts the arm and contributes to the elbow climbing into the chest.
findings.expected: The equine scapula rotates about a centre in its upper part, roughly at the level of the spine's tuber, not about its dorsal border. As the distal end swings forward in protraction, the dorsal border moves back. The scapula also slides on the thoracic wall (no clavicle), so the shoulder joint travels mainly fore-and-aft with little rise.
findings.evidence: index.html:1411-1417 (base = scapSwing·cos(πw), shoulder rotated about r.sc); scapSwing per gait at index.html:204, 214, 222, 230, 238. Measurements: elbowsurf.js shoulder-joint body-frame position at race k=11 LF.

fixOptions.label: Move the pivot
fixOptions.approach: Rotate the scapula about a point about 1/3 of the way down from scapTop (and move the limb-plane abduction pivot with it).
fixOptions.risk: The scapula top then moves visibly under the withers; the skinned trunk does not follow it.

fixOptions.label: Rotation plus translation
fixOptions.approach: Add a small fore-aft slide of the whole scapula (a few cm, in phase with the swing) to model the thoracic sling.
fixOptions.risk: Needs the chest skin or shoulder mesh to hide the sliding blade.

references: Back W et al. Equine Vet J 1995;27:31-38 (scapular rotation in trotting horses)
Clayton HM, Back W (eds). Equine Locomotion, 2nd ed., 2013
Getty R (ed). Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 1975

findings.title: Forelimb segment proportions: the humerus is as long as the scapula, and the forearm is long
findings.observed: Joint-centre lengths at rest: scapula (scapTop to shoulder joint) 0.356 m, humerus 0.354 m, forearm (elbow to knee) 0.460 m, cannon (knee to fetlock) 0.291 m, pastern 0.140 m. The humerus-to-scapula ratio is 0.99 and the forearm is 1.30 × the humerus. The long humerus also slopes only 47.7° below horizontal, with a scapulohumeral angle of 99°, which makes for a long, flat arm that has to swing through a large arc (see the elbow findings).
findings.expected: In horses of this size the scapula is clearly the longer bone: about 0.40-0.45 m including the cartilage, against a humerus of about 0.30-0.33 m (joint-centre distance about 0.27-0.30), a ratio of about 0.7-0.75. The radius is about 0.35-0.37 m, giving an elbow-to-carpus distance of roughly 0.38-0.42 m. The cannon (0.29) and pastern (0.14) are about right.
findings.evidence: index.html:536 FORE = { sc [0.5,1.5], sh [0.72,1.22], el [0.48,0.96], kn [0.48,0.5] }; stand.js segment lengths and angles from measurements.json static.standing.

fixOptions.label: Re-proportion the arm
fixOptions.approach: Shorten the humerus to about 0.29-0.30 (move sh down and back or el forward and up) and lengthen the scapula by raising sc about 4-5 cm. Shorten the forearm about 4 cm by lowering the elbow.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the chest and arm mesh fit, the elbow-to-chest relationship and every gait's IK tuning.

fixOptions.label: Leave as stylisation, document it
fixOptions.approach: Keep the lengths but note the deliberate exaggeration, and rely on the motion fixes to hide the side effects.
fixOptions.risk: The anatomical inaccuracy stays.

references: Getty R (ed). Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 1975: equine scapula, humerus, radius dimensions
Anderson TM, McIlwraith CW. Equine Vet J 2004;36:563-570 (PMID 15581319)

findings.title: Knee (carpus): no accessory-carpal bump behind the knee, and the joint is locked exactly straight through every stance
findings.observed: Shape: the back of the knee is flush. The forearm ends at a back depth of 0.04 and the cannon starts at 0.038-0.042, so there is no caudal projection; the knee shows only as a 1.6 cm swelling at the front and a colour change (00-stand 'foreleg, right side'). Motion: carpal flexion is between -0.2° and +0.3° in every stance sample of every gait (flex is set to 0 in stance for the fore).
findings.expected: The accessory carpal bone projects about 3-4 cm behind the knee and gives the familiar bump at the back of the knee in profile. Back et al. (1995): 'The carpal joint rapidly snaps into overextension at the beginning of the stance phase to enable the forelimb to work as a propulsive strut', i.e. a few degrees past straight under load.
findings.evidence: index.html:1171-1172 forearm and cannon cross-section tables (back depth 0.04 → 0.038/0.042); index.html:1360 stance flex 0 for the fore; index.html:1418-1421. Measurements: knee flexion in stance per gait (summary.js).

fixOptions.label: Add the accessory carpal
fixOptions.approach: Add a small caudal bulge (back depth about 0.07 at t≈0 of the cannon, or a separate small block on the cannon joint) behind the knee.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Check it doesn't poke through the forearm at full carpal flexion.

fixOptions.label: Stance overextension
fixOptions.approach: Let the fore cannon go 3-5° past the forearm under load (flex = -k·load in stance).
fixOptions.risk: If overdone it reads as 'back at the knee', a conformation fault.

references: Back W et al. How the horse moves 1. Equine Vet J 1995;27:31-38 (PMID 7774544)
Getty R (ed). Sisson and Grossman's The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, 1975: carpus, accessory carpal bone

findings.title: Jockey's feet are not in the irons: no stirrup leathers, irons left run-up on the saddle, legs hang about 13 cm off the barrel
findings.observed: Measured in-page (Symboli Rudolf, Tokyo, race gait, 8 phases). The jockey's feet hang in the air: the toe and ankle stay 12.6-12.8 cm from the trunk surface all through the stride (foot at z=0.31, barrel half-width about 0.18). The knee is 30.6-31.6 cm from any horse surface (z=0.27-0.29, 26 cm above the back). The irons are the same 'run up' boxes used for a riderless saddle, at (0.36, top-0.07, z ~0.19). That puts them about 17 cm from the feet, and nothing links them, because there are no leathers. Sheet 06 'jockey close' tiles show a black boot hanging straight down beside the cloth. The '3/4 front g=0.3' tile shows splayed legs. My close-ups sm-a1/sm-a2 show the iron sitting on the cloth well away from the foot.
findings.expected: In the modern race seat the jockey stands in very short irons. The irons hang on leathers from the stirrup bars at the front of the saddle, with the ball of the foot on the iron. The inside of the knee and the lower leg rest against the saddle flap and the horse's upper barrel and shoulder, so the legs grip the horse instead of floating 10-30 cm away. Pfau et al. 2009 show this crouch over short irons, and the jockey's mass is carried through the irons.
findings.evidence: index.html:957 (reviewed snapshot :921) jockey leg points Hj/K/A/Toe = (0.18,T+0.30,±0.10)/(0.44,T+0.26,±0.28)/(0.30,T-0.12,±0.31)/(0.42,T-0.15,±0.31). index.html:868 (:832) irons placed at the run-up spot whether or not there is a rider ('with no rider the irons are run up'). No leather geometry exists. Sheet 06 tiles 'jockey close, right side g=0.1/0.6' and 'jockey, 3/4 front g=0.3'. Screenshots C:/Users/Aaron/.playwright-mcp/sm-a1.png and sm-a2.png.

fixOptions.label: Irons + leathers under the feet
fixOptions.approach: When look.jockey is set, put the iron boxes under the jockey's balls of the feet. Add two thin strap boxes from the stirrup bar (front of the saddle, x≈0.38, y≈top(0.38)) down to each iron. Parent them to jockeyPivot, or skin them to the trunk at the top and the pivot at the bottom (as addReins does).
fixOptions.risk: Low. Only tack geometry. Leathers may clip the saddle cloth slightly.

fixOptions.label: Re-pose the legs onto the horse
fixOptions.approach: Compute knee and foot z from rowAt(x) instead of constants. Put the knee at the trunk half-width + ~0.05 at the withers and the foot/iron at barrel half-width + ~0.04, so the knee and calf touch the saddle flap and shoulder. Keep the hip/knee angles.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. Calves may intersect the protruding scapula/arm shells (see the scapula finding) as the shoulder swings. Needs a clearance check over the stride.

fixOptions.label: Leg IK pinned to the irons
fixOptions.approach: Give the jockey two-bone leg IK: feet fixed in irons that hang from the saddle (skinned to the trunk), hips on the jockey pivot. The knees are solved, so the legs absorb the relative motion. This is also needed for the decoupled-rider fix in the next finding.
fixOptions.risk: Moderate. Per-frame IK cost on 18-horse fields and possible knee flips. Must stay a pure function of the phase.

references: Pfau T, Spence A, Starke S, Ferrari M, Wilson A (2009) Modern riding style improves horse racing times. Science 325:289 (PMID 19608909)
Winter DA (2009) Biomechanics and Motor Control of Human Movement, 4th ed., Wiley (segment proportions used to sanity-check leg reach)

findings.title: The rider is bolted to the spine: the jockey's head bobs 14 cm per racing stride, more than the withers, and the pose is the same at every gait
findings.observed: jockeyPivot is a child of the spine bone. Only 70% of the back's pitch is cancelled, and translation is not filtered at all. Over one race stride (32 samples): withers vertical range 12.6 cm (1.479-1.605 m), jockey seat 12.6 cm, jockey head 14.1 cm (2.004-2.145 m). These are in phase with the withers, so the rider amplifies the horse's motion instead of absorbing it. Hands move 19.7 cm vertically and 10.5 cm fore-aft. The crouch, hand position and leg pose are also identical at walk, trot, canter, gallop and race (my sm-a3: the full race crouch at a walk).
findings.expected: Jockeys in the crouch 'move to isolate themselves from the movement of their mount', so the horse does not have to move the jockey through each stride path (Pfau et al. 2009). Legg et al. 2025 measured jockey head displacement with accelerometers: median 0.06 m (IQR 0.05-0.09) in trial (race-speed) riding versus 0.12 m in exercise riding, and it fell with speed. Horan et al. 2021 also report jockey centre-of-mass displacements smaller than the horse's at the gallop. At a walk or slow trot the rider sits or stands more upright with a longer rein. The full crouch belongs to fast work.
findings.evidence: index.html:884 (:848) rig.jockeyPivot = joint(spine, …). index.html:1726-1731 (:1659-1663) the pivot only counter-rotates -0.7·pitch. BODY.race spine.position.y = rest-0.085+0.05·cyc (index.html:1545, :1508). In-page measurement: head y range 0.141 m, withers 0.126 m, seat 0.126 m, spine 0.100 m. buildJockey has one fixed pose (index.html:877-964).

fixOptions.label: Low-pass the rider's vertical motion
fixOptions.approach: In poseGait, offset jockeyPivot.position.y by -k·(spine bob about its stride mean), k≈0.5-0.6, written as the same cyc() terms so the loop stays seamless. That gives about 6 cm of head travel at race speed. Pair it with leg IK or stretchable legs so the feet stay in the irons.
fixOptions.risk: Rigid legs would lift out of or sink into the horse by about 6 cm without the IK fix from the previous finding.

fixOptions.label: Phase-lagged spring rider
fixOptions.approach: Model the rider's torso as a periodic, critically damped response to the withers trajectory (Fourier terms of the stride), with a small lag and reduced amplitude. Legs are solved by IK between the irons and the hips.
fixOptions.risk: Moderate. Tuning per gait, and reins and hands must follow the new torso position.

fixOptions.label: Gait-dependent rider posture
fixOptions.approach: Blend the torso pitch, seat height and hand position per gait: upright with a longer rein at walk/trot, half-crouch at canter, full crouch at gallop/race. Use the existing 0.6 s gait blend.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Rein lengths and the hand/arm reach must be retuned per pose.

references: Pfau T et al. (2009) Science 325:289 (PMID 19608909): jockeys isolate themselves from the movement of their mount

Legg KA, Cochrane DJ, Gee EK, Chin YY, Rogers CW (2025) Relationship between experience and head kinematics in race riding jockeys. Sci Rep 15 (PMID 40287497): head displacement 0.06 m (trial) vs 0.12 m (exercise), decreasing with speed
Horan K, Kourdache K, Coburn J, … Pfau T (2021) The effect of horseshoes and surfaces on horse and jockey centre of mass displacements. PLoS One (PMID 34813584)

findings.title: The hind thigh is a rigid slab that pushes through the flank at protraction and peels off the buttock at extension
findings.observed: The femur shell (thigh mass, back half-depth up to 0.22 m) is a rigid loft on the femur node. The trunk skin around it only follows spine/hips/chest. In the race gait the femur swings from -9° to +89° from vertical (measurements.json, RH hip->stifle). Rest is +33° and walk spans 0..67°. At protraction (race g≈0.75-0.94, femur 86-89°) the stifle end of the shell sticks out of the flank as a hard-edged horizontal shelf, with 24-27% of the shell outside the trunk by up to 6.3 cm (close-up sm-a4.png, race g=27/32). At extension (g≈0.31-0.38, femur -8/-9°) 50-52% of the shell is outside by up to 12.5 cm. The hamstring edge then reads as a separate vertical panel behind the trunk's own rounded rump (sm-a5.png). Visible in sheet 05 tiles g=5/8-7/8 as a lump under the loin.
findings.expected: The thigh muscles (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, quadriceps) are part of one continuous hindquarter. The skin and the stifle fold stretch and slide over the femur instead of moving rigidly with it. Skin over the greater trochanter moves 13-17 cm relative to the bone at the walk and up to 14.2 cm at the trot (van Weeren et al. 1990). The outline from croup to gaskin stays smooth through the stride.
findings.evidence: index.html:1223 (:1186) attach(L.fem, limb(hip, st, [[-0.2,0.08,0.12,0.09],[0.1,0.11,0.2,0.11],[0.5,0.11,0.22,0.11],…])). index.html:748 (:711) trunk skin weights only [-0.55 hips … 0.45 chest]. FEMUR_RANGE index.html:1432 (:1395) is applied only in the swing, while the stance reaches 89°. Sheet 05-race tiles g=5/8-7/8. Screenshots C:/Users/Aaron/.playwright-mcp/sm-a4.png and sm-a5.png.

fixOptions.label: Skin the upper thigh into the body
fixOptions.approach: Move the proximal femur shell (or a flank/buttock region of the trunk loft) into the skinned body. Weight it hips→femur, e.g. 0→0.6 from the hip joint to the stifle, so the flank and buttock deform with the leg. Leave the gaskin and below rigid.
fixOptions.risk: Linear-blend volume loss at large angles. The femur would have to become a Bone in the body skeleton (it is already a node in the merged skeleton, so this is feasible).

fixOptions.label: Stifle-fold strip
fixOptions.approach: Add a short skinned strip from the stifle to the belly/flank, weighted femur↔spine with sliding weights (the same technique as addReins). It hides the edge and the gap as the femur rotates.
fixOptions.risk: Medium. Extra geometry, and the strip may show its own crease at the extremes.

fixOptions.label: Reshape the rigid shell
fixOptions.approach: Round and shrink the upper-front (stifle) and upper-back sections of the femur shell so they stay inside the trunk across -10..90°. Extend the trunk loft's flank and buttock down so it covers what the shell no longer does.
fixOptions.risk: Changes the standing silhouette, so the anatomy reviewers' proportions need a recheck. It does not fully remove the hard edge.

references: van Weeren PR, van den Bogert AJ, Barneveld A (1990) Quantification of skin displacement in the proximal parts of the limbs of the walking horse. Equine Vet J Suppl 9:101-109 (PMID 9259818): 1-4 cm (distal scapula) to 13-17 cm (greater trochanter)
van Weeren PR et al. (1990) A quantitative analysis of skin displacement in the trotting horse. Equine Vet J Suppl 9 (PMID 9259817): up to 142 mm at the greater trochanter
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, gallop plates (continuous hindquarter outline)

findings.title: The shoulder blade and arm are separate plates standing up to 12-15 cm proud of the chest wall and withers
findings.observed: The scapula is a rigid lofted plate on the scapula node, with the limb plane at z=0.165 and the blade's top cap at the withers. 77-88% of its upper 30% lies outside the trunk at every gait, by 10.4-11.9 cm (walk g=0 through race g=0.375). The humerus/arm shell's upper part is outside by up to 13.7-14.6 cm at race g=0.25-0.375. At g=0.31 the elbow reaches x=0.81, level with the front of the chest. From a front 3/4 view the blade reads as a fin with a step all round (sm-a10.png, walk). From the side the arm reads as a block bolted to the chest (sm-a6.png, race g=0.31). During the race the blade swings ±18° (scapSwing) about its top, sliding its edge across the chest wall.
findings.expected: The scapula lies flat against the thoracic wall under skin and muscle (trapezius, deltoid, triceps). The withers and shoulder form one continuous surface, and the skin over the distal scapula moves only 1-4 cm relative to the bone at the walk (van Weeren 1990). The bone moves under the skin, never through it.
findings.evidence: index.html:1201 (:1164) scapula limb() with sections up to 0.12 m deep at z=FORE.z. index.html:1440-1451 (:1410-1414) scapula rotation.z = scapSwing·cos about sc (the top). TRUNK rows near the withers are narrow at the top (wu 0.42-0.58, index.html:507-525). In-page inside/outside test against the posed trunk shell. Screenshots C:/Users/Aaron/.playwright-mcp/sm-a10.png and sm-a6.png. Sheet 00 'chest + forelegs, front'.

fixOptions.label: Tuck the blade into the chest wall
fixOptions.approach: Tilt the scapula plane so its top sits near z≈0.08-0.10 and the point of shoulder at 0.165. Thin the top two sections so the dorsal border stays inside the trunk.
fixOptions.risk: Low. It exposes the trunk's narrow withers, which the anatomy reviewers may want widened instead.

fixOptions.label: Skin the shoulder region
fixOptions.approach: Weight trunk vertices over the shoulder (x 0.45-0.75, below the withers) partly to the scapula/humerus nodes, e.g. 30-60%. Then the chest wall follows the blade, and the rigid plate shrinks to the point-of-shoulder/arm mass.
fixOptions.risk: Linear-blend pinching at the girth and the base of the neck. The scapula node must join the body skeleton.

fixOptions.label: Move the scapular pivot down
fixOptions.approach: Rotate the scapula about a point in its upper third instead of its top, so the dorsal border moves back as the point of shoulder moves forward. This cuts the outward sweep of the top cap.
fixOptions.risk: Changes forelimb reach. Coordinate with the forelimb and gait reviewers.

references: van Weeren PR, van den Bogert AJ, Barneveld A (1990) Equine Vet J Suppl 9:101-109 (PMID 9259818): skin over the distal scapula moves 1-4 cm relative to bone
Sisson & Grossman, The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals (Getty ed. 1975), equine thoracic limb: scapula against the lateral thoracic wall

findings.title: The mane is a stiff comb that ignores gravity: blades stand horizontal or upward and part on both sides of the neck
findings.observed: Measured blade directions (5 sample blades, withers to poll). At every gait the blades point 74-123° from straight down, i.e. horizontal to 33° above horizontal, and 0-29° above the local crest line. Walk: 87-117° from down, 9-25° above the crest. Race: 74-123°, -9..+16°. So the mane hardly changes between a walk and 16 m/s. The side roll (Euler X 0.95-1.15 rad applied after the Z tilt) only acts on the blade's leftover vertical component. As a result the withers blades fall to the LEFT (-11..-36°), the poll blades to the RIGHT (+27..+31°), and mid-neck blades stay upright: the mane parts on both sides. In grazers the 'falls to one side' pose (x=1.05) leaves blades sticking out sideways and horizontally from a lowered neck (sm-a7.png). Sheet 00 'head, right side' shows a punk-style crest of spikes pointing up and back.
findings.expected: At rest the mane hangs under gravity and lies flat on one side of the neck. It is traditionally trained to the off (right) side, and racing manes are pulled short. It lifts and streams back only in an airflow. At racing speed (~16 m/s, dynamic pressure about 150 Pa) it streams back and up, as in Muybridge's gallop plates. At walk and stand it should lie roughly 0-40° from straight down against the neck.
findings.evidence: index.html:1102-1122 (:1066-1086), especially :1118 (:1082) mount.rotation.set(0.95 + 0.2·rnd(), 0, atan2(-up.x, up.y) + 62°). Per-gait mane rotation in BODY: race index.html:1558-1561 (:1521-1524), walk :1632-1635 (:1595-1598), graze :1655 (:1618). In-page blade-direction measurements. Screenshots C:/Users/Aaron/.playwright-mcp/sm-a3.png (walk) and sm-a7.png (graze). Sheet 00 tile 'stand: head, right side'.

fixOptions.label: Mount blades in a crest frame
fixOptions.approach: Build each blade's rest direction from an explicit basis (crest tangent t, crest normal n, side s): dir = -t·cos(a) + (n·cos(b) + s·sin(b))·sin(a), with b≈70-90° toward one side. Add a 'maneSide' parameter (off, near, standing/hogged) for horse quirks.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The forelock and hood logic stay unchanged.

fixOptions.label: Speed and gravity driven lift
fixOptions.approach: Blend each blade between a 'hanging' rest (corrected for the parent bone's world rotation, so it hangs down even when grazing) and a 'streaming' pose by (v/v_race)², plus the existing stride-locked flutter. All of it is a pure function of g, p and gait speed.
fixOptions.risk: Low to moderate. Needs per-gait speed in the gait table (already implied by stride/T).

fixOptions.label: Skinned mane strips
fixOptions.approach: Replace the 16 rigid cones with 3-4 skinned strips along the crest, 2-3 joints each, driven by an analytic (Fourier) damped response to the neck motion and the wind.
fixOptions.risk: Performance with 18 runners and seamless-loop constraints. Larger visual change.

references: Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, gallop plates: mane lifted and streaming at speed
The Pony Club (UK) Manual of Horsemanship, grooming: the mane is trained to lie on the off side

findings.title: Ears never point forward, move in lock-step at speed, and the new ear sliders don't reach 'pricked' or 'pinned'
findings.observed: World tilt of the ear axis from vertical (forward = +), per gait over the stride: walk -2..-11°, trot -13..-14°, canter -13..-16°, gallop -14..-29°, race -18..-34°. The ears are always swept back and never ahead of vertical. The idle walk/trot flick (idleEars) only adds rotation backwards (+0.45 rad). At canter, gallop and race both ears follow the same formula (left-right difference ≤4-6°), oscillating twice per stride at gallop/race (about 4.6 Hz flapping). On HEAD e73d9ca, run.earsAtSpeed=-1 ('pricked forward') gives -16..0° at race, and +1 ('pinned flat back') only -35..-51°. conf.earTilt=-1 ('pricked forward') gives -11° at walk. Sheets 05/06 show permanently laid-back ears.
findings.expected: Attentive horses hold their ears forward toward what they are attending to, with the tips ahead of the bases (Wathan & McComb 2014). The ears are mobile and independent. EquiFACS codes EAD101 ears forward, EAD102 adductor, EAD103 flattener and EAD104 rotator. Racehorses commonly gallop with both ears forward or one ear forward and one back toward the rider. Pinned ears are flattened caudally almost against the poll and neck, roughly 70-90° back from vertical, not 35-50°.
findings.evidence: index.html:997 (:961) mount rest tilt HEAD_TILT+58° (16° back). BODY.gallop ears index.html:1524-1527 (:1487-1490), race :1554-1557 (:1517-1519), canter :1605-1608 (:1568-1571). idleEars :1664-1670 (:1627-1633), whose flick is only backwards. applyRun earsAtSpeed ±0.3 rad (index.html:1718, new). In-page measurement with the sliders driven through the UI.

fixOptions.label: Re-base the ear carriage and slider ranges
fixOptions.approach: Make the neutral ear about +5..+15° forward of vertical at walk/trot. Map earsAtSpeed -1 to about +20..+30° forward and +1 to about -80° (flat). Let the idle flick go both forward and back.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Hood ear covers ride on the ear mesh and follow automatically.

fixOptions.label: Independent ears
fixOptions.approach: Give each ear its own offset and phase at canter/gallop/race. Add an occasional, per-horse-seeded 'one forward, one back to the jockey' state with whole cycles per loop, and replace the 2×/stride flap with a small passive bounce at 1×/stride.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

fixOptions.label: Ear yaw (pinna rotation) channel
fixOptions.approach: Add rotation of the pinna about its own long axis plus an 'earYaw' customization so ears can turn their opening sideways or backwards (needs the ear-shape fix below).
fixOptions.risk: Medium. Needs a pinna with an opening to read.

references: Wathan J, McComb K (2014) The eyes and ears are visual indicators of attention in domestic horses. Curr Biol 24(15):R677-R679
Wathan J, Burrows AM, Waller BM, McComb K (2015) EquiFACS: The Equine Facial Action Coding System. PLoS One 10(8):e0131738 (EAD101-104 ear actions)

findings.title: Reins pass through the neck and the hands hover 6-10 cm off it
findings.observed: Each rein is a straight strap from the hand (z=±0.08) to the bit (z=±0.08), with a 5 cm built-in sag. 15-24% of the rein sample points lie inside the neck shell, up to 3.3 cm deep, at every race phase tested (8/8). The rein visibly disappears into the neck between crest and throat (sm-a2.png, sm-a3.png, sm-a9.png). The hand centroid stays 6.3-9.9 cm off the neck surface over the stride, while forearm vertices dip into the neck (up to 20 of 696 at g=0.5). Rein length varies only 2.4 cm, so the give-and-take itself works.
findings.expected: Reins run from the bit along the outside of the neck to the hands. The hands rest on or just above the crest, often joined in a bridge across it, and are pushed along the neck in the finish. A rein never passes through the neck. At racing speed with contact the reins are taut rather than sagging.
findings.evidence: addReins index.html:1245-1291 (:1208-1254): straight lerp plus -0.05·4t(1-t) sag at :1260 (:1223). Hand point Hn=(0.83,T+0.23,±0.08) at index.html:945 (:909). Bit end index.html:1073 (:1037). In-page point-in-neck-shell test and distance to the neck. Screenshots C:/Users/Aaron/.playwright-mcp/sm-a2.png, sm-a3.png, sm-a9.png.

fixOptions.label: Route the rein around the neck
fixOptions.approach: Give the rein a middle waypoint on a marker on neck2 placed at the neck's half-width + 1.5 cm on each side. Skin the strap across three markers (hand → neck waypoint → bit) and drop the sag at race speed.
fixOptions.risk: Low. One extra marker per rein.

fixOptions.label: Hands onto the neck
fixOptions.approach: Place Hn at z = ±(neck half-width at that x + 0.02) and lower the hands onto the crest sides (a bridge). Clamp the slide so the hands stay in contact.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The arm reach changes slightly and the arm-slide clamp needs retuning.

fixOptions.label: Per-frame push-out
fixOptions.approach: Each frame, project rein vertices that fall inside the neck out to the surface using the NECK_ROWS cross-sections.
fixOptions.risk: Minor CPU cost per runner. The strap could jitter at the facets.

references: Pfau T et al. (2009) Science 325:289 (race-riding crouch with hands forward on the neck)

findings.title: Grazing neck folds through itself at the base: crest stretched about 2× and throat inverted; mane roots slide up to 12 cm off the crest
findings.observed: Grazer pose (BODY.graze): chest -12°, neck1 -64°, neck2 -6°, head +55°. Nearly all of the neck bend sits between the chest and neck1, blended over the first two of only six neck rings. On the skinned neck the crest edge from the withers to ring 2 stretches 0.225 → 0.442 m (×1.96). The throat line turns 146° and 162° at its first two rings, i.e. it folds back on itself, leaving a hard crease at the base of the neck (sm-a7.png). The mane blades are rigid on chest/neck1/neck2 while the skin blends, so their roots slip by up to 11.9 cm relative to the crest when grazing (2.3, 6.2, 1.6, 11.9, 8.0 and 0.9 cm along the neck). At race the slip is ≤3.5 cm.
findings.expected: Neck flexion is spread over the cervical joints. The atlanto-occipital joint gives only about 32% of the total dorsoventral range (86° there), and the rest is shared by C2-T1 (Clayton & Townsend 1989). A grazing horse's neck is a smooth curve. Skin wrinkles under the throat but never folds through itself, and the mane stays rooted in the crest.
findings.evidence: BODY.graze index.html:1643-1661 (:1606-1624), neck1 -65° at :1651 (:1614). Neck skin weights index.html:762 (:725) [[0,2],[0.28,3],[0.62,4],[0.97,5]] over six NECK rows (index.html:526-533). Mane parent choice index.html:1115 (:1079). In-page posed vs rest crest/throat polylines on the Hidaka grazer. Screenshot C:/Users/Aaron/.playwright-mcp/sm-a7.png.

fixOptions.label: Spread the bend
fixOptions.approach: Redistribute the graze pose, e.g. chest -10°, neck1 -35°, neck2 -25°, head +45°, so no single blend carries more than about 35°. Recheck the muzzle height (2-10 cm above the ground, as the code comment says).
fixOptions.risk: Low. Pose tuning only.

fixOptions.label: More rings and a base bone
fixOptions.approach: Add 2-3 intermediate neck rings near the base and a 'neck0' bone at the cervicothoracic junction, with wider smoothstep windows.
fixOptions.risk: Moderate. Touches the skin weights used by the mane, the gear and the rein routing.

fixOptions.label: Skin the mane roots
fixOptions.approach: In mergeRigid, give each mane blade the same two-bone weights as the crest point under it, instead of 100% to its own node, so the roots ride on the skin.
fixOptions.risk: Low to moderate. mergeRigid currently assumes one bone per rigid part, so this is a small special case.

references: Clayton HM, Townsend HGG (1989) Kinematics of the cervical spine of the adult horse. Equine Vet J 21(3):189-192 (PMID 2731506): atlanto-occipital joint 86.4°, 32% of total dorsoventral cervical movement

findings.title: Cold-weather breath puffs: two exhalations per stride at the canter and gallop, and a double puff per breath at the walk
findings.observed: At the snowy-field location, buildBreath gives puff i the age wrap01(n·p − i/4). That staggers the puffs by a quarter of a breath cycle within one breath, instead of making them successive breaths. With two puffs enabled, every cycle emits a second puff 0.25 cycle after the first. Measured: gallop and race emit puffs at g=0 and g=0.25 every stride (≈4.6-4.8 Hz at race). The walk emits two puffs 0.625 s apart every 2.5 s. The first puff of each stride comes at g=0 (trailing hind touchdown).
findings.expected: Horses take exactly one breath per stride at the canter and gallop, with locomotor-respiratory coupling at 1:1 (Young et al. 1992 on Thoroughbreds at 9-11 m/s; Bramble & Carrier 1983; Attenburrow 1982). Expiration is commonly placed in the forelimb-support part of the stride, as the head and neck lower and the viscera move forward, and inspiration in the hind-support/suspension part. At walk and trot breathing is not locked to the stride, so one puff per breath is right.
findings.evidence: buildBreath index.html:2969-2993 (:2902-2926). Age formula at index.html:2982. Visible-count rule ceil(life·n/loop)+1 = 2. In-page sampling of puff visibility over 32 phases at the walk, gallop and race.

fixOptions.label: Fix the puff indexing
fixOptions.approach: Make puff i the breath from i cycles ago: age = (wrap01(n·p)/n + i/n)·loopPeriod, with enough puffs to cover the puff lifetime.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

fixOptions.label: Lock the exhale to the stride
fixOptions.approach: For coupled gaits, offset the exhale phase to the forelimb support (e.g. at G.land of the trailing fore, ≈0.27-0.30 in race/gallop) instead of g=0.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The cited timing is moderately certain, so keep it as a tunable constant.

references: Young IS, Alexander RMcN, Woakes AJ, Butler PJ, Anderson L (1992) The synchronization of ventilation and locomotion in horses (Equus caballus). J Exp Biol 166:19-31 (PMID 1602274)
Bramble DM, Carrier DR (1983) Running and breathing in mammals. Science 219:251-256 (PMID 6849136)
Attenburrow DP (1982) Time relationship between the respiratory cycle and limb cycle in the horse. Equine Vet J 14:69-72 (PMID 7084182)

findings.title: No respiratory or flank motion and static nostrils, even at racing speed
findings.observed: Nothing in BODY.* changes the barrel's shape over the breathing cycle, at any gait. The only breathing-like motion is a 4 mm spine bob on a ~4 s cycle in the grazing pose. The nostrils are fixed dark octahedra (0.018 m, scale 1.4×0.9×0.5) that never dilate. At race speed the flank, belly and nostrils are completely still.
findings.expected: At rest horses breathe about 8-16 times a minute, with visible rise and fall of the flank and ribcage. At the canter and gallop breathing is coupled 1:1 with the stride (Young et al. 1992), so the flank and abdomen pulse once per stride. Horses are obligate nasal breathers, and the nostrils flare widely at maximal exercise.
findings.evidence: BODY functions index.html:1508-1662 (:1471-1625): no barrel or nostril channel. graze spine bob 0.004·cyc at :1647 (:1610). Nostril geometry index.html:987-989 (:951-953).

fixOptions.label: Nostril flare
fixOptions.approach: Scale the nostril meshes 1.0→1.6 with gait speed and pulse them with the breath phase from the breath-puff finding.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The nostrils are separate rigid parts in the eye-material merge.

fixOptions.label: Barrel breathing via a skin bone
fixOptions.approach: Add a 'ribs' bone at the mid-barrel whose scale (y,z) breathes ±1-2%. Blend trunk vertices between x≈-0.3 and 0.4 to it. Drive it at 1:1 with the stride at canter/gallop and on whole cycles per loop at rest.
fixOptions.risk: Moderate. The saddle, cloth and girth share the trunk weights and would breathe too, which is acceptable.

references: Young IS et al. (1992) J Exp Biol 166:19-31 (PMID 1602274)
Reed SM, Bayly WM, Sellon DC, Equine Internal Medicine (normal resting respiratory rate 8-16/min)

findings.title: Ear shape has no pinna opening: a solid 4-sided pyramid whose broad faces point sideways
findings.observed: Each ear is ConeGeometry(0.036, 0.15, 4) scaled 0.62 front-to-back. It is a solid, symmetric pyramid with no concave conch, and its broadest faces face outward (±z). In sheet 00 'head, front' and 'head, right side' the ears read as spikes. Without an opening, the direction the ear is listening in, which is the main ear signal, cannot be shown, and the earSet/earTilt customizations only tilt a spike.
findings.expected: The equine pinna is a funnel or scoop open on one side, with a pale haired inner surface. Horses rotate it toward a sound through a wide arc (EquiFACS EAD104 'ear rotator'). Seen from the front, attentive ears show their openings forward; relaxed or 'airplane' ears show them sideways.

findings.title: Girth and overgirth: the overgirth floats 4-6 cm off the barrel, and both pass through the elbow and triceps for half the racing stride
findings.observed: The overgirth is a full-ring shell grown 0.056 m in every direction, so on the sides and belly it floats 4.2-6.1 cm off the skin. The girth sits 1.0-2.9 cm off. During the race the elbow travels back to x=0.30-0.36, behind the girth band at x=0.355-0.39. From g=0.50 to 0.88, up to 30 of 108 girth/overgirth vertices lie inside the arm, forearm or triceps shells, up to 3.8 cm deep.
findings.expected: The girth sits in the girth groove about a hand's width behind the elbow and lies on the skin. The overgirth (surcingle) passes over the saddle and lies flat on the girth. The elbow slides close to the girth but does not pass through it.
findings.evidence: index.html:866-867 (:830-831) girth = shell(0.355,0.39,1,0.022), over = shell(0.3,0.325,1,0.056). Elbow x range 0.29-0.80 at race (measurements.json RF.elbow). In-page point-in-shell test and distance to the skin.

fixOptions.label: Height-dependent overgirth offset
fixOptions.approach: Grow the overgirth 0.056 only where it crosses the saddle (y > top-0.06) and about 0.025 elsewhere, e.g. grow = lerp(0.025, 0.056, smoothstep(top-0.1, top, y)).
fixOptions.risk: Low.

fixOptions.label: Move the girth back or limit elbow travel
fixOptions.approach: Shift the girth and overgirth 4-6 cm caudally (x ≈ 0.30-0.34), or limit the humerus's caudal travel in late stance (coordinate with the forelimb reviewer, ARM_RANGE index.html:1431).
fixOptions.risk: Low for the tack move. Limiting the elbow changes the forelimb motion.

findings.title: Jockey's thighs and upper arms are proportionally too short
findings.observed: From the joint points in buildJockey: thigh (hip→knee) 0.32 m, shank (knee→ankle) 0.41 m, ratio 0.78. Upper arm (shoulder→elbow) 0.23 m, forearm (elbow→hand) 0.28 m, ratio 0.81. Torso hip→shoulder 0.43 m. The sum suggests a rider about 1.45-1.5 m tall, with stubby thighs and upper arms (visible in sheet 06 close tiles: short white thighs and short sleeves).
findings.expected: Human segment proportions (Winter 2009) are thigh 0.245H and shank 0.246H (ratio ≈1.0), upper arm 0.186H and forearm 0.146H (ratio ≈1.27). For a 1.58 m jockey that is thigh ≈0.39, shank ≈0.39, upper arm ≈0.29, forearm ≈0.23 m.

fixOptions.label: Jockey build parameters

fixOptions.risk: Low. Data and UI work.

findings.title: At racing speed the tail is a stiff club that droops, and the 'Tail at speed' slider only re-angles the dock
findings.observed: Race gait: the dock moves -10..+15° about horizontal, but the six rigid segments keep a built-in +9° per segment droop. The last segment points 21-44° below horizontal, the maximum bend between segments is only 5-12°, and the tip swings 0.96-1.45 m high (49 cm) each stride, like a pivoting rod (sheet 05 tiles). run.tailCarriage (HEAD e73d9ca) only rotates segment 0 by ±0.3 rad: dock -27..-3° ('clamped') or +8..+32° ('streaming'), with the rest of the tail shape unchanged. Walk (dock -39..-44°, tip ±14 cm lateral swing once per stride) and trot look plausible.
findings.expected: At racing speed, air drag streams the tail hair nearly straight back from a raised dock. The hair fans and the whole length flexes in a travelling wave, rather than hanging down at the end (Muybridge's gallop plates). How high the tail is carried at speed is a real individual trait, so a tail-at-speed parameter should change the whole tail's shape, not just the dock angle.
findings.evidence: Tail build index.html:1124-1144 (:1088-1108), tAng += 9° per segment at :1143. BODY.race tail index.html:1562-1566 (:1525-1529). applyRun tailCarriage index.html:1719. In-page tail angle sweep with the slider at -1/0/+1.

fixOptions.label: Speed-dependent curvature
fixOptions.approach: Interpolate the per-segment droop from 9° (walk) toward 0-2° at race speed and add more per-segment lag, so the tail straightens into a streaming line. Have tailCarriage scale the whole curve as well as the dock.
fixOptions.risk: Low.

fixOptions.label: Analytic damped tail
fixOptions.approach: Drive each segment angle by a periodic (Fourier) damped response to croup pitch and vertical acceleration plus a wind term ∝ v², which keeps the loop seamless.
fixOptions.risk: Moderate tuning effort.

references: Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, gallop plates (tail streaming behind at speed)

findings.title: At the trot, the forefoot clips the same-side hind cannon at each diagonal changeover
findings.observed: Ipsilateral limb collision test (closed limb shells only; hooves with racing plates excluded as targets). At trot g≈0.97-0.00 the RF pastern/hoof sits inside the RH cannon/tibia shell (8-25 vertices, 1.3-1.6 cm deep). At g≈0.47-0.50 the LF does the same with the LH (8-26 vertices, ≤1.6 cm). No contact at walk, canter, gallop or race. The fore swing's default 'flick' (0.4 of the swing spent moving back at ground speed) carries the lifting forefoot back toward the landing hind, and the fore and hind limb planes are only 1 cm apart (z 0.165 vs 0.175).
findings.expected: At a working trot the forefoot breaks over and folds up out of the way just before the ipsilateral hind lands in or behind its print ('tracking up'). Hind-toe-to-fore-foot contact is the gait fault called forging (interference).
findings.evidence: GAITS.trot index.html:221-226 (:219-224). Default flick in footPath index.html:1406 (:1369). FORE.z/HIND.z index.html:552-553 (:536-537). In-page shell interpenetration sweep (32 phases per gait).

fixOptions.label: Less fore flick at trot
fixOptions.approach: Set fore.flick ≈0.2-0.25 for the trot so the forefoot leaves straight up and forward instead of swinging back into the hind's path.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The swing path changes slightly, so check the zero-slip claim at lift-off.

fixOptions.label: Separate the tracks
fixOptions.approach: Widen the hind limb plane slightly (e.g. HIND.z 0.175 → 0.19) or narrow the fore plane, so the ipsilateral distal limbs pass beside each other.
fixOptions.risk: Low. Changes the stance width seen from front and rear, so coordinate with the conformation reviewer.

references: Clayton HM (1994) Comparison of the stride kinematics of the collected, working, medium and extended trot in horses. Equine Vet J 26(3):230-234 (fore/hind placement at the trot)
Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion, trotting plates

findings.title: Hind limb stands ~15 cm too far forward under the body (camped under behind); the hip joint sits directly under the croup peak
findings.observed: Standing pose (measurements.json static.standing): the point of buttock (tuber ischii) is at x=-0.858 (the loft cap reaches -0.91). The hock joint is at x=-0.614 and the point of hock (cannon section t=-0.02, back 0.085) is at about -0.70, so a plumb line from the buttock falls 0.16 m behind the point of hock, 0.27 m behind the hind heel (about -0.587) and 0.37 m behind the hind toe (-0.491). The hip joint is at x=-0.515, the same x as the croup peak (-0.525), and 0.343 m in front of the tuber ischii. The hind hoof stands under the hip joint. The base of support is short: fore toe to hind toe is 1.12 m on a body about 1.66-1.77 m long. In 00-stand 'left side', 'right side' and 'hindleg, right side' the quarters visibly overhang the hind leg, and the leg comes out of the middle of the rump.
findings.expected: Side view of a correctly built horse: a vertical from the tuber ischii touches the point of the hock, runs down the back of the cannon and meets the ground 7.5-10 cm behind the heel (Stashak). A limb placed forward of that line is 'standing under behind'. The acetabulum lies caudoventral to the tuber sacrale, roughly midway between the point of hip and the point of buttock, about 20 cm in front of the tuber ischii, not directly under the croup peak. The model's own joint angles (stifle 110 deg, hock 146 deg) already match measured TB values (115 and 149 deg). Moving the hip joint back about 14 cm with those angles kept puts the point of hock within about 1-2 cm of the buttock plumb line.

fixOptions.label: Shorten the rear overhang
fixOptions.approach: Pull the TRUNK rows at x <= -0.68 (and the tail root / tail head) forward about 6-8 cm so the tuber ischii ends about 20 cm behind the hip joint. The legs and gaits stay as they are.

findings.title: Shoulder blades stand vertical at z=+/-0.165 and stick out beside the withers and neck base as flat fins
findings.observed: The scapula mesh runs in the limb plane z=+/-0.165, which is vertical with no medial lean. At its top (x 0.485, y 1.52) its inner face is at z=0.143 and its outer face at 0.187. The trunk there is only about 0.09 m half-wide (the TRUNK row at x=0.46 has wu=0.42), and the neck root is about 0.12. So the upper half of each blade stands 3-9 cm proud of the body. In 00-stand 'stand: front' and 'stand: head, front' two vertical rectangular plates rise on either side of the neck base, like epaulettes.
findings.expected: The scapulae lie flat against the curved cranial thorax and lean inward at the top. Their dorsal borders and cartilages sit just lateral to the spinous processes of T2-T7, a few cm either side of the midline at the withers, while the shoulder joints are about 0.35-0.45 m apart. The shoulder therefore has no step at its upper border, and from the front the withers and neck base read as one smooth wedge.

fixOptions.label: Lean the scapula inward
fixOptions.approach: Give FORE.sc its own z (about +/-0.08-0.10), so the scapula joint and mesh run from near the withers out to the shoulder joint at +/-0.165.
fixOptions.risk: Breaks the planar-limb assumption: the scapula swing about z, solveLeg and abductedZ all assume one plane. At the gallop the swing would add lateral wobble unless the swing axis is tilted too.

fixOptions.label: Reshape the blade mesh only
fixOptions.approach: Add a per-section inward z offset to the scapula limb() rings that grows toward the top (like the femur's `inward`), and thin or sink the top section into the body.
fixOptions.risk: Low. The blade may clip into the neck when it swings forward at the gallop or race.

fixOptions.label: Fill the withers region out to the blade
fixOptions.approach: Raise the top-width factor (wu) of the TRUNK rows at x 0.34-0.58 and the half-width of NECK row 0 so the body surface covers the blade top.
fixOptions.risk: Softens the sharp withers ridge and makes the forehand look heavier from the front. The saddle drape reads these rows.

findings.title: Head about 15-20% too long for a Thoroughbred and neck short relative to it (neck:head 1.18)
findings.observed: Poll to muzzle is 0.661 m, 40.8% of withers height. Poll to withers (neck topline, straight) is 0.783 m, only 1.18 times the head length. The neck is about 0.80 of the back length (withers to croup 0.982 m). The HEAD loft spans x -0.05..0.63 (caps -0.08..0.66), and the jowl is 0.32 m deep (top 0.085 + bottom 0.235 at x=0.15). The neck's underside, from throatlatch (about 1.07, 1.69) to chest (0.74, 1.14), is about 0.60 m, so topline to bottomline is only about 1.3:1. In 00-stand 'left side' and 'right side' the head looks large on a short neck, the opposite of the TB's refined head on a long neck.
findings.expected: Measured TBs: head length 54.8 +/- 2.5 cm at 157.9 cm withers height (34.7%), which scales to about 0.565 m at 163 cm (Ünal et al. 2025). Jumping TBs: neck length 100.7 +/- 5.6 cm with a back/neck ratio of 0.92 (Senna et al. 2015). The neck is therefore roughly 1.6-1.8 times the head, against 1.18 in the model, and longer than the back. A common conformation guide is a neck topline about twice the bottomline. The code comment's 0.76 m target for poll to withers looks low against these data.

findings.title: Femur too short and tibia too long (thigh:gaskin 0.69); the thigh reads stubby and the gaskin over-long
findings.observed: Joint-centre lengths are femur (hip to stifle) 0.306 m and tibia (stifle to hock) 0.444 m, a ratio of 0.69. The hind cannon is 0.347 m. The hip joint is 1.171 m high and the stifle 0.915 m, only 4.5 cm below the elbow (0.96 m). In 00-stand 'hindleg, right side' the thigh barely shows below the trunk, and a long gaskin runs from just under the flank to the hock. The joint angles themselves (stifle 110 deg, hock 146 deg, hind fetlock 147 deg) are within published TB ranges, so the problem is the segment lengths.
findings.expected: The equine femur is longer than the tibia. Withers-height factors from greatest bone lengths (Kiesewalter, used in archaeozoology) give a tibia of about 37 cm and a femur of about 42-46 cm at 163 cm, so joint-centre femur:tibia is about 1.0-1.1. Surface-landmark data on jumping TBs give thigh 49.7 cm and gaskin 53.1 cm (0.94). Horse-proportional leg models use thigh 0.40 m to crus 0.36 m (1.11). So the femur should be about 0.37-0.40 m and the tibia about 0.36-0.40 m. At the model's angles this lowers the stifle to about 0.85-0.87 m and moves the hip joint back, toward its correct place within the pelvis.

fixOptions.approach: Lower HIND.st to about 0.84 (femur about 0.37) and move the hock back so the tibia is about 0.38.

Including the pointed loft caps (front 0.86, rear -0.91), the trunk spans 1.77 m (1.09 x WH). Front part (point of shoulder to withers) is about 0.34 m, back 0.98 m, croup to buttock horizontal 0.33 m. In 00-stand 'left side' and '3/4 front-right' the body looks long and sausage-like for a racehorse, and the short base of support (toe to toe 1.12 m) adds overhang at both ends.

Scaled to 163 cm the back is about 0.84 m, roughly 14 cm shorter than the model's. Classic TB conformation is a short, strong back with a long underline and long sloping hip, in a frame about as long as it is tall.
